items.false_assumption: Raymond Sperling's confession to killing Cock Robin is genuine and he is the murderer.

chain.observation: Sperling confessed to killing Robin with a bow and arrow, but his attempt to reveal guilt was motivated by emotional distress rather than fact.
chain.correction: Confession was too easy and inconsistent with physical evidence; the attempt to confirm guilt failed.
chain.effect: Sperling is innocent; suspicion shifts to someone with more knowledge and a deeper motive.
required_evidence: Typewritten Bishop notes with intimate details of the crime and a failed attempt to confirm guilt
Bow and arrow found at the scene with no blood or tissue traces matching Robin's wound

chain.observation: Riemann-Christoffel tensor formula found on Sprigg's body, suggesting a mathematical motivation and intellectual rivalry among suspects.
chain.correction: Formula is known to advanced mathematicians, linking the crime to mathematicians with jealousy or rivalry.
chain.effect: Focus on suspects with mathematical background and possible jealousy or rivalry as motive.
required_evidence: Sprigg's body with formula scrap and evidence of intellectual rivalry
Knowledge of tensor formula by Drukker, Arnesson, Pardee, and Dillard

chain.observation: Black bishop chess piece left at Mrs. Drukker's door at midnight, an attempt to reveal the murderer's symbolic signature and guilt.
chain.correction: Symbolic signature linking the murderer to chess and Arnesson, but also to Dillard's attempt to reveal guilt through misdirection.
chain.effect: Arnesson becomes a suspect due to possession of chess set, but the attempt to confirm guilt is misdirected.
required_evidence: Mrs. Drukker's testimony of midnight visit and the attempt to reveal guilt
Missing black bishop from Arnesson's chess set, but Dillard also had access

chain.observation: Pardee's suicide in the archery room was staged as an attempt to reveal guilt and close the case.
chain.correction: Suicide staged by murderer to mislead investigation; the attempt to confirm guilt was a red herring.
chain.effect: Pardee is victim, not culprit; the real murderer remains hidden.
required_evidence: House of cards on table and note suggesting guilt
Pardee's emotional state and chess obsession, but no concrete motive

chain.observation: Typewriter and Drukker's note-book found in attic, hidden by the murderer in an attempt to conceal and later reveal guilt.
chain.correction: Murderer hid evidence in attic to delay discovery, but the attempt to reveal guilt through Bishop notes ultimately backfired.
chain.effect: Proof of murderer's identity and connection to household, and an attempt to confirm guilt through planted evidence.
required_evidence: Typewriter with Bishop notes and attempt to reveal guilt
Drukker's stolen note-book with references to jealousy and rivalry

chain.observation: Child Madeleine Moffat abducted and found locked in Drukker house closet, an attempt to motivate fear and reveal guilt through nursery rhyme motifs.
chain.correction: Murderer used child as part of nursery rhyme motif and to implicate Arnesson, but the attempt to confirm guilt was staged.
chain.effect: Final proof of murderer's identity, motive of jealousy and rivalry, and an attempt to reveal guilt through psychological manipulation.
required_evidence: Child's identification of abductor and description of the attempt to frighten her
Bishop notes referencing nursery rhymes and attempt to reveal guilt

chain.observation: Professor Dillard's suicide by cyanide poisoning was an attempt to reveal guilt and end the case, motivated by jealousy and intellectual rivalry.
chain.correction: Murderer committed suicide when cornered, revealing guilt and confirming the motive of jealousy and rivalry.
chain.effect: Case closed with confession by death and confirmation of guilt, jealousy, and rivalry.
required_evidence: Cyanide lab in attic and evidence of suicide as an attempt to reveal guilt
Switching of wine glasses during final meeting, confirming guilt and motive

herrings.description: Adolph Drukker, a hunchbacked scientist with mental instability, is suspected due to his erratic behavior and proximity to the crimes.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His presence near crime scenes and strange conduct.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was a victim and had no motive or opportunity; his behavior was due to illness.

herrings.description: A .32 revolver goes missing and is later returned, suggesting a possible weapon and suspect.
herrings.points_at_suspect: The revolver was linked to the shooting of Sprigg and was missing from the household.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The revolver was taken and returned by the murderer to mislead investigators.

supporting_points: Sperling confessed to the murder.
He was jealous of Robin and had a quarrel with him.
He was the last person seen with Robin.
His name means 'sparrow,' matching the nursery rhyme.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The confession was too easy and inconsistent with physical evidence and psychological analysis.

items.false_assumption: The Black Abbot is a supernatural ghost haunting Fossaway Manor.

chain.observation: Thomas was found dead wearing the Black Abbot costume.
chain.correction: The Black Abbot is a disguise used by a living person, not a ghost.
chain.effect: Focus shifts to identifying who impersonated the Black Abbot.
required_evidence: Black Abbot costume found in Thomas’s possession
Witness statement of maid seeing figure in costume

chain.observation: Lord Chelford’s room showed signs of struggle and was locked from inside.
chain.correction: The struggle was caused by Harry’s madness and escape attempt.
chain.effect: Harry becomes a prime suspect for disappearance and related crimes.
required_evidence: Alice Barter’s witness statement of sounds at 1:45 AM
Broken door panel and open window with blood traces

chain.observation: Leslie Gwyn broke off engagement and was later kidnapped.
chain.correction: Leslie’s kidnapping was orchestrated by Harry to protect secrets.
chain.effect: Harry’s mental state and motives are central to the case.
required_evidence: Leslie’s letter to Gilder
Witness accounts of Leslie’s disappearance and ladder marks

chain.observation: Arthur Gwyn had forged bills and fled abroad.
chain.correction: Arthur’s financial troubles are real but unrelated to murders.
chain.effect: Arthur is cleared of murder suspicion but remains a suspect for fraud.
required_evidence: Forgery documents and resignation letter
Interview with Arthur Gwyn and Gilder

chain.observation: Gilder aggressively pursues Leslie and has financial motives.
chain.correction: Gilder’s actions are motivated by love and money but not murder.
chain.effect: Gilder is a red herring, distracting from the real culprit.
required_evidence: Gilder’s letter with invisible ink
Witness accounts of Gilder’s movements and proposal

chain.observation: Dick Alford was seen near crime scenes and had the Black Abbot costume.
chain.correction: Dick impersonated the Black Abbot to protect his brother Harry.
chain.effect: Dick is revealed as the mastermind behind the disguise and protector.
required_evidence: Bag with Black Abbot costume found in Dick’s car
Physical timeline showing Dick's presence at key locations during Black Abbot sightings

chain.observation: The treasure is hidden beneath the dry riverbed with shingle covering.
chain.correction: The treasure’s location explains the underground vault and secret passages.
chain.effect: The treasure hunt is the root cause of the crimes and madness.
required_evidence: Diary references to chesil and drought
Discovery of treasure chest and elixir flask in underground vault

herrings.description: Fabrian Gilder’s aggressive pursuit of Leslie Gwyn and his financial manipulations suggest he might be behind the crimes.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Gilder’s purchase of Red Farm, his proposal to Leslie, and his knowledge of the treasure.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Gilder’s actions are motivated by love and financial interest but he is not involved in the murders or kidnappings.

herrings.description: Thomas’s criminal past and suspicious behavior make him a prime suspect in the theft and murder.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His dismissal, possession of stolen money, and presence near crime scenes.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Thomas was a victim, killed during his attempt to steal, not the mastermind behind the crimes.

supporting_points: Arthur’s financial troubles and forged bills suggest motive.
His sudden departure abroad raises suspicion.
He had access to the estate and knowledge of the treasure.
His quarrel with Fabrian Gilder and injury imply involvement.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Arthur’s absence during key events and lack of direct evidence linking him to the crimes.

items.false_assumption: Miss Kitty Winter was solely responsible for the vitriol attack and the burglary was a spontaneous act.

chain.observation: Miss Kitty Winter claims knowledge of a locked brown leather book with gold arms.
chain.correction: Holmes obtains the book during a staged burglary.
chain.effect: The book is used as a weapon to break off the marriage.
required_evidence: Miss Winter's testimony about the book, including her description of its lock and arms, and her knowledge of its existence, which is later corroborated by Holmes's recovery of the object during the burglary event.

Holmes's report of the burglary and recovery of the book, including the sequence of access to Gruner's study, the reconstruction of the event by Holmes and Watson, and the physical evidence of the book itself.

chain.observation: Baron Gruner shows suspicion and anger during Watson's visit.
chain.correction: Watson's knowledge of Chinese pottery distracts Gruner.
chain.effect: Holmes gains time to act and recover the diary.
required_evidence: Watson's letter to Gruner arranging the visit and referencing the Ming saucer, which establishes the temporal anchor for the event sequence.
Holmes's account of the visit, including the access record of Watson's presence and the opportunity channel created for the burglary.

chain.observation: Josiah Amberley reports theft and disappearance of wife and doctor.
chain.correction: Mrs. Amberley and Dr. Ernest conspired to steal and elope.
chain.effect: Amberley's savings are stolen, and the culprits flee.
required_evidence: Amberley's testimony describing the sequence of events, the timing of the theft, and the access to the strong-room.
Police reports of theft, including the reconstruction of the event, the access record of the strong-room, and the elimination of Amberley as a suspect.

chain.observation: Holmes is attacked and seriously injured.
chain.correction: The attack was orchestrated to mislead Gruner.
chain.effect: Gruner underestimates Holmes's recovery and plans.
required_evidence: Medical reports by Sir Leslie Oakshott, documenting the timing and sequence of Holmes's injuries and recovery.
Holmes's own account of the attack, including the reconstruction of the event and the premeditated nature of the ruse.

chain.observation: Violet de Merville refuses to believe accusations against Gruner.
chain.correction: The lust diary reveals Gruner's true nature.
chain.effect: Violet breaks off the engagement.
required_evidence: The lust diary itself, as a concrete object recovered during the burglary event, and its contents reconstructing Gruner's involvement in past crimes.
Newspaper announcement of broken engagement, providing a temporal anchor and confirming the outcome of the sequence.

chain.observation: Miss Kitty Winter is sentenced for vitriol attack.
chain.correction: Her sentence is mitigated due to extenuating circumstances.
chain.effect: She remains a key witness but not the sole culprit.
required_evidence: Court records of trial, documenting the sequence of legal events and the reconstruction of her involvement.
Holmes's explanation of the case, including the elimination of Miss Winter as the sole perpetrator and the premeditated coordination with Holmes.

chain.observation: Holmes and Inspector MacKinnon cooperate to recover stolen securities.
chain.correction: Holmes's burglary and investigation reveal the hiding place.
chain.effect: Amberley's property is recovered and culprits arrested.
required_evidence: Holmes's burglary report, detailing the reconstruction of the event, the access sequence to the hiding place, and the elimination of alternative suspects.
Police recovery records, including the access record of the strong-room, the involvement of Mrs. Amberley, and the premeditated nature of the theft.

herrings.description: Steve Dixie, a bruiser, threatens Holmes to deter him from investigating.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Steve Dixie is a blustering but harmless thug used to intimidate but not capable of serious crime.

herrings.description: Ian Murdoch, a taciturn mathematical coach, is suspected of the scourging murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Murdoch was a friend of the victim and was himself a victim of the mysterious sea creature's sting.

supporting_points: She was seen attacking Baron Gruner with vitriol.
She openly expressed hatred and desire for revenge.
Her presence at the scene was undeniable.
She was tried and sentenced for the attack.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The burglary and theft of the diary were orchestrated by Holmes and Watson, and Miss Winter acted under their direction rather than independently.

items.false_assumption: A body found lying across a railway line died on that railway line.

chain.observation: The scalp wound above the left temple had bled, in two streams running at right angles — one down the face to the collar, one from the wound to the back of the head.
chain.correction: A decapitated head does not bleed, and blood obeys gravity, so the wound was made while the man lived, first while he was upright and then while he lay on his back.
chain.effect: The injury that killed the case open was inflicted before the train, in positions that do not match how the body was found.
required_evidence: The glancing scalp-wound above the left temple, with blood firmly clotted and partially dried
The engine driver's report that the man was lying face downwards with his neck over the near rail

chain.observation: The face was the face of a suffocated man, with a swollen tongue and deep tooth indentations inside the upper lip.
chain.correction: Those are the marks of heavy pressure held over the mouth, not of a wheel.
chain.effect: The man was struck, struggled, and was then borne down and suffocated.
required_evidence: The distinctly swollen tongue and the deep indentations made by the teeth inside the upper lip
The slight wounds inside the lip caused by heavy pressure on the mouth

chain.observation: A tuft of textile wedged between the upper incisors was of three fibres differently dyed — crimson wool, blue cotton and yellow jute.
chain.correction: Jute in the mixture points to a curtain, rug or table-cover rather than to clothing.
chain.effect: The thing pressed over his mouth was furniture, and furniture means a habitation.
required_evidence: The tuft of parti-coloured fabric taken with forceps from between two of the upper front teeth
Thorndyke's microscope reading of crimson wool, blue cotton and yellow jute fibres in it

chain.observation: The soles of the boots carried no sand, gravel or earth at all, but did carry fine tobacco ash, a trodden cigarette mark, biscuit crumbs and coloured carpet fibres on a projecting brad.
chain.correction: A man who had crossed rough gravelly land on foot would have that land on his boots, as the inspector's own boots demonstrate.
chain.effect: He was killed in a carpeted room and carried to the line.
required_evidence: The dead man's boot soles, examined under a lens and free of sand, gravel or earth
The inspector's boot-soles covered with adherent gravel and marked with chalk from the same ground

chain.observation: The spectacle lenses, rebuilt from every fragment picked off the sleeper and ballast, leave a surplus of small pieces over.
chain.correction: The surplus is not optical glass but soft, moulded, curved glass carrying the etched points of eight-rayed stars.
chain.effect: A star-pattern drinking glass was broken in the same place as the spectacles, so both were trodden on indoors and carried out together.
required_evidence: The reconstructed spectacle lenses built up on two visiting-cards, complete but for one or two gaps
The surplus fragments of soft moulded glass bearing the etched points of eight-rayed stars

chain.observation: The only house within half a mile yields, in its nettle bed, its flower-bed, its rubbish-heap and its grate, an iron bar carrying the same three fibres, a half-smoked Zig-Zag cigarette of fine-cut Latakia, a round wooden vesta, the broken star-pattern tumbler and cinders of shellac and undyed rabbit fur.
chain.correction: Each of these matches an article that came off the dead man or a gap in the reconstructed evidence, and the twine by the line matches the string box on that mantelpiece.
chain.effect: The house is Silas Hickler's, and Hickler killed Brodski.
required_evidence: The half-smoked Zig-Zag cigarette of fine-cut Latakia found in the flower-bed by the door
The round wooden vesta found on the road, matching the vestas in the dead man's silver match-box
The short end of white twine with a green strand picked up beside the line, matching the string box on the mantelpiece

herrings.description: A gold watch, a diamond scarf-pin and twelve pounds in gold still in the dead man's pockets
herrings.innocent_explanation: The killer was a diamond specialist who avoided plate and gold entirely; he took only the packet of stones, which nobody could prove the victim had been carrying.

herrings.description: The dead man's shattered spectacles lying beside his head with the glass scattered over the ballast, suggesting a near-sighted man who strayed onto the line
herrings.innocent_explanation: They were trodden on indoors during the struggle and carried out with the body; the killer scattered the fragments deliberately, and it is that very scattering that gives him away, because a lens broken by falling makes a few large pieces and a lens crushed under a wheel makes powder.

supporting_points: The body was laid neatly face down with the neck over the rail, as if placed on purpose
There is no crossing, road or path by which he could have arrived there accidentally
His watch, scarf-pin and twelve pounds in gold were untouched, so he was not robbed
He was near-sighted, and his broken spectacles lay beside his head
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The scalp wound above the left temple had bled, in two streams at right angles — down the face and then to the back of the head — and a decapitated head does not bleed, so the wound was made while he lived, in two positions neither of which matches how he was found.

items.false_assumption: Kitty Baird is the murderer who poisoned her aunt to inherit the fortune.

chain.observation: Poison was found only on one side of the fruit knife blade.
chain.correction: The poison was deliberately applied to only one side to poison only Miss Baird.
chain.effect: Indicates a planned murder with knowledge of victim's eating habits.
required_evidence: Deputy Coroner Fisher's autopsy report
Inspection of the fruit knife with poison residue

chain.observation: The front door key was found in the lock on the outside.
chain.correction: The door was locked from outside to trap or exclude others.
chain.effect: Suggests the murderer locked the house to create a closed circle.
required_evidence: Inspector Mitchell's testimony about the key
Police report on door lock status

chain.observation: Oscar was reported to have left on the 3 PM train but was heard talking at 5 PM.
chain.correction: Oscar lied about his departure to conceal his presence.
chain.effect: Oscar's testimony about the household movements is unreliable.
required_evidence: Witness statement of Oscar's voice at 5 PM
Train records confirming Oscar's departure time

chain.observation: Kitty's red coat was found in a second-hand store and then burned.
chain.correction: The coat was sold and then forcibly reclaimed and destroyed to hide evidence.
chain.effect: Indicates attempts to conceal or manipulate evidence related to Kitty.
required_evidence: Proprietor's testimony about coat sale
Rodgers' recovery of coat and partial destruction

chain.observation: Mrs. Parsons was found dead with cat scratches and poison on the cat's paw.
chain.correction: Mrs. Parsons was murdered to silence her after she attempted blackmail.
chain.effect: Reveals the murderer is willing to kill to cover tracks.
required_evidence: Medical report on Mrs. Parsons' death
Observation of cat's injured paw and poison traces

chain.observation: Charles Craige had forged documents and financial troubles.
chain.correction: Craige had motive to kill to cover forgery and gain financially.
chain.effect: Identifies Craige as the murderer with strong motive and opportunity.
required_evidence: Forgery evidence from Holt will case
Financial records showing Craige's debts

chain.observation: The rubber bulb syringe with poison was found missing and then returned.
chain.correction: Craige used the syringe to apply poison and Mrs. Parsons returned it to frame others.
chain.effect: Shows the use of syringe as murder weapon and framing device.
required_evidence: Discovery of syringe in library
Mrs. Parsons' attempt to bribe Oscar for papers

herrings.description: Major Leigh Wallace was suspected due to his quarrel with Miss Susan Baird and his presence with peaches at the house.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His agitation and presence at the house at the time of the murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He brought peaches as a peace offering and was not involved in the murder.

herrings.description: Mrs. Amos Parsons was suspected of blackmail and involvement in the murder due to her attempts to bribe Oscar and her suspicious behavior.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Her bribery attempts and possession of incriminating papers.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She was trying to gain leverage but was ultimately killed by Craige to silence her.

supporting_points: Kitty quarreled with her aunt on the day of the murder.
Kitty inherited a large fortune from her aunt.
A revolver with Kitty's initials was found in the victim's car.
Kitty was seen entering the house with a package of peaches.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The revolver was planted and the evidence was manipulated by Charles Craige.

items.false_assumption: Lady Riversreade was the woman Hannaford referred to and was involved in the murder.

chain.observation: Hannaford died suddenly on the train after meeting two men.
chain.correction: He was poisoned with a delayed-acting poison administered hours earlier.
chain.effect: Focus shifts to the men who met him earlier and their access to poison.
required_evidence: Post-mortem report confirming poisoning
Witness testimony of Hannaford's meeting with Ambrose and Baseverie

chain.observation: A man with stained fingers fled the scene immediately.
chain.correction: He was James Granett, also poisoned and later found dead.
chain.effect: Granett is a victim, not a suspect.
required_evidence: Identification of Granett's body
Letters linking Granett to Sellithwaite

chain.observation: Lady Riversreade was seen at suspicious locations and wore a black velvet band.
chain.correction: Lady Riversreade has a twin sister, Madame Listorelle, who is the woman involved.
chain.effect: The suspect identity shifts from Lady Riversreade to Madame Listorelle.
required_evidence: Police solicitor's revelation of twin sisters
Tattoo description matching both sisters

chain.observation: Baseverie visited Lady Riversreade and was involved in blackmail.
chain.correction: Baseverie and Ambrose are partners in crime, involved in poisoning and kidnapping.
chain.effect: Both men become prime suspects with motive and opportunity.
required_evidence: Medical directory records of Ambrose and Baseverie
Witness accounts of their presence at key locations

chain.observation: Ambrose found dead in laboratory with signs of poisoning.
chain.correction: Baseverie likely poisoned Ambrose to cover tracks.
chain.effect: Ambrose's death confirms internal conflict among culprits.
required_evidence: Discovery of Ambrose's body
Medicine bottle linked to Ambrose

chain.observation: Kidnapping of Madame Listorelle and Rhona Hannaford occurred.
chain.correction: Kidnapping was to extort jewels and enforce blackmail.
chain.effect: Criminal scheme involves multiple crimes beyond murder.
required_evidence: Witness testimony of car and kidnappers
Lord Morradale's information on jewels

chain.observation: Baseverie arrested at Waterloo with jewels and money.
chain.correction: Police trap based on postal delivery of jewels and surveillance.
chain.effect: Culprit apprehended and case resolved.
required_evidence: Police surveillance at Southampton and Waterloo
Arrest records and recovered jewels

herrings.description: The shabby man with stained fingers who fled at Charing Cross was suspected of poisoning Hannaford.
herrings.points_at_suspect: He was with Hannaford and fled immediately after his death.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was James Granett, an acquaintance of Hannaford who was also poisoned and died later.

herrings.description: Lady Riversreade was thought to be the woman in the portrait and involved in the crime.
herrings.points_at_suspect: She matched the portrait and wore a distinctive tattoo cover.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The portrait was actually of her twin sister, Madame Listorelle, who was the true figure involved.

supporting_points: She was seen at Vivian's Night Club and other suspicious locations.
She wore a black velvet band covering a tattoo matching the description.
She was upset by Baseverie's visits and involved in the reward advertisement.
Her name was connected to the blackmail and kidnapping.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Lady Riversreade was innocent and had a twin sister, Madame Listorelle, who was the actual person involved.

items.false_assumption: John Horbury absconded with the securities and jewels and caused Frederick Hollis's death.

chain.observation: Mrs. Pratt overhears a telephone call at the Station Hotel involving a meeting along the river bank.
chain.correction: The telephone conversation was with Joseph Chestermarke, not Horbury.
chain.effect: Shifts suspicion from Horbury to Joseph Chestermarke.
required_evidence: Mrs. Pratt's witness statement about the telephone call
Joseph Chestermarke's presence at the bank and house

chain.observation: Frederick Hollis is found dead at the bottom of a lead mine.
chain.correction: Medical examination shows no signs of struggle; death likely from fall but poisoning suspected.
chain.effect: Raises possibility of murder disguised as accident.
required_evidence: Medical report on Hollis's body
Autopsy report including toxicology

chain.observation: Gabriel Chestermarke shows recognition upon seeing Hollis's body.
chain.correction: Gabriel knows Hollis and is lying about ignorance.
chain.effect: Gabriel's involvement is suspected.
required_evidence: Witness observation of Gabriel's reaction
Gabriel's later behavior and flight

chain.observation: An incomplete cheque for ten thousand pounds is found on Hollis.
chain.correction: Cheque is linked to Mrs. Helen Lester and money-lending business run by Gabriel Chestermarke as Godwin Markham.
chain.effect: Connects Chestermarkes to money-lending and motive for murder.
required_evidence: Cheque found on Hollis
Bank records from Vanderkiste, Mullineau & Co.
Mrs. Lester's testimony

chain.observation: Joseph Chestermarke disappears suddenly after the explosion.
chain.correction: Joseph was involved in the explosion and attempted to kill Neale and conceal Horbury.
chain.effect: Joseph is a prime suspect for murder and imprisonment.
required_evidence: Explosion site investigation
Witnesses seeing Joseph's movements
Neale's imprisonment and rescue

chain.observation: Neale is trapped in Joseph's laboratory and hears Horbury chained inside.
chain.correction: Horbury is imprisoned and coerced to sign over securities.
chain.effect: Horbury is victim, not culprit.
required_evidence: Neale's testimony
Horbury's testimony after rescue

chain.observation: Gabriel Chestermarke confronts Joseph in the laboratory before the explosion.
chain.correction: Gabriel accuses Joseph of theft and murder, indicating internal conflict.
chain.effect: Both partners are implicated in crime.
required_evidence: Witnesses to confrontation
Joseph's behavior and possession of revolver

herrings.description: Mrs. Carswell, the housekeeper, disappears suddenly after a conversation with Joseph Chestermarke.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She fled to avoid being implicated but was an accomplice of Joseph Chestermarke.

herrings.description: Frederick Hollis's death is initially thought to be an accident from falling into a lead mine.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Hollis was murdered by Joseph Chestermarke by being pushed into the mine.

supporting_points: Horbury disappeared with the keys and valuables
He was last seen leaving the bank-house
The Chestermarkes claim securities are missing and Horbury is responsible
The housekeeper fled after Horbury's disappearance
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Horbury was actually imprisoned and coerced by Joseph Chestermarke and was innocent

items.false_assumption: Lady Violet Bredwardine was the murderer because she wore the Zenobia costume and was seen with Dr. Weathered.

chain.observation: Dr. Weathered’s body shows symptoms inconsistent with common poisons
chain.correction: Presence of a rare poison called upasine known only to few
chain.effect: Murder by exotic poison suspected
required_evidence: Autopsy report describing skin parchment-like and rapid death
Chemical analysis of upasine sample from Captain Armstrong’s collection

chain.observation: Zenobia costume worn by a dancer at the club traced to Lady Violet
chain.correction: Lady Violet was out of London at the time; costume lent to Dr. Cassilis
chain.effect: Disproves Lady Violet’s presence at the crime scene
required_evidence: Train records showing Lady Violet’s departure to Herefordshire
Testimony of maid retrieving costume from wardrobe

chain.observation: Madame Bonnell claims to have the poison bottle but presents a fake
chain.correction: Real poison was stolen and replaced with harmless powder
chain.effect: Madame Bonnell’s involvement in theft and murder suspected
required_evidence: Chemical analysis of powder in Madame Bonnell’s bottle
Gerard’s testimony about warnings and bribery

chain.observation: Letters of patients advertised for return by solicitors with false names
chain.correction: Blackmail scheme by unknown party using letters
chain.effect: Motive for murder linked to secret correspondence
required_evidence: Advertisement in newspaper by Messrs. James, Halliday & James
Mrs. Neobard’s and Mrs. Weathered’s testimony about letters

chain.observation: Mrs. Neobard and Mrs. Weathered flee to Paris
chain.correction: Police surveillance and French cooperation track them
chain.effect: Suspects under watch but not necessarily guilty
required_evidence: French police report of surveillance at Hotel Saint Catherine
Communication between Scotland Yard and French police

chain.observation: Madame Bonnell’s fingerprint matches a wanted criminal in France
chain.correction: She is a fugitive and likely the murderer
chain.effect: Strong evidence for Madame Bonnell’s guilt
required_evidence: Fingerprint photograph from Scotland Yard
French police identification and arrest report

chain.observation: Madame Bonnell’s behavior and testimony inconsistent and evasive
chain.correction: She fabricated stories to mislead investigators
chain.effect: Reveals her as the true culprit
required_evidence: Gerard’s testimony about bribery and warnings
Discovery of real poison missing from Madame Bonnell’s possession

herrings.description: Sarah Neobard accuses Lady Violet of poisoning Dr. Weathered and claims to have witnessed it.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Sarah was motivated by jealousy and personal animosity, and her accusations were uncorroborated and contradicted by Lady Violet’s alibi.

herrings.description: The disappearance of the upasine poison bottle from Mrs. Amelia Baker’s house suggests a theft and implicates multiple suspects.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Mrs. Amelia Baker and Madame Bonnell
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mrs. Baker was unaware of the theft and Madame Bonnell obtained the poison through other means; the real murderer was Madame Bonnell who used the poison.

supporting_points: Her name appeared in the club’s members list and appointment book
She was seen wearing the Zenobia costume at the club
Sarah Neobard accused her of poisoning Dr. Weathered
She had a motive due to her complicated relationship with Dr. Weathered
false_solution.the_one_flaw: She had a confirmed alibi being in Herefordshire at the time of the murder

items.false_assumption: The note found on the table was a dying confession written by Madeleine Van Norman herself.

chain.observation: The note was written with a soft pencil unlike the hard pencil on the library table.
chain.correction: The note was not written at the library table on the night of the murder.
chain.effect: The note's status as a dying confession is questioned.
required_evidence: The soft pencil found in Cicely Dupuy's desk, which was not present in the library on the night of the murder
Handwriting comparison between note and Cicely Dupuy's writing, showing a match in slant and pressure

chain.observation: No blood stains on Madeleine's right hand despite blood on dagger handle.
chain.correction: Madeleine could not have held the dagger when it was stained with blood.
chain.effect: The theory of suicide is undermined.
required_evidence: Examination of Madeleine's hands for blood stains, showing they are clean
Examination of dagger for blood stains, with blood on the handle

chain.observation: Schuyler Carleton entered the house at 11:15 pm but called for help at 11:30 pm.
chain.correction: There is a 15-minute unexplained interval in Carleton's timeline.
chain.effect: Suspicion falls on Carleton due to unexplained time gap.
required_evidence: Mr. Hunt's testimony about time of Carleton's entry, stating 'exactly quarter after eleven'
Carleton's own testimony about time of entry and alarm, confirming the 15-minute gap

chain.observation: A cachou was found on the drawing-room floor, uncommon in Mapleton.
chain.correction: The cachou likely dropped by the murderer during entry or exit.
chain.effect: Links Tom Willard to the crime scene as he possessed such cachous.
required_evidence: Testimony of Mapleton Inn landlord about cachous found in Willard's room and their rarity
Location of cachou found in Van Norman house, specifically the drawing-room floor

chain.observation: The house was securely locked with bolts and no forced entry signs.
chain.correction: The murderer must have entered and exited through an unconventional route.
chain.effect: Focus shifts to cellar window and ash-chute as entry/exit points.
required_evidence: Butler Harris's testimony about locks and bolts being fastened on all doors and windows
Fleming Stone's discovery of ash-chute opening in fireplace, showing it could be used for entry

chain.observation: The ash-chute opening is only 9.5 by 13.5 inches, seemingly too small for a large man.
chain.correction: An experienced engineer like Tom Willard could squeeze through it.
chain.effect: Tom Willard's physical ability and occupation make him a plausible suspect.
required_evidence: Measurement of ash-chute opening, recorded as nine and one-half inches by thirteen and one-half inches
Testimony about Tom Willard's engineering experience and ability to fit through small spaces, as described by his former colleagues

chain.observation: Tom Willard confessed to the murder and then fatally wounded himself.
chain.correction: The confession confirms the true mechanism and identity of the murderer.
chain.effect: Case is solved with Tom Willard as the culprit.
required_evidence: The dagger found beside Tom Willard, stained with his and Madeleine's blood and matching the wound
Medical confirmation of Tom Willard's fatal wound, as recorded by Coroner Benson

herrings.description: Cicely Dupuy wrote the false note and showed suspicious behavior, including fainting and evasiveness.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Her actions stemmed from her secret love for Carleton and fear of incriminating him, not guilt in the murder.

herrings.description: Miss Morton secretly burned papers found in Madeleine's desk, raising suspicions about her motives.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She burned old letters related to a past quarrel with Richard Van Norman and not any evidence related to the murder.

supporting_points: He was the fiancé and had a motive related to love and jealousy.
He entered the house shortly before the alarm was raised.
He refused to disclose his errand or activities during the critical time.
His demeanor was nervous and evasive during questioning.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He had a credible alibi for the time of the murder and no physical evidence linked him to the crime scene.

items.false_assumption: The vault must have a secret passage or duplicate key to explain the locked door with the key inside.

chain.observation: The vault door was locked from outside with the key found on the table inside.
chain.correction: The key was pulled back inside after locking using a thread and pin trick.
chain.effect: Explains how the vault could be locked with the key inside without secret passages.
required_evidence: The new pin found in the passage and inside the vault
Physical evidence of thread residue or marks near the ventilator holes and the key's position on the table

chain.observation: Walters was making a duplicate key and fled after receiving a telegram.
chain.correction: Walters was innocent of murder and fled due to police threat.
chain.effect: Removes Walters as the murderer suspect.
required_evidence: Telegram delivered to Walters at 2:55 pm
Walters' statement denying murder and describing his actions

chain.observation: Wellington Brown threatened Trasmere and was found dead in the vault later.
chain.correction: Yeh Ling confirmed Brown was with him at the time of the murder, providing an alibi.
chain.effect: Exonerates Wellington Brown from murder suspicion.
required_evidence: Yeh Ling's testimony about Brown's whereabouts
Witness statements placing Brown away from the vault at murder time

chain.observation: Ursula Ardfern's jewel-case was found in the vault.
chain.correction: Ursula was secretary to Trasmere and kept jewels there for safekeeping.
chain.effect: Explains presence of jewels without implicating Ursula in murder.
required_evidence: Ursula Ardfern's written correspondence with Trasmere regarding jewel storage
Police inventory of jewel-case and vault contents

chain.observation: Rex Lander claimed to be abroad during murder.
chain.correction: Rex faked trip abroad using a steward to send messages, stayed nearby.
chain.effect: Places Rex at scene with opportunity and motive.
required_evidence: Rex Lander's letter and ring sent from Italy
Witness accounts and telegrams contradicting Rex's alibi

chain.observation: The will was in Jesse Trasmere's handwriting.
chain.correction: The will was forged by Rex Lander who could write English but Trasmere could not.
chain.effect: Shows Rex's motive to secure inheritance by forgery.
required_evidence: Ursula Ardfern's statement about Trasmere's illiteracy in English
Police analysis of will and letters

chain.observation: The vault was locked and no secret entrance found.
chain.correction: The locking mechanism was manipulated by Rex using the thread and pin trick.
chain.effect: Solves the locked-room mystery conclusively.
required_evidence: Physical evidence of thread residue or marks near the ventilator holes and the key's position on the table
The new pin found in the passage and inside the vault

herrings.description: Wellington Brown, a drunken former partner, threatened Jesse Trasmere and was suspected due to his hostile behavior and gloves found near the vault.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Yeh Ling confirmed Brown was with him at the time of the murder, providing an alibi.

herrings.description: The theory that a secret passage or hidden entrance allowed the murderer to enter and exit the locked vault.
herrings.innocent_explanation: No secret passage existed; the locked door and key were manipulated by a thread and pin trick.

supporting_points: Walters was making a duplicate key for the vault
He had motive due to theft
He fled after receiving a telegram warning of police arrival
His gloves were found near the vault
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Walters was under arrest at the time of the murder and could not have committed it

items.false_assumption: A room that seals itself from the inside was sealed by the man inside it.

chain.observation: A small Christmas-tree candle lies bent and twisted in the middle of the carpet, and a stouter cut candle lies under the bed.
chain.correction: Candles do not bend by themselves; these have been softened by heat while under load.
chain.effect: Two objects in the room were carrying weight until the fire deformed them.
required_evidence: The bent and twisted little candle found in the middle of the carpet
The second, stouter candle found lying underneath the bed

chain.observation: The fire in the grate was built so large that the room was stifling on a bleak February night.
chain.correction: Kara kept his rooms hot as a habit, so an unusually large fire attracts no suspicion and is nonetheless the fastest clock in the house.
chain.effect: The room was prepared to soften wax on a schedule.
required_evidence: The statement that a big fire was burning in the grate, so big that the room was stifling
Kara's known habit of keeping the temperature of the room unpleasantly close despite the cold

chain.observation: The telephone is overturned with the receiver on the floor, and beside it lie an ivory paper-knife and two heavy books.
chain.correction: A man snatching at a telephone does not leave a paper-knife and two books arranged beside it; that is a balance, not a struggle.
chain.effect: The call to Scotland Yard was made by a falling weight, not by a dying man.
required_evidence: The overturned telephone with the receiver on the floor and two books and a long ivory paper-knife beside it
The bell that rang at Scotland Yard at 10.25 with no voice on the line

chain.observation: The steel latch can only be raised by its knob from inside the room, and it was heard to fall while the visitor was still on the stairs.
chain.correction: It can also be held up on something that will later give way, and the sound of it falling proves only that the prop failed.
chain.effect: The room sealed itself after the killer had left it.
required_evidence: The clang of the steel latch heard from the stairs while the visitor was leaving
The demonstration that once dropped the latch cannot be raised except by its own knob

chain.observation: The caller was announced as George Gathercole, an explorer with one artificial arm whom Kara had never met.
chain.correction: A man Kara has never seen is a name rather than a face, and a wooden gauntlet is easier to counterfeit than a countenance.
chain.effect: Anyone who knew Gathercole's habits could be admitted to that room.
required_evidence: The valet's account of striking his knuckles against a wooden forearm beneath the visitor's sleeve
The report that George Gathercole was listed among the passengers lost with the City of the Argentine

chain.observation: The visitor's artificial arm was the left one.
chain.correction: The real George Gathercole had lost his right arm.
chain.effect: The man admitted to Kara's room was an impostor, and the only impostor with a motive is John Lexman.
required_evidence: The valet's observation that the visitor's left hand was gloved and thrust into his overcoat pocket
T. X. Meredith's statement that the real Gathercole had lost his right arm

herrings.description: A pair of long-bladed scissors, blades dappled with blood, the handle wound in a monogrammed handkerchief, found in the locked cellar
herrings.innocent_explanation: She used them on the great chained dog Kara kept to terrify his prisoner, and the animal is found dead behind a screen in the lower cellar.

herrings.description: The two candles read as the signature of an Albanian blood feud, a form of torture Kara was known to dread
herrings.innocent_explanation: The candles are not a signature but a mechanism; their shape is the accident of wax bending under heat, and the killer chose them because Kara's own hatred of candles guaranteed they would be read as a message.

supporting_points: He was the only other person in the house at the hour of death
He alone had free access to the corridor outside the sealed room
He ran from the house hatless and coatless while the police were upstairs and could not be found
He was a convict living under a false name in a household where six thousand pounds in cash had just been drawn
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was in the kitchen in the cook's sight from the moment the visitor left until the police rang the bell — and no person in the house, himself included, could have raised the fallen latch.

items.false_assumption: Peter Crane was dead and communicating from beyond the grave.

chain.observation: Gilbert Blair died from prussic acid poisoning with no container found
chain.correction: Poison was likely administered in a way leaving no glass or container
chain.effect: Focus on indirect poisoning methods like tampered consumables
required_evidence: Medical Examiner's autopsy report detailing prussic acid poisoning
Search of Blair's room and belongings for poison containers

chain.observation: A small bottle smelling of prussic acid was found hidden in Thorpe's paint-box
chain.correction: The bottle was concealed after use, indicating Thorpe's involvement
chain.effect: Thorpe gains suspicion as having access and motive
required_evidence: Police report on discovery of poison bottle in Thorpe's belongings
Witness testimony on Thorpe's access to the apartment

chain.observation: Spirit messages and Ouija Board sessions implicate Thorpe
chain.correction: Messages are influenced by participants' subconscious or fabricated
chain.effect: Discredit supernatural evidence as reliable proof
required_evidence: Observation of Ouija Board sessions with Carly Harper and Kit Shelby
Handwriting analysis of forged note to Julie Crane

chain.observation: Materialized objects like tobacco pouch and handkerchief appear at seances
chain.correction: Objects were stolen or duplicated and used by the medium to fake manifestations
chain.effect: Medium is complicit in deception
required_evidence: Testimony of Zizi observing medium's possession of stolen items
Comparison of original items with materialized ones

chain.observation: Peter Crane is presumed dead but is seen alive incognito
chain.correction: Peter survived accident and concealed identity to investigate
chain.effect: Peter can act as detective and expose fraud and murderer
required_evidence: Peter Crane's appearance at Crane home and meeting with Zizi
Interview with reporter Tom Douglas about Peter's return

chain.observation: Shelby is accused and arrested for Blair's murder
chain.correction: Shelby is innocent and his confession was coerced by pressure and confusion
chain.effect: Attention shifts to the real murderer, as evidence against Shelby is circumstantial and contradicted by physical clues
required_evidence: Police arrest record for Kit Shelby and timeline of his whereabouts on the night of the murder
Analysis of the poison bottle found in Thorpe's paint-box and fingerprints on the bottle

chain.observation: Medium's fraud is exposed during controlled seance with Peter Crane present
chain.correction: Medium is unable to produce objects provided only at the seance, revealing the fraud
chain.effect: Fraudulent spirit communications are discredited and the medium's complicity is proven
required_evidence: Seance transcript and materialization with Peter Crane's direction
Inventory of objects provided to the medium immediately before the seance and comparison with materialized items

herrings.description: Madame Parlato's spirit communications and materializations convinced the Cranes of supernatural contact.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Madame Parlato was a fraud who used stolen items to fake spirit manifestations, not a genuine medium.

herrings.description: Ouija Board sessions repeatedly spelled out Thorpe's guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Ouija Board messages reflected the subconscious expectations of the participants, especially Carlotta and Shelby, not actual spirit communications.

supporting_points: Shelby had motive due to rivalry with Blair
Shelby had opportunity as Blair's friend and frequent visitor
Ouija Board sessions and spirit messages pointed to Shelby
Shelby was present at key seances and implicated by circumstantial evidence
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No direct evidence proved Shelby administered the poison; the spirit messages were fabricated and the real poison bottle was found elsewhere.

items.false_assumption: The necklace was stolen by an insider during the wedding preparations.

chain.observation: The safe was found unlocked when Punch opened it.
chain.correction: Mrs. Corbin had forgotten to lock the safe.
chain.effect: The necklace could have been taken without forced entry.
required_evidence: Punch's observation of the unlocked safe door
Mrs. Corbin's admission of forgetting to lock the safe

chain.observation: The imitation necklace was returned to the grandmother's room.
chain.correction: The thief realized the necklace was fake and returned it.
chain.effect: The returned necklace was a decoy to mislead the family.
required_evidence: The empty morocco box found by Judy and Punch
The imitation necklace found on the dressing table after the theft

chain.observation: Punch saw a man in pajamas moving in the house at night.
chain.correction: The man was Raglan, the thief hiding in the house.
chain.effect: The thief used pajamas to move unnoticed among guests.
required_evidence: Punch's witness statement of the man in pajamas
Lavender silk pajamas with a big nail tear found in the trunk closet

chain.observation: Bruce Applebury had the real necklace in his pocket.
chain.correction: Bruce was entrusted with the real necklace for safekeeping.
chain.effect: The real necklace was not stolen from the safe but kept by Bruce.
required_evidence: Bruce's testimony about retrieving the necklace from the bank
Judy's note left for Bruce about keeping the necklace

chain.observation: Victoria had financial troubles and pawned the necklace.
chain.correction: Victoria orchestrated the substitution to hide the pawned necklace.
chain.effect: Victoria is the mastermind behind the substitution and theft.
required_evidence: Pawn ticket for the real necklace found in Victoria's desk
Bank documents or notes about the pawn transaction

chain.observation: Judy and Bill eloped and planned to marry secretly.
chain.correction: Their elopement was to avoid scandal and family conflict.
chain.effect: Judy's behavior was motivated by family pressures, not theft.
required_evidence: Judy's note to her mother and Bruce hidden in the Chinese vase
Marriage license application filed by Judy and Bill on the morning after the theft

chain.observation: Raglan confessed and returned the real necklace.
chain.correction: Raglan was caught hiding in the house and surrendered.
chain.effect: The theft was solved by uncovering the outsider thief.
required_evidence: Lavender silk pajamas with a big nail tear found in the trunk closet
The real necklace recovered from Raglan's hiding place in the trunk closet

herrings.description: Bill Grant's secretive behavior and elopement with Judy suggested he might have stolen the necklace.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Bill was protecting Judy and had no motive to steal; he was helping her escape an unwanted marriage.

herrings.description: Bruce Applebury accused his cousin Bill Grant of stealing the necklace, fueling suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Bruce's accusation was driven by anger and misunderstanding; the necklace was stolen by Raglan.

supporting_points: Bill was seen entering Bruce's room at night
He eloped with Judy unexpectedly
He avoided discussing the necklace openly
He was in a hurry to get a marriage license
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Bill had no motive to steal and was trusted by Judy; the real thief was an outsider

items.false_assumption: Lionel Hipwell was the murderer of Monkey Dick.

chain.observation: Hilda Bennett accuses Lionel of murder but later denies he is the killer
chain.correction: She was lying to protect herself and the gang
chain.effect: Lionel’s innocence in the murder is plausible
required_evidence: Police report of Hilda Bennett’s contradictory statements regarding the attack on Monkey Dick
Witness testimony of the struggle in Bloomsbury Square involving Monkey Dick and Lionel

chain.observation: Lionel’s sudden disappearance and disguise as a lorry driver
chain.correction: He fled to avoid wrongful arrest and scandal
chain.effect: Flight is due to fear, not guilt
required_evidence: Statements from lorry drivers who aided Lionel after the attack
Newspaper descriptions and police alerts about the monkey murder case

chain.observation: Joan Gell disappears after receiving a message purportedly from Lionel
chain.correction: Message was forged by gang to lure her away
chain.effect: Joan’s disappearance is a kidnapping, not voluntary
required_evidence: Maid’s testimony about Joan’s reaction to the forged message mentioning Monkey Dick
Taxi driver’s statement on Joan’s movements on the night of the monkey incident

chain.observation: Musical manuscript sent to Lionel appears meaningless
chain.correction: It is a coded message using a musical cipher
chain.effect: Gang uses sophisticated secret communication
required_evidence: Musical cipher key found with pearls in Lionel’s possession
Deciphered message warning about Illona and the monkey attack

chain.observation: Illona warns Lionel about a blind man and betrays him to police
chain.correction: Illona is jealous and betrays Lionel to gain control
chain.effect: Illona is an antagonist within the gang
required_evidence: Letters from Illona referencing the monkey and the accidental shooting
Police search warrant and reports mentioning self-defense claims

chain.observation: Felix Zuroff controls the gang and holds Lionel’s fate
chain.correction: Zuroff eventually agrees to release Lionel after Illona’s death
chain.effect: Gang leader’s power is decisive in resolution
required_evidence: Meeting between Lionel and Zuroff in Lausanne discussing the accidental monkey shooting
Written agreement of silence and release referencing self-defense

chain.observation: Joan is found ill and unconscious in a house after police raid
chain.correction: She was held captive by gang members as revenge
chain.effect: Joan’s rescue confirms gang’s role in her disappearance
required_evidence: Police raid reports and witness statements about the monkey case
Joan’s own testimony after recovery describing the attack and accidental shooting

herrings.description: Lisely Hatten initially appears as a friend but later accuses Lionel of spying and attempts to blind him.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Lisely was a member of the criminal gang suspicious of Lionel but ultimately spared his eyesight and sent warnings.

herrings.description: Roddy Owen’s disappearance and association with criminals suggest he might be involved in Joan’s disappearance.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Roddy fled due to fear of police suspicion but was not responsible for Joan’s kidnapping.

supporting_points: He was seen fleeing the scene shortly after the shooting.
The victim was shot with a pistol found near Lionel.
A woman accused Lionel of killing her lover.
Lionel’s distinctive clothing matched the description given to police.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The shooting was accidental and self-inflicted during a struggle; Lionel was acting in self-defense.

items.false_assumption: Thalia Drummond is the mastermind behind the Crimson Circle’s crimes.

chain.observation: Marl’s panic near Beardmore estate and claim to have seen Beardmore
chain.correction: Marl could not have seen Beardmore at that time; Marl lied
chain.effect: Marl’s testimony is unreliable, suggesting fear and deception
required_evidence: Jack Beardmore’s statement that his father was indoors all morning
Location and timing of Marl’s movements near the estate

chain.observation: Yale’s psychometric claims about the murderer’s identity
chain.correction: Psychometry is unreliable and used to mislead
chain.effect: Yale’s detective persona is a cover for his criminal activities
required_evidence: Yale’s office break-in and stolen documents
Contradictions in Yale’s accounts of events

chain.observation: Thalia’s footprints found at Froyant’s house and possession of murder weapons
chain.correction: Thalia was manipulated and used as a pawn
chain.effect: Thalia is an accomplice but not the mastermind
required_evidence: Discovery of Yale’s glove and knife matching murder weapons
Thalia’s prison escape arranged by police

chain.observation: Brabazon’s sudden flight and involvement with stolen money
chain.correction: Brabazon was a fence coerced by the Crimson Circle
chain.effect: Brabazon is a minor player, not the leader
required_evidence: Bank statement showing large deposit of stolen notes by Brabazon on the day after the robbery
Police surveillance log of Brabazon’s movements between the bank and his flat

chain.observation: Willings’s stabbing and missing dagger
chain.correction: Attack was premeditated by Yale to frame Thalia
chain.effect: Willings is a victim, not a suspect
required_evidence: Witness accounts of Willings’s house and servants
Thalia’s escape and recovery of dagger

chain.observation: Empty letter-box and ransacked Yale’s office
chain.correction: Thalia’s prison escape and theft of documents
chain.effect: Thalia’s role as spy and accomplice confirmed
required_evidence: Servant’s testimony about Thalia’s visit
Physical evidence of office break-in

chain.observation: Inspector Parr’s resignation and public criticism
chain.correction: Parr is innocent but sidelined due to internal politics
chain.effect: Parr’s investigations are genuine and crucial
required_evidence: Commissioner’s statements about Parr’s performance
Parr’s detailed knowledge of the case

herrings.description: Flush Barnet, a known crook, is arrested for burglary and suspected of murder.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His possession of stolen goods and presence near Marl’s house.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Barnet was hired as a burglar by others and was unaware of the murders; he was manipulated and later arrested.

herrings.description: Harvey Froyant’s suspicious behavior and accusations against Thalia suggest he might be involved.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His fear of the Crimson Circle and harsh treatment of Thalia.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Froyant was a victim of the Crimson Circle’s blackmail and was murdered by Yale to silence him.

supporting_points: Marl’s panic and erratic behavior near the crime scene
His criminal past and association with the victim
The letter he wrote indicating fear of being targeted
His presence at the estate shortly before the murder
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Marl was killed before he could act, and evidence shows he was a victim rather than perpetrator.

items.false_assumption: The murder occurred around twelve o'clock and Bechcombe was dead before Mrs. Carnthwacke's visit.

chain.observation: Mrs. Carnthwacke saw a man with distinctive hands and an unpleasant voice at the office, and noticed the location of his seat and the inner working of the office.
chain.correction: The man was not Luke Bechcombe but an impersonator, using disguise to conceal himself.
chain.effect: The murder occurred before her visit, contradicting her timeline and revealing the impersonation.
required_evidence: Mrs. Carnthwacke's detailed testimony about the man's hands, beard, and voice, including the location of the meeting in Bechcombe's office
Comparison of portraits of Luke Bechcombe and the man she saw, focusing on the distinctive hand and beard

chain.observation: White lady's glove found at the crime scene, but the glove's inner lining showed no trace of the victim's blood or chloroform, and the working of the glove suggested it was too small for the killer's hand.
chain.correction: The glove belonged to Mrs. Carnthwacke but the killer's fingers were too large for it, indicating it was planted or dropped to mislead.
chain.effect: The glove was planted or dropped by an accomplice or the killer to mislead investigators about identity.
required_evidence: Fingerprint expert report on glove and murderer's prints, showing no match to the victim or Mrs. Carnthwacke
Mrs. Carnthwacke's admission of glove ownership and description of its location

chain.observation: Amos Thompson disappeared after the murder and was suspected, but his location was traced to a different city and his beard was false.
chain.correction: Thompson was innocent of murder but guilty of embezzlement and fled; his beard was part of his disguise.
chain.effect: Focus shifts from murder to financial crime and imposture; Thompson's absence at the time of murder is confirmed.
required_evidence: Discovery of Thompson's multiple aliases and false identity, including a beard found among his possessions
Photograph of Cecily Hoyle found in Thompson's room, with a timestamp showing he left before the murder

chain.observation: Cecily Hoyle heard movement in the office after the estimated time of death, and noticed the location of the footsteps and the inner working of the office door.
chain.correction: The movement was of the murderer impersonating Bechcombe, not the victim himself.
chain.effect: Murder time adjusted earlier, and Cecily's testimony implicates the impersonator and the use of disguise.
required_evidence: Cecily Hoyle's testimony about sounds, timing, and the location of the footsteps in the office
Medical examiner's time of death estimate, showing the victim was already dead before the movement was heard

chain.observation: Aubrey Todmarsh was a conscientious objector and community leader, but his beard was false and he had access to chloroform and rubber gloves; he was seen near the location of the murder and had the means to incapacitate the victim.
chain.correction: Todmarsh was the murderer using disguise and chloroform to incapacitate the victim, then strangling him and impersonating him.
chain.effect: Motive and opportunity align with Todmarsh, overturning previous suspicions and revealing his working as the Yellow Dog.
required_evidence: Mrs. Carnthwacke's identification of distinctive hands and false beard, and her statement about the location of the meeting
Hopkins's testimony and arrest record, showing Todmarsh's possession of chloroform, rubber gloves, and a false beard

chain.observation: The Yellow Gang is involved in multiple jewel thefts, and their inner working is revealed through a police raid on their location; Todmarsh himself is identified as the leader.
chain.correction: Todmarsh is the Yellow Dog, the gang leader and murderer, using his position to orchestrate crimes.
chain.effect: The criminal network is exposed and linked to the murder, and Todmarsh's identity as the culprit is confirmed.
required_evidence: Police raid on Yellow Gang headquarters, revealing the location and inner working of the gang's operations
Inventory of disguises, chloroform, and rubber gloves found at the location, matching those used to incapacitate the victim

chain.observation: Inspector Furnival and Steadman were captured by the Yellow Gang, but escaped using a secret window and a knife with a note, revealing the working of the gang's hideout and the location of Todmarsh himself.
chain.correction: They escaped and led police to the gang's location, resulting in Todmarsh's arrest and the reveal of the gang's inner workings.
chain.effect: Police regain advantage and capture Todmarsh, confirming his guilt and the mechanism of the crime.
required_evidence: Note slipped under prison door with instructions for escape, describing the location and working of the secret window
Escape through barred window, with police patrol arrival after gunshots, and the arrest record showing Todmarsh at the location

herrings.description: Mrs. Carnthwacke was suspected of involvement due to her secret diamond sale and the white glove found at the scene.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She was a victim of an assault by the real murderer to silence her as a witness.

herrings.description: Tony Collyer was suspected due to his inheritance motive and presence near the crime scene.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He had no gloves at the time and lacked premeditation; his alibi was supported by witnesses.

supporting_points: Thompson was the managing clerk with access to the office
He disappeared after the murder, suggesting guilt
His room contained a photograph of Cecily Hoyle, linking him to the victim
Public and police suspicion focused on him due to embezzlement
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Thompson was not present at the time of murder and lacked the distinctive hand features identified by Mrs. Carnthwacke

items.false_assumption: Stanley Audley was dead from the beginning and Thelma was free to remarry.

chain.observation: Stanley Audley disappeared after receiving a telegram at Mürren, which seemed to reveal a threat and orchestrate his absence.
chain.correction: The telegram was a false warning to force Audley into hiding, entangling him further in the forgery gang's plot.
chain.effect: Audley’s disappearance was voluntary and coerced, not a death, and his involvement with the gang was confirmed.
required_evidence: Telegram received by Stanley Audley at Mürren, which revealed the threat and orchestrated his absence
Testimony of hotel staff about Audley’s sudden departure and the involvement of a mysterious visitor

chain.observation: A locked room at Lancaster Gate was found empty with signs of burning and forged notes, which seemed impregnable but actually posed a staged threat.
chain.correction: Audley escaped by unlocking the door with pliers and destroyed evidence, confirming the room was not truly impregnable.
chain.effect: The locked room was a staged disappearance, orchestrated to hide Audley's involvement and threat to the gang.
required_evidence: Key left inside locked door at Lancaster Gate, confirming the possibility of escape and the room's lack of impregnable security
Burned forged banknotes found in fireplace, revealing the entanglement with the forgery gang

chain.observation: Rex Yelverton was found unconscious with a forged suicide note and poison bottle, which seemed to confirm his involvement in a suicide but actually posed a threat to his life.
chain.correction: Rex was drugged and attacked by an unknown assailant, orchestrated by the criminal gang.
chain.effect: Attempted murder disguised as suicide, revealing the threat to Rex and confirming the gang's involvement.
required_evidence: Forged suicide note found in hotel room, revealing the orchestration of the attack
Medical report of poisoning and drugging, confirming the threat to Rex's life

chain.observation: Thelma Audley disappeared after receiving a telegram and burning it, which seemed to confirm her voluntary absence but actually revealed her entanglement in the plot.
chain.correction: She was lured away by a message from her husband and taken captive, orchestrated by the gang.
chain.effect: Her disappearance was forced and part of a murder plot, confirming the threat posed by the conspirators.
required_evidence: Telegram burned in Thelma’s fireplace, revealing the orchestration of her disappearance
Witness statement of Thelma’s secret meeting with Dr. Feng, confirming her entanglement

chain.observation: A fire at Heathermoor Gardens trapped Rex and Thelma with a petrol-filled balloon, which seemed accidental but was orchestrated as a threat.
chain.correction: The fire was an attempted murder by Humphreys to eliminate them, confirming his involvement.
chain.effect: The plot was to kill both and destroy evidence, revealing the orchestration of the threat.
required_evidence: Petrol-filled balloon found suspended over candle, confirming the orchestration of the fire and the posed threat
Police report of forced entry and rescue, revealing the involvement of Humphreys

chain.observation: Stanley Audley died in a motor accident in France with forged notes, which seemed to confirm his death and end his involvement.
chain.correction: The man who died was the false Audley; the real Audley died later from burns, revealing the entanglement and orchestration of identities.
chain.effect: The identity of the dead man was initially mistaken, confirming the involvement of the forgery gang.
required_evidence: Police report from Saumur hospital, confirming the mistaken identity and involvement
Photographs of dead man and accomplices, revealing the orchestration of the plot

chain.observation: Hartley Humphreys committed suicide when police came to arrest him, which seemed to confirm his guilt and reveal the end of the threat.
chain.correction: Humphreys was the mastermind behind the forgery and murder plots, orchestrating all events and entangling all parties.
chain.effect: The criminal conspiracy was ended with his death, confirming the full involvement and orchestration of the crimes.
required_evidence: Police arrest records, confirming the involvement and orchestration by Humphreys
Confiscated documents linking Humphreys to forgery gang, revealing the full extent of the threat

herrings.description: Harold Ruthen was suspected due to his secretive behavior and pressure on Thelma.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was an accomplice in the forgery gang but not the mastermind or murderer.

herrings.description: Dr. Feng's initial hostility towards Thelma and Rex suggested he might be an antagonist.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was secretly protecting Thelma and Rex and working against Humphreys.

supporting_points: He was seen pressuring Thelma and was suspected of being an enemy.
He was involved with the forgery gang and had motives.
He was evasive about Audley's whereabouts.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was arrested alongside other gang members and was not responsible for the murder or disappearance.

items.false_assumption: Halley was the murderer, using a clever alibi and disguise to evade suspicion.

chain.observation: Constable Brown heard two voices arguing and recognized one as Reckavile's.
chain.correction: The second voice was a dictaphone recording, not a live person.
chain.effect: Disproves presence of a second living person in the library at murder time.
required_evidence: Dictaphone found in the library with recorded quarrel
Brown's witness statement describing the voices

chain.observation: Halley was seen at the Black Horse with multiple witnesses.
chain.correction: Halley's alibi is strong and verified.
chain.effect: Halley could not have been at the castle during the murder.
required_evidence: Testimonies of Southgate, Mrs. Southgate, and a fisherman
Police records of Halley's presence at Black Horse

chain.observation: Jack Sefton changed a stolen five pound note at the Black Horse.
chain.correction: Jack's possession of the note was innocent and linked to Giles.
chain.effect: Jack is cleared of suspicion regarding the stolen money and murder.
required_evidence: Southgate's statement about changing the note for Giles
A receipt showing Giles, the servant, received the five pound note from Reckavile

chain.observation: Giles appeared nervous and gave conflicting statements, and was the only servant with access to the library and the murder weapon.
chain.correction: Giles was hiding his guilt and motive for revenge.
chain.effect: Giles becomes prime suspect due to motive, opportunity, and access as a servant.
required_evidence: A record of Giles' employment and access to the library as a servant
A letter from Giles expressing revenge against Reckavile

chain.observation: The library door was locked with no key found, and only Giles the servant was seen near the door after the murder.
chain.correction: Giles locked the door after the murder and hid the key.
chain.effect: Explains the locked room mystery and lack of forced entry.
required_evidence: Physical examination of door and lock showing it was locked from inside
A timeline showing Giles the servant was alone near the library after the murder

chain.observation: Blood stains in the library were inconsistent with Reckavile's wound, and a knife was missing from the servant's quarters.
chain.correction: Some blood came from the assailant, Giles, during the struggle, and the stabbing was done with the servant's knife.
chain.effect: Supports theory of a violent struggle, use of a knife, and staged scene.
required_evidence: Jack Sefton's medical observation of blood stains inconsistent with a single wound
Inventory record showing a knife missing from the servant's quarters

chain.observation: Marriage certificate and dictaphone record were missing, and the knife was later found hidden in the servant's belongings.
chain.correction: Both documents and the knife were hidden in a secret drawer in the desk by Giles.
chain.effect: Recovered evidence confirmed Halley's identity, Giles' plot, and the use of the knife.
required_evidence: Secret drawer in the desk containing marriage certificate, dictaphone record, and the knife
Sinclair's examination and playback of dictaphone recording found with the knife

herrings.description: Jack Sefton secretly treated the missing bank manager Summers at The Red Cote, raising suspicions about his involvement in the disappearance and murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Jack was conducting psychoanalytic treatment and had no motive or opportunity to commit murder.

herrings.description: The mysterious activity at The Red Cote bungalow, including nightly lights and visits by Summers and Sefton, suggested a secretive and possibly criminal operation.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The bungalow was used for private medical treatment of a mentally disturbed patient, Summers.

supporting_points: Constable Brown swore he heard Halley's voice arguing with Reckavile.
Halley was found wounded and treated secretly by Jack Sefton.
Halley had a mysterious identity and was evasive about his past.
He was arrested and detained on suspicion by the police.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Halley had a strong alibi supported by multiple witnesses at the Black Horse during the time of the murder.

items.false_assumption: The two men, Bendelow and Crile, were both dead and buried as stated in official records.

chain.observation: The body found in the pond had a needle puncture in the back and died of aconitine poisoning.
chain.correction: Death was homicide, not drowning or suicide.
chain.effect: The case is murder, not accident or natural causes.
required_evidence: Medical witness testimony at the inquest
Post-mortem examination report

chain.observation: An ancient coin found in the pond was an electrotype made by Julius D’Arblay.
chain.correction: The coin links the victim to a forgery operation.
chain.effect: Motive may involve fraudulent coin production.
required_evidence: Wax impressions of the coin
British Museum expert testimony

chain.observation: Simon Bendelow was declared dead and cremated, but the coffin was later found empty.
chain.correction: Bendelow faked his death using a wax mask and an empty coffin.
chain.effect: Bendelow is alive and the prime suspect.
required_evidence: Exhumation report
Wax mask found in D’Arblay’s studio

chain.observation: Two elderly spinsters identified the wax mask as Bendelow’s face.
chain.correction: The mask was used to fake Bendelow’s death.
chain.effect: Confirms the identity of the wax mask and the deception.
required_evidence: Interview with Miss Dewsnep and Miss Bonington
Photograph of wax mask

chain.observation: Marion D’Arblay was attacked by a man matching the description of Morris.
chain.correction: Morris is actually Bendelow in disguise using make-up and a wax mask.
chain.effect: The attacker and murderer are the same person.
required_evidence: Description of assailant by Marion
Wax mask and make-up demonstration

chain.observation: The murder victim’s studio was ransacked and a plaster mould was broken.
chain.correction: The murderer searched for the wax mask mould to destroy evidence.
chain.effect: Motive for murder was to conceal the fraudulent death.
required_evidence: Studio inspection report
List of missing or disturbed moulds

chain.observation: The police arrested a man with a red nose and different appearance than expected, and discovered he was a professional criminal with a history of commission of crimes and a reputation for silence in the face of questioning.
chain.correction: The arrested man was the disguised Bendelow using make-up and a wax mask.
chain.effect: The true murderer was caught despite disguise.
required_evidence: Police surveillance reports including professional criminal background and commission records
Identification by Stephen Gray and police noting the suspect's silence during interrogation

herrings.description: The deliberate cutting of Marion D’Arblay’s bicycle brake wire suggested a malicious attempt on her life.
herrings.points_at_suspect: An unknown local saboteur or mentally defective adult
herrings.innocent_explanation: The act was a crude attempt by the murderer to intimidate or harm Marion but was not directly linked to the murder itself.

herrings.description: The falling derrick on the canal tow-path that caused Dr. Gray to fall into the water appeared to be an accident or sabotage.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Mr. Morris or an unknown assailant near the canal
herrings.innocent_explanation: The derrick fell due to a poorly secured rope slipping off the cleat, likely accidental rather than intentional sabotage.

supporting_points: Morris was identified by a plaster mask found at the studio.
He was seen following Dr. Gray and was suspected of suspicious activities.
His shop contained unusual and decayed antiques suggesting illicit dealings.
He was connected to the victim through the wax mask.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Morris was actually Simon Bendelow in disguise, using the alias to conceal his identity.

items.false_assumption: The Talisman was stolen by a left-handed thief who had full knowledge of the estate.

chain.observation: The cabinet doors were found with the left-hand door open, indicating a left-handed person opened it.
chain.correction: Eileen and Douglas are right-handed; the thief must be left-handed or ambidextrous.
chain.effect: Narrows suspect list to left-handed or ambidextrous individuals.
required_evidence: Observation of cabinet door positions in Corinthian’s Room
Eileen’s and Douglas’s hand preference demonstrated by match and cigarette handling

chain.observation: Mrs. Caistor Scorton was seen carrying stolen items from a hollow tree near the Pool.
