He was absent during the murder, suggesting opportunity for a frame-up
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was away fishing during the time of the murder and had no access to the victim

items.false_assumption: The murder was committed by Jim Egan, the hotel proprietor, due to his secret dealings and silence.

chain.observation: Wristwatch with illuminated dial and damaged numeral two seen on intruder's wrist; motive for the crime included Jennison's desire to marry Barbara and inherit Dan's fortune.
chain.correction: Watch belonged to Harry Jennison, not the taxi driver Okuda; Jennison's motivation and desire to marry Barbara provided a strong motive.
chain.effect: Identifies Jennison as the intruder at the crime scene and establishes motive.
required_evidence: Observation of wristwatch by Miss Minerva Winterslip at 1:20 AM, noting the damaged numeral two
Barbara's letter to John Quincy describing Jennison's desire to marry her and her father's opposition

chain.observation: Corsican cigarette stub found near crime scene, initially thought to implicate Jim Egan.
chain.correction: Tobacco analysis shows different tobacco types in cigarettes linked to suspects.
chain.effect: Exonerates Jim Egan from suspicion based on cigarette evidence.
required_evidence: Tobacco expert testimony from smoking emporium comparing stubs
Comparison of cigarette stubs from Egan, Brade, and Cope by laboratory

chain.observation: Thomas Macan Brade claims to be wronged heir with motive.
chain.correction: Brade was on another island during murder and has no direct evidence.
chain.effect: Removes Brade as a viable suspect.
required_evidence: Sailing records of Brade's travel to Maui showing absence
Testimony from Mrs. Brade about his whereabouts during the murder

chain.observation: Jim Egan refuses to disclose business with Dan Winterslip, raising suspicion of motive.
chain.correction: Egan's silence due to personal reasons and financial troubles, not guilt.
chain.effect: Weakens case against Egan.
required_evidence: Check for $5000 from Dan to Egan, dated before murder
Carlota Egan's testimony about her father's financial troubles and desire to protect family

chain.observation: Jennison claims alibi on ship during murder; timeline shows opportunity.
chain.correction: Jennison swam ashore secretly and returned before dawn.
chain.effect: Disproves Jennison's alibi and places him at the crime scene.
required_evidence: Witness testimony of Jennison's presence on lanai by Miss Minerva Winterslip
Hepworth's and quartermaster's testimony about ship's anchoring and watch during the night

chain.observation: Jennison's wristwatch found and linked to crime; watch was damaged and sold multiple times.
chain.correction: Watch was originally Jennison's and the damaged numeral two matches the one seen at the scene.
chain.effect: Physical evidence linking Jennison to the murder.
required_evidence: Testimony from jeweler Lau Ho about watch repair and sales, including the damaged numeral two
Spaniard José Cabrera's testimony about handling and reselling the watch

chain.observation: Jennison attempts to flee and resists arrest; attempted suicide is a confession.
chain.correction: Jennison's attempted suicide with empty gun is confession.
chain.effect: Final proof of guilt and confession.
required_evidence: Witness testimony of Jennison's behavior at arrest, including attempted suicide
Empty gun found on Jennison after failed suicide attempt

herrings.description: Jim Egan's silence about his business with Dan and the Corsican cigarette stub found near the crime scene suggested his guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Tobacco analysis showed the cigarette stub was of a different tobacco type than those Egan sold, and Egan's refusal to talk was due to personal reasons unrelated to the murder.

herrings.description: Thomas Macan Brade's claim of being wronged by Dan Winterslip and his mysterious absence raised suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Brade was away on another island during the murder and had no opportunity; his claim related to a decades-old family dispute unrelated to the crime.

supporting_points: Egan was the last person to see Dan Winterslip alive
Egan refused to disclose the nature of his business with Dan
Corsican cigarette stub found near the crime scene matched cigarettes sold by Egan
Egan had financial troubles and motive
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The Corsican cigarette evidence was disproven by tobacco analysis showing different tobacco types, and Egan had a strong alibi and no direct evidence linking him to the murder.

items.false_assumption: A man whom nobody notices is a man who was not there.

chain.observation: Laura Hope heard Welkin's voice in an empty street at the exact moment each letter from Smythe reached her.
chain.correction: A letter does not arrive unaccompanied; somebody carried it and stood near enough to speak.
chain.effect: A person was present at both moments who was not counted as present.
required_evidence: Laura Hope's account of hearing a laugh while standing alone outside the shop at the corner
The two letters from Isidore Smythe that arrived at those moments

chain.observation: A strip of stamp paper was gummed along the outside of the shop window while Angus and Laura Hope sat inside.
chain.correction: Gumming a yard and a half of stamp paper to a lit shop window takes minutes in full view of the street.
chain.effect: The enemy can work unhurried in public without any passer-by registering him.
required_evidence: The strip of stamp paper reading 'If you marry Smythe, he will die' found on the shop window
Angus's statement that no paper was on the window fifteen minutes earlier

chain.observation: Grey footprints run through the snow into the entrance, between the legs of the commissionaire who swears nobody entered.
chain.correction: The footprints and the testimony are both true, so the witness's word 'nobody' is narrower than it sounds.
chain.effect: Somebody crossed the threshold in a capacity the watchers do not classify as a visitor.
required_evidence: The stringy pattern of grey footprints stamped on the white snow at the porch
The commissionaire's sworn statement that nobody has been to ask since Angus left

chain.observation: There is blood on the hall floor of the flat but no body anywhere in it.
chain.correction: The body left the building, so whoever removed it carried it out through the watched entrance.
chain.effect: The killer had a container large enough for a small man and unremarkable enough to carry out.
required_evidence: The pool of blood where the note in red ink had lain
Flambeau's five-minute search of every corner and cupboard finding no corpse

chain.observation: Smythe's body is recovered from the canal below the crescent with a stab wound over the heart, not drowned.
chain.correction: He was killed upstairs and carried down, so the carrier passed the four watchers going out as well as coming in.
chain.effect: The same unnoticed capacity accounts for both crossings.
required_evidence: The constable's report of the body found in the canal down below
The constable's statement that he was not drowned but died of a great stab over the heart

chain.observation: Welkin, who took long solitary walks and vanished to seek his fortune, has a postman's round covering the crescent.
chain.correction: A postman in uniform enters any building unchallenged and carries a bag large enough for a small corpse.
chain.effect: The invisible man is a postman, and the sack that carried the body is a light brown postbag.
required_evidence: Laura Hope's account that Welkin went for great walks by himself and left to seek his fortune
The light brown sack sought with the body in the canal
The postman walking the crescent under the trees

herrings.description: The rows of headless clockwork servants standing over the blood stain, one with its arm raised
herrings.innocent_explanation: The machines run on grooves in the floor and are moved by a button in the wall; one was standing over the blood because Smythe summoned a drink from it moments before he was killed.

herrings.description: Angus is a rival suitor who had access to the flat that evening and left just before the killing
herrings.innocent_explanation: Angus was at Lucknow Mansions with Flambeau and Father Brown for the whole interval, and it was he who set the four watchers on the entrance in the first place.

supporting_points: The entrance was watched continuously by four men and there is no back door
All four watchers swear independently that no man went in or out
There is blood on the hall floor but no body anywhere in the flat
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Grey footprints run through the snow into the entrance, between the legs of the commissionaire who swears nobody entered — so somebody crossed a threshold no living person is supposed to have crossed.

items.false_assumption: Paulette Brown is guilty of theft and involved in the murders.

chain.observation: Thompson's letter had a hidden message inside the envelope, whose warning was crucial.
chain.correction: The message was a warning about Macartney's true identity and danger.
chain.effect: Revealed Macartney as the murderer and criminal mastermind.
required_evidence: Thompson's letter with hidden pencil scrawl inside envelope, whose warning was orchestrated to reach Nick Stretton
Thompson's playing cards with secret writing about Macartney's chance to cause harm

chain.observation: Wolf bait was found in the wagon and on the road, showing a chance for wolves to attack.
chain.correction: Macartney used wolf bait to lure wolves to attack Dudley.
chain.effect: Showed Macartney's involvement in Dudley's death.
required_evidence: Broken bottle of wolf bait in wagon, orchestrated by Macartney
Dead wolf with throat cut near corduroy road, whose presence was caused by bait

chain.observation: Four mill men were found dead in the assay office, whose deaths were orchestrated to eliminate witnesses.
chain.correction: Macartney staged a robbery and killed them to eliminate witnesses.
chain.effect: Confirmed Macartney's violent methods to secure control.
required_evidence: Dead mill men with gunshot wounds in assay office, whose deaths were caused by Macartney
Macartney's empty revolver and slashed doorpost, orchestrated as part of the staged robbery

chain.observation: Dunn and Collins were believed dead but reappeared alive, whose disappearance was orchestrated by Macartney.
chain.correction: They were hiding in secret tunnels and allied with Macartney.
chain.effect: Revealed complicity of Dunn and Collins in the conspiracy.
required_evidence: Secret tunnels behind Thompson's stope, whose existence was orchestrated for hiding
Dunn and Collins' presence in Skunk's Misery den, caused by their alliance with Macartney

chain.observation: Paulette Brown's real name and connection to emerald theft, whose identity was used to cause suspicion.
chain.correction: She was innocent and a victim of Macartney's schemes.
chain.effect: Cleared Paulette of theft and implicated Macartney.
required_evidence: Letter signed Tatiana Paulina Valenka, whose contents were orchestrated to protect Paulette
Van Ruyne's emerald necklace found on Macartney, showing cause for suspicion

chain.observation: Macartney was seen with Marcia Wilbraham and had fainting fits, whose behavior was orchestrated to deflect suspicion.
chain.correction: Macartney is Dick Hutton, the criminal mastermind.
chain.effect: Identified Macartney as the true culprit behind murders and theft.
required_evidence: Thompson's deuce of hearts with message, whose warning was orchestrated to reveal Macartney's identity
Macartney's behavior and fainting episodes, caused by his criminal stress

chain.observation: Macartney's men were ambushed and killed by explosion in Thompson's stope, whose fate was orchestrated by Nick Stretton.
chain.correction: Nick Stretton and allies used explosives to trap Macartney's gang.
chain.effect: Led to Macartney's downfall and capture.
required_evidence: High explosive placed in Thompson's stope, whose detonation was orchestrated as a trap
Explosion and collapse of tunnel entrance, causing Macartney's gang to be incapacitated

herrings.description: Paulette Brown's real identity as Tatiana Paulina Valenka and her connection to a stolen emerald necklace.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She was protecting herself from Macartney's threats and was not involved in theft or murder.

herrings.description: Dunn and Collins were believed dead and suspected of conspiracy.
herrings.innocent_explanation: They were alive and hiding in secret tunnels, working against Macartney.

supporting_points: Billy Jones was found near Thompson's body and had a suspicious demeanor.
Dudley Wilbraham accused him of possible murder.
Billy Jones was fired suddenly and mysteriously.
He had no alibi for the time of Thompson's death.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Billy Jones was incapable of the complex conspiracy and had no motive to kill Thompson or Dudley.

items.false_assumption: Penelope Noelson was initially assumed to be the principal thief and accomplice.

chain.observation: A forged cheque was cashed in the name of Solly Gertstein.
chain.correction: The cheque was forged by Adèle Gertstein under blackmail pressure.
chain.effect: Identifies forgery and blackmail as part of the crime.
required_evidence: Letter from Adèle Gertstein to Larry Hughes requesting money
Handwriting analysis report comparing forged cheque and letters

chain.observation: Penelope Noelson gave a forged cheque to the detective and tried to bribe him.
chain.correction: Penelope was acting under coercion and was abducted to prevent testimony.
chain.effect: Shifts suspicion from Penelope as culprit to victim.
required_evidence: Witness statement of Penelope's abduction
Observation of Penelope's fainting and interrogation

chain.observation: No forced entry or broken locks at Streetly House.
chain.correction: Stebbins made wax impressions of keys to gain access.
chain.effect: Explains how the burglary was executed without forced entry.
required_evidence: Recovered duplicate keys matching locks at Streetly House
Wax residue found on keyholes and Stebbins' personal effects

chain.observation: Stolen goods were not found in Larry Hughes' house.
chain.correction: Goods were hidden in a secret tunnel at 'Mope's Bottom'.
chain.effect: Reveals the storage and transport method of stolen goods.
required_evidence: Discovery of secret tunnel and steel boxes
Recovered stolen items from tunnel

chain.observation: Larry Hughes was elusive and not caught during initial raids.
chain.correction: Larry escaped through the tunnel and later was captured after a chase.
chain.effect: Explains Larry's temporary escape and eventual capture.
required_evidence: Witness accounts of Larry's escape
Train confrontation and arrest records

chain.observation: Larry Hughes offered bribes to the detective to drop the case.
chain.correction: Detective refused and continued pursuit leading to capture.
chain.effect: Shows detective's integrity and determination.
required_evidence: Letter from Larry Hughes offering bribe
Detective's testimony rejecting bribe

chain.observation: Penelope Noelson and Mrs. Gertstein were held captive at 'Mope's Bottom'.
chain.correction: They were coerced to prevent testimony and cooperation with police.
chain.effect: Explains their behavior and eventual cooperation.
required_evidence: Statements from Penelope and Mrs. Gertstein
Observation of their captivity and treatment

herrings.description: Adèle Gertstein's forgery and blackmail scheme misleads suspicion towards her as the main culprit.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Her actions were driven by desperation and blackmail, not direct involvement in the burglary.

herrings.description: Gold Dust Teddy's drunkenness and criminal record make him a suspect, but he is more a pawn than mastermind.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was used as a tool by Larry Hughes and was not the organizer.

supporting_points: She gave the detective a forged cheque
She fainted under interrogation, suggesting guilt
She was seen in suspicious circumstances with Larry Hughes
She initially denied knowing Larry Hughes
false_solution.the_one_flaw: She was acting under duress and was abducted to prevent her testimony, not a willing criminal.

items.false_assumption: Eleanore Leavenworth was the murderer because she possessed the key and behaved suspiciously.

chain.observation: Mr. Leavenworth was found murdered in locked library with no sign of forced entry. Detective Gryce arranged for the scene to be secured and observed by police.
chain.correction: Murderer was inside the house and locked the door on exit
chain.effect: Suspects limited to household members and close associates
required_evidence: Testimony of Thomas Dougherty about locked doors and windows
Coroner’s report on locked door and absence of forced entry

chain.observation: Eleanore Leavenworth possessed the key to the library door and refused to explain. The detective arranged for the key to be examined and its discovery was observed by multiple parties.
chain.correction: Key was hidden and later found in her possession, but she denied taking it
chain.effect: Suspicion falls on Eleanore for possible involvement
required_evidence: Discovery of broken-handled key in Eleanore’s possession
Testimony of Mr. Fobbs about Eleanore’s behavior with the key

chain.observation: Mary Leavenworth was secretly married to Henry Ritchie Clavering. Detective Gryce arranged for access records at the hotel to be examined.
chain.correction: Marriage was secret due to family opposition and social prejudice
chain.effect: Mary’s motive for murder is linked to inheritance and secret marriage
required_evidence: Visitor book of Hotel Union at R—— showing presence of Mary and Clavering
Testimony of Timothy Cook about secret marriage at F——

chain.observation: Hannah Chester disappeared and was later found dead under suspicious circumstances. The detective arranged for the room to be searched and observed the discovery of physical evidence.
chain.correction: Hannah was silenced by poison and left a forged letter implicating Mary
chain.effect: Hannah’s death removes key witness and misleads investigation
required_evidence: Printed letter (the forged document) found in Hannah’s bed
Poison detected on paper found in Hannah’s room

chain.observation: James Trueman Harwell accused Henry Clavering of murder in a fit of madness. The detective arranged for Harwell's statements and timeline to be compared with physical evidence.
chain.correction: Harwell was the actual murderer acting out of love and jealousy
chain.effect: Real culprit revealed through document analysis and timeline contradiction
required_evidence: Physical evidence placing Harwell at the scene during the time of the murder
Timeline contradiction between Harwell's account and access records

chain.observation: Forged letter and poison sent to Hannah Chester. The detective arranged for the document to be analyzed and the room to be observed for physical traces.
chain.correction: Harwell forged the letter to mislead and poisoned Hannah to silence her
chain.effect: Investigation focuses on Harwell as true murderer
required_evidence: Analysis of the forged letter showing it was printed, not handwritten, and matching paper to Harwell's possession
Testimony of Mrs. Amy Belden about Hannah’s letters and the delivery of the poisoned paper

chain.observation: Mary Leavenworth’s behavior is secretive and suspicious. The detective arranged for her correspondence and diary to be examined in a secluded setting.
chain.correction: Mary was protecting her secret marriage and unaware of Harwell’s crime
chain.effect: Mary is exonerated and the true murderer is Harwell
required_evidence: Diary entries of Eleanore Leavenworth
Letters and papers found in Mrs. Belden’s possession

herrings.description: The secret marriage of Mary Leavenworth to Henry Ritchie Clavering misleads suspicion towards Mary as the murderer.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mary’s marriage was secret due to family opposition, but she was not involved in the murder.

herrings.description: The disappearance and later death of Hannah Chester creates suspicion of her involvement or knowledge of the crime.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Hannah was a witness who was silenced by the real murderer through poison and a forged confession.

supporting_points: Possession of the library key
Equivocation and refusal to explain certain actions
Handkerchief stained with pistol grease found at the scene
Attempted destruction of incriminating letter
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Lack of direct evidence and the presence of a forged confession and poison implicating another party

items.false_assumption: The Avenger is a respectable young man carrying a newspaper parcel seen by witnesses.

chain.observation: Witnesses describe a man carrying a newspaper parcel near crime scenes
chain.correction: Descriptions are composite and inconsistent; the real murderer carries a leather bag
chain.effect: Official suspect description is misleading
required_evidence: Witness statements from inquest including Lizzie Cole and warehouse wife
Mr. Cannot’s testimony about a man with a leather bag

chain.observation: Blood found on Robert Bunting’s hand after meeting Mr. Sleuth
chain.correction: Blood likely from Mr. Sleuth’s nosebleed or contact with dead animal
chain.effect: Bunting’s guilt is doubtful
required_evidence: Bunting’s account of touching Mr. Sleuth’s damp cape
Mr. Sleuth’s mention of brushing against a dead animal

chain.observation: Mr. Sleuth exhibits eccentric behavior and nocturnal outings
chain.correction: Eccentricity masks homicidal mania and murderous activity
chain.effect: Mr. Sleuth is prime suspect
required_evidence: Mrs. Bunting’s observations of lodger’s habits
Joe Chandler’s police reports on Avenger’s movements

chain.observation: Mr. Sleuth disappears after confrontation at Madame Tussaud’s
chain.correction: Disappearance confirms guilt and ends murder spree
chain.effect: Case closure
required_evidence: Eyewitness account of Mr. Sleuth’s behavior at Madame Tussaud’s
Subsequent lack of lodger’s return

chain.observation: Inquest reveals conflicting witness descriptions and unreliable testimony
chain.correction: Witnesses influenced by fear, press, and confusion
chain.effect: Official descriptions are unreliable
required_evidence: Inquest transcripts
Coroner’s remarks on witness credibility

chain.observation: Police find a peculiar knife and rubber-soled shoe print near crime scenes
chain.correction: Knife and shoe print match Mr. Sleuth’s belongings
chain.effect: Physical evidence linking lodger to murders
required_evidence: Knife found on Primrose Hill wrapped with shoes
Footprint outline published in newspapers

chain.observation: Mr. Sleuth’s landlady and husband harbor suspicions but do not report to police out of fear of social ruin and pity for the lodger, who is suspected to be an escaped lunatic driven by religious mania
chain.correction: Their silence delays police action and allows the religiously motivated escaped lunatic to continue his crimes
chain.effect: Delay in apprehension and continued murders
required_evidence: Mrs. Bunting’s internal monologues and behavior regarding the escaped lunatic
Bunting’s reluctance to involve authorities despite suspicion of religious mania

herrings.description: A barmaid who served a gentleman with a glass of milk paid by a sovereign, suspected to be the Avenger.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The gentleman was a harmless lunatic who gave the barmaid a sovereign out of kindness, unrelated to the murders.

herrings.description: Mr. Cannot claims to have met the murderer on the night of a crime and describes him as a madman carrying a bag.
herrings.innocent_explanation: His testimony was dismissed as unreliable and not corroborated; he was considered a crank.

supporting_points: Blood found on Bunting’s hand
His nervous behavior and secretive actions
His proximity to the crime scenes as the lodger’s landlord
His reluctance to involve the police
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Lack of direct evidence linking him to the murders and his genuine ignorance of the lodger’s true nature

items.false_assumption: Lady Loudwater and Colonel Grey were the murderers motivated by passion.

chain.observation: Lord Loudwater was found stabbed in his smoking-room with a knife from the inkstand
chain.correction: The knife had no fingerprints, indicating the murderer wore gloves
chain.effect: Eliminates suspects who did not wear gloves or left prints
required_evidence: Photographs of fingerprints on the knife handle
Witness statement of Mr. Manley about the knife usage

chain.observation: A forged letter instructed the bank to pay Helena Truslove a large sum
chain.correction: The signature on the letter was a skilled forgery by someone close to Lord Loudwater
chain.effect: Identifies financial motive and implicates someone with access to Lord Loudwater's papers
required_evidence: Letter of instruction to the bank
Comparison of signatures on other letters

chain.observation: Lady Loudwater and Colonel Grey lied about hearing Lord Loudwater snore
chain.correction: They lied to protect each other and to mislead about the time of death
chain.effect: Narrows time window of murder and excludes them as murderers
required_evidence: Statements from Lady Loudwater and Colonel Grey
Mr. Flexen's later interview with Colonel Grey admitting he heard the snore

chain.observation: James Hutchings was discharged and threatened Lord Loudwater
chain.correction: He returned to the castle late but had no solid evidence linking him to the murder
chain.effect: Removes Hutchings as the murderer despite motive and opportunity
required_evidence: Witness statement of Jane Pittaway about Hutchings' presence
Mr. Flexen's interview with Hutchings

chain.observation: A mysterious woman had a quarrel with Lord Loudwater late at night
chain.correction: She was Helena Truslove, who had a financial dispute but did not commit the murder
chain.effect: Focuses suspicion on those close to Lord Loudwater rather than outsiders
required_evidence: Witness statement of Mrs. Carruthers about the quarrel
Mr. Flexen's interview with Helena Truslove

chain.observation: Herbert Manley was secretive and had motive to secure Helena's allowance
chain.correction: Manley forged the letter and murdered Lord Loudwater to protect the forged transaction
chain.effect: Identifies the true culprit and explains the motive and method
required_evidence: Mr. Flexen's analysis of the forged letter
Mr. Carrington's legal assessment of the forged cheque

chain.observation: Mr. Manley claims Lord Loudwater never threatened to halve Helena's allowance
chain.correction: Manley admits he invented the threat to justify his actions
chain.effect: Reveals Manley's manipulation and confirms his guilt
required_evidence: Letter from Lord Loudwater to Helena Truslove confirming her allowance would continue
Comparison of Lord Loudwater's statements about the allowance in his correspondence

herrings.description: William Roper, the under-gamekeeper, spreads scandalous rumors about Lady Loudwater and Colonel Grey, claiming to have witnessed their kiss and suggesting their involvement in the murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He is motivated by ambition to gain promotion and is a known gossip; his stories are exaggerated and unsubstantiated.

herrings.description: An unknown woman visits Lord Loudwater late at night and has a violent quarrel with him, leading to suspicion she may be involved in the murder.
herrings.points_at_suspect: The mysterious woman, later identified as Helena Truslove
herrings.innocent_explanation: She had a legitimate grievance over her allowance and did not commit the murder; the quarrel was genuine but non-lethal.

supporting_points: He was discharged by Lord Loudwater and threatened him
He was seen entering and leaving the castle late at night
He had a violent temper and was disliked by many
He was found to be nervous and under strain
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No concrete evidence linked him to the murder, and the glove on the knife excluded his fingerprints

items.false_assumption: Jonathan Ingle died naturally and was cremated with proper certificates.

chain.observation: The magic casket’s bottom is a Japanese magic mirror with an etched design.
chain.correction: The design is a secret message etched invisibly on the mirror’s reflective surface.
chain.effect: The message reveals the hiding place of the stolen pearls.
required_evidence: The magic casket with the mirror bottom
Photograph of the reflected light showing Japanese characters

chain.observation: Jonathan Ingle’s cremated ashes contain no human bones or teeth.
chain.correction: The ashes are mostly butcher’s mutton legs preserved with formalin.
chain.effect: Ingle’s death was faked using a dummy body to commit fraud.
required_evidence: Analysis of cremation ashes
Undertaker’s statement about the body not being seen

chain.observation: A suffragist letter is found in the murder compartment of Burnham.
chain.correction: The letter was planted by the real murderer to frame Miss Dalby.
chain.effect: Miss Dalby’s guilt is a false assumption.
required_evidence: Duplicated circular letters with secret messages
Secret message revealing the real murderer’s plan

chain.observation: Duck-weed species in ditch where Cyrus Pedley’s body was found differs from drowning site.
chain.correction: Pedley was drowned elsewhere and his body transported to mislead investigators.
chain.effect: The death is a murder, not suicide or accident.
required_evidence: Botanical analysis of duck-weed species
Footprints and tire tracks near the ditch

chain.observation: Millicent Fawcett’s wounds and blood stains inconsistent with suicide.
chain.correction: She was murdered by Frederick Barnett with assistance from James Barnett and Mrs. Barnett.
chain.effect: The Barnetts’ false alibi is exposed by the phonograph recording.
required_evidence: Cast of distinctive footprint
Phonograph cylinder with recorded practice

chain.observation: Tattoo on dismembered arm found in Chapman’s box matches Rebecca Mings.
chain.correction: The tattoo was applied post-mortem to fake identity; the box was swapped.
chain.effect: Chapman is innocent; Mings and Gamble conspired to fake death and frame him.
required_evidence: Microscopic examination of tattoo marks
Lock and sales records of luggage boxes

chain.observation: Blood in Joseph Riggs’s hall is not his nor Robert Fletcher’s.
chain.correction: Blood belongs to a negro with filariasis and elephantiasis, who was present at the time.
chain.effect: Riggs died by suicide; the negro’s testimony confirms this.
required_evidence: Microscopic examination of blood samples
Testimony of Robert Bruce (Kwaku Mensah)

herrings.description: Japanese men shadowing Miss Bonney and attempting to recover the magic casket.
herrings.innocent_explanation: They were after the casket for the secret message, not directly involved in the murder.

herrings.description: The noisy practice of the Barnetts and the phonograph alibi for Millicent Fawcett’s murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Ponting’s alibi was genuine, but the Barnetts used a phonograph to create a false alibi.

supporting_points: A suffragist letter was found in the murder compartment.
Miss Dalby was seen carrying a similar bag to the one found empty.
Circumstantial evidence suggested she was near the crime scene.
She was arrested and charged with the murder.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The letter was planted by the real murderer to frame her, and she had a solid alibi.

items.false_assumption: The murderer was a lame man who used the walking-stick found at the scene.

chain.observation: Walking-stick found at murder scene had wear across heel, not sides, which is unusual for a lame man but typical for a blind man using it to feel his way in public places such as a garden in London.
chain.correction: Walking-stick wear indicates use in darkness, consistent with blind man's use and not a lame man's.
chain.effect: Murderer not lame; walking-stick belongs to Kinloch.
required_evidence: Walking-stick with sole bevelled across heel, found in the public garden in London where Kinloch was expected to wait.
Dr. Dunn's testimony on Kinloch's blindness and use of stick, confirming Kinloch's identity as the blind man.

chain.observation: Fingerprints on broken glass at scene were compared to those of Dick Hollins, a suspected impostor, to reveal whether the woman who visited Kinloch in the public garden was involved.
chain.correction: Fingerprints do not match suspect Dick Hollins, who was a red herring.
chain.effect: Fingerprints likely belong to murderer, not Kinloch or Hollins.
required_evidence: Fingerprint analysis from Scotland Yard, confirming the identity of the person present at the scene.
Comparison of fingerprints taken from Dick Hollins, revealing he was not involved.

chain.observation: Kinloch was blind but later regained sight after surgery, which was not public knowledge and thus prevented exposure of the murderer's political ambition.
chain.correction: Murderers unaware of Kinloch's regained sight, increasing his danger.
chain.effect: Kinloch becomes a threat to murderer and target for elimination.
required_evidence: Dr. Dunn's statement on Kinloch's eye operation, confirming the timing and recovery.
McNab's report of Kinloch's regained sight, revealing Kinloch's new ability to identify the woman.

chain.observation: Lady Wye fainted near Kinloch and was emotionally involved, and her visits to the public garden in London were expected to reveal her identity and confirm her role.
chain.correction: Lady Wye is protecting Kinloch and involved in concealment.
chain.effect: Lady Wye is an accomplice but not the murderer.
required_evidence: Constable Howley's witness statement about Lady Wye's behavior in the public garden.
Mrs. Spedding's gossip and observations about the woman visiting Kinloch, confirming her identity.

chain.observation: Sir Stephen Wye had an alibi of being at home, but the timing of his movements and access records in London public spaces contradict his story and reveal his attempt to prevent exposure of his political ambition.
chain.correction: Alibi was staged; he left house secretly to commit murder.
chain.effect: Sir Stephen Wye is the murderer despite alibi.
required_evidence: Butler James Brown's testimony about Sir Stephen's absence from home at the relevant time.
Inspector Snargrove's investigation of alibi and access records in London, confirming the contradiction.

chain.observation: Murderer left no footprints on brick path but car tracks with embedded cartridge were found, and the car was seen leaving a public garden in London, which was not expected by the police.
chain.correction: Murderer escaped by car with solid rubber tyres, no hoof marks.
chain.effect: Car tracks help locate murderer's escape route.
required_evidence: McNab's observation of wheel marks on driveway and in the public garden in London.
Brass cap of cartridge embedded in tyre tread, confirming the car's identity.

chain.observation: Kinloch was forcibly removed from murder scene and hidden in a remote village, but his dialect and knowledge of London public gardens revealed his location and confirmed the woman's involvement.
chain.correction: Kinloch was taken to remote village to hide him.
chain.effect: Kinloch's location discovered through dialect and local names.
required_evidence: Mrs. Spedding's gossip about local names and the woman who visited Kinloch in the public garden.
Kinloch's recognition of dialect words and place names, confirming his identity and location.

herrings.description: Dick Hollins, a blind man reading in Enderby Gardens, was suspected to be Kinloch but was an impostor.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Dick Hollins was thought to be the blind man involved in the case.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Dick Hollins was a genuine blind man unrelated to the murder or Kinloch.

herrings.description: Lady Wye's fainting and emotional breakdown suggested guilt or involvement in the murder.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Her behavior indicated she might be hiding something or involved.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Her distress was due to fear and protective feelings for Kinloch and the situation, not guilt.

supporting_points: Walking-stick found at the scene matched Kinloch's.
Bloodstains and fingerprints could be attributed to Kinloch.
Kinloch was present at the murder scene and fled.
Kinloch had no alibi and was found in suspicious circumstances.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Kinloch was blind and incapable of the expert stabbing; the walking-stick belonged to him and not the murderer.

items.false_assumption: The deaths of police officers at the tower were caused by Prince Michael's violent escape.

chain.observation: The statue of Britannia was found toppled with a body beneath it.
chain.correction: The body was placed there after death; the statue fell after the murder.
chain.effect: The death was staged to look like an accident.
required_evidence: Pools of blood around the statue and body
Doctor Prince's wound analysis of the throat cut

chain.observation: Two swords of identical pattern were present at the scene.
chain.correction: One sword was used in the duel; the other was a duplicate brought by Horne Fisher.
chain.effect: The murder weapon was not unique, complicating identification.
required_evidence: Description of swords with wavy edges and jeweled hilts
Horne Fisher's admission of bringing duplicate swords

chain.observation: Horne Hewitt's coat was removed before death.
chain.correction: He removed it himself to prepare for the duel.
chain.effect: Explains how the murderer could remove the coat without suspicion.
required_evidence: Absence of struggle signs on the coat
Coat found folded on the garden bench before the duel

chain.observation: Sir Henry Harland Fisher was found in captivity in a locked room.
chain.correction: He was captured by his brother Horne Fisher after the murder.
chain.effect: Reveals the family betrayal and motive.
required_evidence: Description of locked room with iron grating
Horne Fisher's testimony about captivity

chain.observation: Lord Bulmer disappeared after a cry was heard at daybreak.
chain.correction: He was murdered on the ice by a deliberate crack and sabotage.
chain.effect: The disappearance was a murder disguised as an accident.
required_evidence: Description of cracked ice and thawing
Witness statements about Bulmer's last movements

chain.observation: Prince Michael was accused of killing police officers at the tower.
chain.correction: Police officer Wilson killed his comrades to remove obstacles to promotion.
chain.effect: Prince Michael was innocent of the murders.
required_evidence: Wilson's firing pattern and revolver charges
Nolan's dying gesture identifying Wilson

chain.observation: The relic St. Paul's Penny was stolen from a locked glass case.
chain.correction: It was removed using a magnet on a string through a hole in the floor.
chain.effect: The theft was a clever mechanical trick, not a supernatural event.
required_evidence: Description of broken wire and hole in floor
Mesmerist's trance observations

herrings.description: Prince Michael's supposed violent escape and killing of police officers.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The murders were actually committed by police officer Wilson, who killed his comrades for personal gain.

herrings.description: Leonard Crane's quarrel with Lord Bulmer and disappearance raised suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Crane did not kill Bulmer; Bulmer disappeared mysteriously and was later found dead due to other causes.

supporting_points: Hugo was a discharged bodyguard with a grudge against Sir Isaac Hook.
Hugo was seen near the scene and had a threatening letter found.
The police arrested Hugo based on circumstantial evidence.
Hugo had a motive of revenge and was a fugitive.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Hugo was not present at the time of the murder and had an alibi; the real murder occurred earlier and was staged.

items.false_assumption: Bob Maillard was the Midnight Masquer and accidentally killed his father.

chain.observation: Bob Maillard was found changing out of the aviator's costume shortly after the murder.
chain.correction: He was not the original Midnight Masquer; the costume was stolen from Gramont's car.
chain.effect: Bob's guilt as the bandit and murderer is questioned.
required_evidence: The aviator costume found in Ben Chacherre's possession
Witness statement of Bob changing costume after the murder

chain.observation: Ben Chacherre was found with the stolen loot and the aviator's costume.
chain.correction: Chacherre was acting under orders from Jachin Fell and committed the murder.
chain.effect: Chacherre is identified as the murderer, not Bob Maillard.
required_evidence: Bloodied knife with Chacherre's name
A telegram sent by Chacherre instructing an associate to destroy evidence

chain.observation: Oil seepage was found on Lucie Ledanois' land.
chain.correction: The oil seepage was planted by Jachin Fell to inflate land value.
chain.effect: The oil discovery is a fraud to manipulate the oil company deal.
required_evidence: Lease option on adjoining land
Statement by Jachin Fell admitting planting oil seepage

chain.observation: Jachin Fell is a respected lawyer and chess master.
chain.correction: He is the head of the criminal gang and lottery operation.
chain.effect: Fell's public persona conceals his criminal mastermind role.
required_evidence: Gang members' testimony
Evidence of lottery operations and stolen cars at Gumberts' place

chain.observation: Gramont was the original Midnight Masquer.
chain.correction: He acted to expose the gang and protect Lucie Ledanois.
chain.effect: Gramont is innocent and a key investigator.
required_evidence: Gramont's commission from the governor
A telegram sent by Gramont instructing his associate to meet at Houma

chain.observation: Jachin Fell's influence prevents his arrest by local police.
chain.correction: He is a secret special agent of the Department of Justice.
chain.effect: Fell's criminal activities are part of a covert government operation.
required_evidence: Fell's claim of being a special agent
Federal agents' refusal to arrest Fell

chain.observation: Ben Chacherre tries to frame Hammond for murder.
chain.correction: Chacherre is the real murderer; Hammond is innocent.
chain.effect: Hammond's arrest is a frame-up by the gang.
required_evidence: Hammond's knife without blood
A destroyed bundle of evidence found in Chacherre's associate's possession

herrings.description: Henry Gramont was suspected to be the Midnight Masquer and possibly involved in the crimes.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His possession of the aviator costume and involvement in the robberies.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Gramont was the original Midnight Masquer acting to expose the criminal gang and protect Lucie Ledanois.

herrings.description: Ben Chacherre was initially suspected of stealing the loot and being involved in the murder.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Found with stolen loot and implicated by fingerprint evidence.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Chacherre was the murderer but acted under Fell's orders; his arrest was part of the larger plan to dismantle the gang.

supporting_points: Found changing out of the aviator's costume shortly after the murder.
Known for drunkenness and wild behavior.
Circumstantial evidence linking him to the crime scene.
His story about the murder was weak and inconsistent.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He had no motive to kill his father and was not the original Midnight Masquer; the real murderer was Ben Chacherre.

items.false_assumption: Mrs. Braxfield saw John Harborough near Markenmore Hollow from her bedroom window at the time of the murder.

chain.observation: Mrs. Braxfield testified seeing John Harborough near Markenmore Hollow from her bedroom window
chain.correction: Physical geography and witness testimony show she could not see that spot from her window but from a spinney nearby
chain.effect: Mrs. Braxfield’s testimony about seeing Harborough is unreliable and may confuse suspect identity
required_evidence: Ordnance Map showing Woodland Cottage and Markenmore Hollow with intervening hill
Mrs. Braxfield’s inquest testimony and later police interview

chain.observation: An automatic pistol was found in a badger hole near Deep Lane
chain.correction: The pistol was identified as sold to Harry Markenmore but was used by Mrs. Braxfield to scare foxes and later discarded
chain.effect: Suspicion on Mrs. Braxfield for murder based on pistol possession is weakened
required_evidence: Gunsmith’s sales record of pistol to Harry Markenmore
Mrs. Braxfield’s admission and police interview

chain.observation: Guy Markenmore had three thousand pounds in cash and secret formula papers on him the night before murder
chain.correction: The secret formula was highly valuable and motive for murder was to obtain it along with the money
chain.effect: Murder motive shifts from simple robbery or family jealousy to acquisition of valuable trade secret
required_evidence: Testimony of Eustace Spindler about formula and price
Professor Sir Thomas Hodges-Wilkins expert opinion letter

chain.observation: Two men were with Guy Markenmore at the Sceptre Inn late Monday night
chain.correction: One was Edward Lansbury, the other Baron von Eckhardstein, neither suspected of murder
chain.effect: Focus shifts away from these men as culprits
required_evidence: Testimony of Charles Grimsdale, landlord of Sceptre Inn
Edward Lansbury’s and Baron von Eckhardstein’s accounts

chain.observation: John Harborough had threatened to kill Guy Markenmore years ago
chain.correction: Harborough’s anger had cooled and he had an alibi at time of murder
chain.effect: Harborough is cleared as suspect
required_evidence: Harborough’s testimony at inquest
Witness Elizabeth Braxfield’s statement of seeing Harborough at 4:10 am

chain.observation: Jim Roper threatened Guy Markenmore and had motive for revenge
chain.correction: Roper denies involvement and is unlikely to conceal a successful revenge
chain.effect: Roper is considered innocent but possibly knowledgeable
required_evidence: Daffy Halliwell’s testimony about Roper
Roper’s own statements to Blick and Professor

chain.observation: Mr. Carter was seen with Guy Markenmore and later died from a fall
chain.correction: Carter was the murderer who killed Markenmore for formula and money and died accidentally while evading capture
chain.effect: Carter identified as the true culprit
required_evidence: Discovery of Carter’s body with formula and money
Professor Sir Thomas Hodges-Wilkins and Blick’s analysis

herrings.description: Mrs. Braxfield’s use of an automatic pistol to scare foxes near Markenmore Hollow suggested she could have used it to kill Guy Markenmore.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She used the pistol only to scare foxes and threw it away after the murder out of nervousness.

herrings.description: John Harborough was accused by Mrs. Tretheroe of murdering Guy Markenmore out of jealousy, supported by a threatening letter he wrote years earlier.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Harborough had an alibi and denied seeing Guy Markenmore at the time of the murder; he had lost his anger years before.

supporting_points: She was seen near Markenmore Hollow early morning
She admitted to using an automatic pistol to scare foxes
The automatic pistol found near the murder scene was identified as hers
She was highly ambitious for her daughter to become Lady Markenmore
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Mrs. Braxfield had no motive to murder and denied firing the pistol at the victim; evidence showed she was not at the murder scene at the time of death.

items.false_assumption: Gilbert Standerton is the criminal burglar stealing jewels for personal profit.

chain.observation: Gilbert is seen with the stolen necklace in his pocket and is suspected of being the burglar.
chain.correction: Gilbert claims he found it and intends to return it, and suggests a reenactment could recreate the scenario to observe whether he could have taken it silently.
chain.effect: Suspicion arises but motive is unclear; the possibility to recreate and observe the scenario is considered.
required_evidence: The necklace found in Gilbert's pocket under electric light, as observed by Edith
Gilbert's calm explanation to Edith about finding the necklace and his willingness to recreate the scenario

chain.observation: George Wallis is under constant police surveillance and has alibis, but the police cannot observe whether he is the legitimate suspect or a double.
chain.correction: Wallis uses a double disguised as a chauffeur to mislead police, silently removing himself from suspicion.
chain.effect: Wallis's movements are deceptive, complicating police tracking and removing legitimate suspicion from himself.
required_evidence: Inspector Goldberg's observation of Wallis's flat and chauffeur, noting the possibility to observe silently from the street
The discovery of the disguised double at Wallis's residence, which removes suspicion from Wallis at key times

chain.observation: A mysterious masked man interrupts the gang during a burglary, and the gang cannot determine whether he is a suspect or a legitimate rival.
chain.correction: The masked man is Gilbert, observing and later robbing the gang, recreating the scenario of a burglary within a burglary.
chain.effect: Gilbert is revealed as the intruder disrupting the gang, and the scenario can be recreated to observe his actions silently.
required_evidence: Description of the masked man holding a revolver during the safecracking, as observed by the gang
Gilbert's admission of watching the gang and taking money, which can be tested by reenactment

chain.observation: The 'Melody in F' played by a violinist triggers Gilbert's distress, and the police observe his behavior silently.
chain.correction: The melody is linked to a cancer diagnosis message sent wrongly, removing suspicion from Gilbert's legitimate actions.
chain.effect: Gilbert's change in behavior is explained by health fears, and the police can observe whether his actions are legitimate or not.
required_evidence: Doctor Barclay-Seymour's story of the wrong card sent with 'Melody in F', as observed by Edith
May Wing's testimony about the letter and playing the melody, which can be observed in the household

chain.observation: Gilbert resigns from the Foreign Office and takes up stock trading, and the police observe whether his financial activities are legitimate or suspect.
chain.correction: He uses stock trading to launder and increase stolen money, but the transactions are legitimate and can be observed in records.
chain.effect: Gilbert's financial activities support his secret mission, and the legitimacy can be tested by observing records.
required_evidence: Gilbert's discussions with Leslie Frankfort about investments, as observed in the office
Broker Warrell's statements about Gilbert's stock transactions, which can be observed in financial records

chain.observation: The gang's safe agency sells safes with keys allowing access, and the police consider whether this scenario can be recreated to observe how the safes are accessed silently.
chain.correction: The gang uses this to access clients' valuables for theft, and the scenario can be recreated to test whether the keys and combination allow silent entry.
chain.effect: The safe agency is a front for burglaries, and the reenactment can observe whether the suspect can remove items silently and legitimately.
required_evidence: Wallis's explanation of the safe agency scheme to Gilbert, which can be observed in the agency office
Gilbert's purchase and inspection of a safe at the agency, recreating the scenario and observing the process

chain.observation: Gilbert is locked in the gang's safe room for 48 hours, and the police observe whether he can remove himself or items silently and legitimately.
chain.correction: Wallis intends to rob Gilbert but is unaware of his true role; the scenario can be recreated to observe whether Gilbert can remove items without detection.
chain.effect: The confrontation reveals Gilbert's knowledge and intentions, and the reenactment can observe whether the removal of items is possible silently and legitimately.
required_evidence: Wallis locking Gilbert in the safe room and providing food, as observed by the gang
Gilbert's calm demeanor and explanation during captivity, which can be observed and tested by recreating the scenario

herrings.description: Mrs. Cathcart's financial losses and secret deposit of the necklace suggest possible involvement in theft.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She deposited the necklace as security and was unaware of the burglary; her financial troubles are unrelated to the crime.

herrings.description: Presence of a mysterious fourth man at the bank robbery suggests a second independent criminal.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The fourth man was a bystander who helped the bound guard and was not involved in the robbery.

supporting_points: He possesses the stolen necklace found in his pocket.
He is absent from home during the times of burglaries.
He has financial motives due to disinheritance and debts.
His behavior is secretive and nervous.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Gilbert's actions are aimed at recovering stolen goods and not personal enrichment; he does not fence stolen items but invests legitimately.

items.false_assumption: Fitzroy Simpson was the murderer who kidnapped the horse and killed Straker.

chain.observation: Stable-boy's curried mutton contained powdered opium, which was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy.
chain.correction: Opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy.
chain.effect: Eliminates Simpson as the drugger since he could not have added opium unnoticed.
required_evidence: Chemical analysis report of curried mutton showing presence of powdered opium
Stable-boy Ned Hunter's testimony about supper and timeline of when the dish was set aside

chain.observation: The dog did not bark during the night despite intruder presence.
chain.correction: The intruder was known to the dog.
chain.effect: Suggests the intruder was someone familiar, likely Straker himself.
required_evidence: Stable-boy's account of the intruder and the dog's behavior
Dog's behavior report from the night of the murder

chain.observation: Straker held a delicate cataract knife with blood stains, a tool used for surgical procedures.
chain.correction: Knife was used for a precise operation, not as a weapon.
chain.effect: Indicates Straker intended to perform a surgical act on the horse.
required_evidence: Examination of the knife revealing it is a cataract knife suitable for surgically nicking a tendon
Holmes's knowledge of surgical instruments and their typical uses

chain.observation: Straker's pockets contained a milliner's account addressed to William Derbyshire, revealing his secret life and debts.
chain.correction: Straker was leading a double life under an alias.
chain.effect: Provides motive for Straker to sabotage the horse to cover debts.
required_evidence: Milliner's account addressed to William Derbyshire found in Straker's pocket
Mrs. Straker's testimony about Derbyshire and Straker's financial situation

chain.observation: Horse tracks and square-toed boot prints were found leading to and from Mapleton stables, and Silas Brown was seen attempting to cover up the tracks.
chain.correction: Horse was hidden at Mapleton by Silas Brown, who attempted to conceal the evidence.
chain.effect: Locates missing horse and implicates Brown in concealment and attempted deception.
required_evidence: Horse track impressions and square-toed boot prints leading to Mapleton stables
Observation of Silas Brown attempting to cover the tracks and acting nervously

chain.observation: Silas Brown's demeanor changed after Holmes confronted him, and he was caught in an attempt to mislead Holmes about the horse's whereabouts.
chain.correction: Brown admitted to hiding Silver Blaze to protect himself and profit from the situation.
chain.effect: Confirms Brown's guilt in horse concealment and attempted deception for financial gain.
required_evidence: Holmes's interrogation notes describing Brown's nervousness and attempt to mislead
Observation of Brown's attempt to keep Silver Blaze hidden and his blaze of panic when discovered

chain.observation: Straker's head wound was consistent with a horse's hoof strike, and the wound on his thigh was surgically inflicted during his attempt to sabotage Silver Blaze.
chain.correction: Straker was killed accidentally by the horse during his sabotage attempt, which involved a surgical nick to the tendon.
chain.effect: Reveals true cause of death and exonerates Simpson; the blaze of panic in the horse led to Straker's fatal injury.
required_evidence: Medical examination of Straker's wounds showing hoof-shaped head injury and surgically inflicted thigh wound
Holmes's reconstruction of events, including the attempt to surgically nick the tendon and the horse's blaze of panic

herrings.description: Fitzroy Simpson, the gambler, was suspected due to his presence near the scene and betting against Silver Blaze.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Simpson was merely seeking information and had no involvement in the murder or horse disappearance.

herrings.description: Gypsies camped nearby were suspected of kidnapping Silver Blaze.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Gypsies fled the area before the crime and had no motive or opportunity to steal such a valuable horse.

supporting_points: Found near the murder scene with the victim's cravat in his hand.
Had a heavy stick similar to the murder weapon.
Had bet heavily against Silver Blaze, providing a motive.
His wet clothing indicated presence during the stormy night.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No wound was found on Simpson, and the knife wound on Straker was likely self-inflicted during his fall.

items.false_assumption: Anne Meredith was the murderer based on her fingerprints and hair on the victim.

chain.observation: Hair found on victim's jacket was chestnut but Fernando claimed white
chain.correction: Fernando lied to protect Anne
chain.effect: Discredits Fernando's testimony and raises suspicion on Armstrong
required_evidence: Inspector Mitchell's statement about chestnut hair wound around button
Physical sample of chestnut hair from victim's jacket, preserved in evidence envelope

chain.observation: Missing prenuptial agreement and codicil documents
chain.correction: Mrs. Meredith took the documents secretly
chain.effect: Shifts suspicion from Anne to Mrs. Meredith
required_evidence: Inventory sheet with notation of prenuptial agreement and codicil last seen on Meredith's bed
Hollister's testimony about documents last seen on bed

chain.observation: Murder weapon found in wrong fern box
chain.correction: Weapon was thrown into a different box than expected
chain.effect: Invalidates Anne's theory of suicide
required_evidence: Inspector Mitchell's reenactment of knife drop
Location of scalpel in fern box

chain.observation: Mrs. Hull confessed to stabbing Meredith
chain.correction: Wound was superficial and non-fatal
chain.effect: Indicates another person inflicted fatal wound
required_evidence: Post-mortem examination report
Curtis' testimony on wound depth

chain.observation: Armstrong absent during murder time but returned later
chain.correction: Armstrong had opportunity to commit murder after returning
chain.effect: Establishes Armstrong's opportunity and motive
required_evidence: Hollister's testimony on Armstrong's departure and return
Armstrong's note excusing absence from inquest

chain.observation: Monkey's paw severed and used to send message
chain.correction: Armstrong used monkey to test if Curtis was awake
chain.effect: Links Armstrong to attempted burglary and murder
required_evidence: Sergeant Brown's testimony on monkey's injury
Curtis' testimony on monkey's visit

chain.observation: Duplicate Yale key found in safe deposit box and on Anne's chain
chain.correction: Key opens secret compartment with money and documents
chain.effect: Connects Anne and Meredith's secret assets
required_evidence: Curtis' discovery of secret compartment
Hollister and Mitchell's search for lock matching key

herrings.description: The parrot repeatedly cries 'Anne—I’ve caught you—you devil!' seeming to implicate Anne Meredith.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The parrot was chloroformed and its cries were a repetition of the victim's last words, not a true accusation.

herrings.description: The disappearance of the prenuptial agreement and codicil suggested Anne Meredith stole them to secure inheritance.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mrs. Meredith secretly took the documents to protect Anne's interests.

supporting_points: Fingerprints found on the murder weapon
Hair matching Anne's found on the victim's jacket
Witnesses overheard threatening conversations involving Anne
The parrot's repeated phrase implicating Anne
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The evidence was circumstantial and manipulated; the hair color was inconsistent and the actual fatal wound was inflicted by another person.

items.false_assumption: Langton Hyde was the murderer who killed Ashton for robbery.

chain.observation: Hyde was seen fleeing the passage with a ring
chain.correction: Hyde only picked up the ring after the murder
chain.effect: Hyde is likely innocent of murder
required_evidence: Viner's witness statement of seeing Hyde flee
Hyde's testimony at magistrate's court

chain.observation: Valuables found in shed where Hyde stayed
chain.correction: Valuables were planted to frame Hyde
chain.effect: Real murderer is someone else
required_evidence: Papers with chemical smell wrapping found in shed
Hyde's lack of money and starvation

chain.observation: Claimant produces documents proving identity
chain.correction: Documents were stolen from Ashton and used in conspiracy
chain.effect: Claimant is a cat's-paw
required_evidence: Methley and Woodlesford's solicitor testimony
Mr. Cave's inconsistent story and missing finger

chain.observation: Miss Penkridge identifies typewriter and stationery clues
chain.correction: Dr. Cortelyon owns the defective typewriter and stationery
chain.effect: Cortelyon is linked to forged documents and conspiracy
required_evidence: Bigglesforth's testimony about Cortelyon's stationery and typewriter
Typewritten letter with defective letter 'o'

chain.observation: Mrs. Killenhall cashed a check for ten thousand pounds
chain.correction: She defrauded Miss Wickham using a blank check
chain.effect: Mrs. Killenhall is involved in criminal conspiracy
required_evidence: Bank manager's statement of check cashing
Miss Wickham's testimony about usual check amounts

chain.observation: Dr. Cortelyon found with stolen diamond, ring, and papers; evidence of secret motive, greed, and conspiracy for wealth
chain.correction: He is the murderer and mastermind, motivated by greed for secret papers and wealth
chain.effect: Cortelyon is the true culprit
required_evidence: Police seizure of items from Cortelyon's possession
Letters and documents showing Cortelyon's secret motive, greed, and desire for wealth

chain.observation: Claimant's missing finger was recently amputated
chain.correction: Finger removal was a deliberate attempt to imitate real Lord Marketstoke
chain.effect: Claimant is an impostor
required_evidence: Portlethwaite's medical observation of finger scar
Historical record of Lord Marketstoke's missing finger

herrings.description: Hyde's attempt to pawn a diamond ring taken from the victim was used as evidence of guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Hyde was starving and desperate, unaware of the ring's true value and innocence of the murder.

herrings.description: A man claiming to be the missing Lord Marketstoke appeared with documents stolen from Ashton, confusing the inheritance issue.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The claimant was a cat's-paw used by the real murderer to mislead the investigation.

supporting_points: Seen running away from the murder scene
Found with one of Ashton's diamond rings
Possessed a knife similar to the murder weapon
Confessed to picking up the ring near the body
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Hyde had no motive to kill and was starving, making it unlikely he committed the murder; planted evidence was used to implicate him.

items.false_assumption: Stephen Aylmore murdered John Marbury to silence him.

chain.observation: Scrap of grey paper with Ronald Breton's name found on victim
chain.correction: Victim was seeking legal advice from Breton
chain.effect: Links victim to Breton and legal circles
required_evidence: Scrap of grey paper found in victim's waistcoat pocket
Witness testimony of Breton not recognizing victim

chain.observation: Victim identified as John Marbury, but no papers found
chain.correction: Victim's real identity is John Maitland, ex-convict
chain.effect: Reveals victim's criminal past and motive for murder
required_evidence: Market Milcaster newspaper report on John Maitland's trial
Silver ticket linked to Maitland's family

chain.observation: Stephen Aylmore arrested due to possession of murder weapon
chain.correction: Weapon was stolen and planted to frame Aylmore
chain.effect: Aylmore is innocent of murder
required_evidence: Murder weapon found in sewer trap
Testimony of woman who recognized weapon from Aylmore's chambers

chain.observation: Elphick and Cardlestone flee and destroy papers
chain.correction: They are involved in conspiracy and cover-up
chain.effect: They are prime suspects in murder and conspiracy
required_evidence: Burned papers and chaotic chambers found after their flight
Porter testimony of their early morning departure

chain.observation: Rare Australian stamps found in Cardlestone's chambers
chain.correction: Victim had been at Cardlestone's chambers before murder
chain.effect: Places victim at scene with suspects
required_evidence: Testimony of stamp dealer Criedir
Stamps found by Spargo in Cardlestone's rooms

chain.observation: Myerst claims knowledge but denies murder
chain.correction: Myerst involved in blackmail and conspiracy but not murder
chain.effect: Separates Myerst's role from actual murder
required_evidence: Myerst's possession of cheques and securities
Cheques and securities found in Myerst's safe deposit box

chain.observation: Victim found murdered at foot of Cardlestone's stairs
chain.correction: Murder committed by Cardlestone or with his knowledge
chain.effect: Identifies true murderers
required_evidence: Myerst's testimony about finding the body
Evidence of victim's valuables in Cardlestone's possession

herrings.description: Stephen Aylmore is arrested and suspected due to his criminal past and possession of the murder weapon.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Aylmore was innocent and was framed by the real culprits; the murder weapon was stolen from his chambers.

herrings.description: The victim's identity as John Marbury misleads investigators about his past and connections.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The victim was actually John Maitland, an ex-convict with a complex history unrelated to the immediate suspects.

supporting_points: Murder weapon found in his chambers with victim's hair and blood
His identity as an ex-convict was revealed, suggesting motive
He was last seen with the victim before the murder
He refused to fully disclose his past, arousing suspicion
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Lack of direct evidence linking him to the murder and his eventual exoneration

items.false_assumption: The locked study room and missing weapon prove that John Waring was murdered.

chain.observation: The study door was locked from the inside with no secret passage found.
chain.correction: Waring locked the door himself after the fatal act.
chain.effect: Eliminates possibility of murderer entering or leaving after the stabbing.
required_evidence: Photographs of the study showing no secret exits
Statements from Mrs. Peyton and Ito about door locking

chain.observation: No murder weapon was found despite a stab wound.
chain.correction: The weapon was an icicle that melted in the wound.
chain.effect: Explains absence of weapon and supports suicide theory.
required_evidence: Nogi's testimony about Waring opening the window
Photograph of icicles on the window with one missing

chain.observation: Anita Austin possessed Waring's money and ruby pin.
chain.correction: Waring gave these to Anita as gifts during her visit.
chain.effect: Removes motive of theft or murder from Anita.
required_evidence: Anita's testimony about receiving gifts
Check stub for $10,000 dated on day of death

chain.observation: Fingerprints and dress button imprints found on chair in study.
chain.correction: Anita visited the study and sat in the chair before the death.
chain.effect: Confirms Anita's presence but not guilt.
required_evidence: Fingerprint analysis report
Helen Peyton's testimony about dress button pattern

chain.observation: Nogi disappeared after the death. The Japanese servant was last seen moving quickly through the house, and his movement included taking the water tray from the study.
chain.correction: Nogi fled in fear after witnessing the death, not as a murderer.
chain.effect: Removes Nogi as a suspect.
required_evidence: Saltonstall Adams' witness statement of Nogi leaving on milk train
Nogi's own testimony after being found, describing his movement and actions as a Japanese servant on the night of the death

chain.observation: Lockwood smoothed the chair back after body was found.
chain.correction: Lockwood erased incriminating marks to protect Anita.
chain.effect: Shows Lockwood's loyalty, not guilt.
required_evidence: Ito and Mrs. Peyton's witness statements
Lockwood's own admission and behavior

chain.observation: A red circular mark was found on Waring's forehead.
chain.correction: Waring rested his head on the telephone transmitter before death.
chain.effect: Explains the mark as accidental, not a sign of murder.
required_evidence: Medical Examiner's report on mark
Fibsy's observation of red ring on his own forehead

herrings.description: Nogi, the Japanese servant, disappears after the death, suggesting guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Nogi fled in fear after witnessing Waring's sudden death and had no involvement in the crime.

herrings.description: Lockwood's smoothing of the chair and possession of a penholder matching the wound size raise suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Lockwood was erasing accidental evidence to protect Anita and had no motive or opportunity to commit murder.

supporting_points: She was seen entering and leaving the study on the night of the death.
She possessed the missing money and ruby pin.
Her fingerprints and dress button imprints were found on the chair in the study.
She had a mysterious background and contradictory statements.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The physical impossibility of entering or leaving the locked study without detection and the absence of a murder weapon.

items.false_assumption: The second will was genuine and executed by Jeffrey Blackmore himself in the presence of witnesses.

chain.observation: The cuneiform inscription photograph was hung upside down in Jeffrey Blackmore's chambers.
chain.correction: The tenant of the chambers was not Jeffrey Blackmore but an impersonator.
chain.effect: Raises suspicion that the will signed there may be forged.
required_evidence: Photograph of the cuneiform inscription in the chambers
Testimony of Stephen Blackmore about his uncle's expertise

chain.observation: The patient Mr. Graves had symptoms of morphine poisoning and a tremulous iris in the right eye.
chain.correction: Mr. Graves is identified as Jeffrey Blackmore, who was secretly confined and poisoned.
chain.effect: Establishes identity of victim and suggests foul play.
required_evidence: Medical examination notes by Dr. Jervis
Optician's and oculist's letters describing Jeffrey's spectacles and eye condition

chain.observation: The signatures on cheques and wills show abrupt changes but consistent personal character.
chain.correction: The changes correspond to intermittent opium use and possible forgery by a relative.
chain.effect: Supports theory of impersonation and forgery by John Blackmore.
required_evidence: Photographs of signatures
Expert opinion by bank partner Mr. Britton

chain.observation: Pieces of peculiar spectacles and Japanese brush found in New Inn chambers.
chain.correction: These items link John Blackmore (tenant of New Inn) and Mr. Weiss (disguised identity).
chain.effect: Supports that Weiss and John Blackmore are the same person.
required_evidence: Fragments of spectacles recovered from New Inn
Description of Mr. Weiss's spectacles by Dr. Jervis

chain.observation: Cabman Wilkins testifies to a man and woman arriving at New Inn on the night of Jeffrey's death.
chain.correction: The woman was Jeffrey Blackmore disguised, the man was John Blackmore impersonating Jeffrey.
chain.effect: Explains presence of two persons and supports impersonation theory.
required_evidence: Signed statement of cabman Samuel Wilkins
Description of the woman and man by Wilkins

chain.observation: Dr. Jervis recreated the carriage journey using compass and timing notes, recording each turn and stop in his notebook.
chain.correction: The compass bearings and timings allowed the precise location of the secret house to be plotted on a map.
chain.effect: Enables the investigators to find where Jeffrey Blackmore was imprisoned and poisoned.
required_evidence: Notebook with compass bearings and timings from the carriage journey
Map showing the plotted route and final location of the house

chain.observation: Lump of sugar in tea contained aconitine poison.
chain.correction: Mrs. Schallibaum attempted to poison Dr. Jervis to prevent investigation.
chain.effect: Confirms active criminal intent and danger to investigators.
required_evidence: Chemical analysis of lump of sugar
Observation of Mrs. Schallibaum's behavior in tea shop

herrings.description: Mrs. Schallibaum's controllable squint suggested she was disguising her identity.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Her squint was a natural condition she could control voluntarily.

herrings.description: The patient's symptoms were initially suspected to be sleeping sickness.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The symptoms were actually due to morphine poisoning, not sleeping sickness.

supporting_points: He was the main beneficiary under the first will
He was present in London at the time of the death
He had a motive to inherit quickly
He was mentioned in connection with the will's execution
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He had no access to the secret house or opportunity to administer poison, and the evidence of impersonation and carriage journeys points elsewhere.

items.false_assumption: Brian Fitzgerald was the man who got into the cab with Oliver Whyte and murdered him.

chain.observation: Cabman Royston identified the man in the light coat as Brian Fitzgerald.
chain.correction: Royston was intoxicated and only saw partial features; the man was actually Roger Moreland impersonating Fitzgerald.
chain.effect: Initial suspicion on Fitzgerald was misplaced.
required_evidence: Testimony of Sal Rawlins about meeting Fitzgerald at the slum
Appearance and behavior of the man in the cab as described by multiple witnesses

chain.observation: Fitzgerald was seen entering his lodgings at Powlett Street shortly before 2 am.
chain.correction: The kitchen clock was 10 minutes fast; corrected time shows Fitzgerald was home before the murder occurred.
chain.effect: Fitzgerald's alibi is confirmed.
required_evidence: Testimony of Mrs. Sampson about the kitchen clock
Watchmaker Dendy's testimony about correcting the clock

chain.observation: A diamond ring was seen on the man who left the cab at Powlett Street.
chain.correction: Fitzgerald never wore rings; Moreland wore a ring on the forefinger of the right hand.
chain.effect: Evidence points away from Fitzgerald and towards Moreland.
required_evidence: Testimony of cabman Rankin about the ring
Testimony of Felix Rolleston about Fitzgerald's dislike of rings

chain.observation: Whyte was murdered for valuable papers he carried.
chain.correction: The papers were the secret marriage certificate of Frettlby and Rosanna Moore.
chain.effect: Motive for murder is to protect Frettlby's secret.
required_evidence: Marriage certificate found in Whyte's secret pocket
Testimony of Sal Rawlins about the papers

chain.observation: Mother Guttersnipe claimed to be Rosanna Moore's mother and Sal Rawlins' grandmother.
chain.correction: Her testimony is partially unreliable due to drunkenness and malice.
chain.effect: Some details need corroboration.
required_evidence: Testimony of Sal Rawlins
Medical testimony about Mother Guttersnipe's condition

chain.observation: Moreland claimed innocence and gave conflicting stories.
chain.correction: Moreland confessed to the murder after arrest.
chain.effect: True murderer identified.
required_evidence: Discovery of Whyte's coat in Fitzroy Gardens
Purchase record of chloroform by Whyte

chain.observation: Frettby died suddenly after a mysterious visit from Moreland.
chain.correction: Frettby's death was caused by heart disease exacerbated by shock from exposure of his secret.
chain.effect: Frettby's guilt and secret marriage revealed posthumously.
required_evidence: Medical testimony of Dr. Chinston
Marriage certificate found in Whyte's secret pocket

herrings.description: Roger Moreland was suspected due to his suspicious behavior and possession of Whyte's coat.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Moreland was actually the murderer, so suspicion was correct but incomplete without Frettlby's involvement.

herrings.description: Moreland claimed to be a barman and very drunk on the night of the murder to deflect suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Moreland was feigning drunkenness to cover his crime.

supporting_points: Cabman Royston identified him as the man who entered the cab
Fitzgerald had threatened Whyte previously
Fitzgerald was found with Whyte's glove in his coat pocket
Fitzgerald could not initially provide an alibi
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The alibi provided by Sal Rawlins and the discovery of the real murderer Moreland disproved Fitzgerald's guilt.

items.false_assumption: The skeleton found in the city wall is the actual body of Angelina Frood.

chain.observation: Skeleton found buried in city wall with personal effects of Angelina Frood
chain.correction: The skeleton was ancient and purchased, not Angelina's real body
chain.effect: Disproves that Angelina is dead and body in wall is hers
required_evidence: Bill from Oscar Hammerstein for purchase of skeleton dated April 19th
Photographic comparison of Mr. Bundy and Angelina Frood

chain.observation: Mr. Bundy appears as a man with masculine clothing and manner
chain.correction: Mr. Bundy is actually Angelina Frood in disguise
chain.effect: Explains the presence of 'Mr. Bundy' and faked disappearance
required_evidence: Fingerprints on tumbler and bottle matching Angelina Frood
Photographic composites and expert testimony by Dr. Thorndyke

chain.observation: Nicholas Frood is missing and suspected of murder
chain.correction: Nicholas Frood died earlier from cocaine overdose
