chain.effect: Removes Nicholas Frood as suspect in Angelina's disappearance
required_evidence: Identification of Nicholas Frood's body at St. Barnabas hospital
Witness testimony of landlady and Dr. Strangeways

chain.observation: Quicklime burial believed to destroy bodies
chain.correction: Quicklime preserves bodies by drying, not destroying
chain.effect: Skeleton in wall could not be recent and is not Angelina's
required_evidence: Experiments by Mr. A. Lucas and Dr. Thorndyke on quicklime effects
Expert testimony at inquest

chain.observation: Clues found progressively up the river and lane
chain.correction: Clues were deliberately planted to mislead investigators
chain.effect: Supports theory of staged disappearance and deception
required_evidence: Map of find locations from brooch to gate key
Testimony of Sergeant Cobbledick and Dr. Thorndyke

chain.observation: Fingerprints on household objects match Angelina Frood
chain.correction: Confirms that Angelina was present in the house disguised
chain.effect: Supports identity of Mr. Bundy as Angelina Frood
required_evidence: Photographs of fingerprints on tumbler, bottle, and kitchen objects
Expert analysis by Dr. Thorndyke

chain.observation: Mr. Bundy and Angelina Frood never seen together
chain.correction: They are the same person using disguise and deception
chain.effect: Explains how the deception was maintained
required_evidence: Testimony of Dr. Strangeways and photographic evidence
Expert testimony on disguise and personation

herrings.description: A man with a mole on his nose pawned Angelina's brooch, suggesting a suspicious character.
herrings.points_at_suspect: An unknown local man possibly involved in the crime
herrings.innocent_explanation: The man likely found the brooch and pawned it without involvement in the crime.

herrings.description: The disappearance of the gate key to the city wall patch where the skeleton was found.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Someone with access to the wall area, possibly the murderer
herrings.innocent_explanation: The key was lost or taken as a prank and thrown over the fence, unrelated to the crime.

supporting_points: He was known to be violent and addicted to drugs
He was searching for Angelina and had threatened her life
He carried a sheath-knife and had a motive of jealousy
He disappeared suspiciously around the time of Angelina's disappearance
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Nicholas Frood died before Angelina's disappearance and could not have committed the crime.

items.false_assumption: The murderer escaped through a secret passage or trapdoor in the locked room.

chain.observation: The door of The Yellow Room was locked and bolted from inside after the attack. The arrangement of the locks and bolts was carefully watched by the investigators, who trusted the testimony of those present in the apartment.
chain.correction: The murderer was not inside the room when the door was locked.
chain.effect: The attacker must have left before the door was locked.
required_evidence: Testimony of Monsieur Stangerson about door being locked
Physical examination of door and bolt

chain.observation: Footprints of a man with large boots and a handkerchief were found inside and outside the pavilion. The arrangement of the footprints suggested someone tried to mislead the watch kept on the apartment.
chain.correction: The footprints were planted to mislead and frame Daddy Jacques or Darzac.
chain.effect: The real murderer disguised evidence to misdirect suspicion.
required_evidence: Pattern of footprints matching Daddy Jacques’s boots
Handkerchief found in The Yellow Room

chain.observation: Frédéric Larsan appeared drugged and inactive during the night of the attack. Rouletabille arranged for a watch to be kept on Larsan’s apartment, trusting his assistants to observe any suspicious activity.
chain.correction: He feigned being drugged to avoid suspicion and to carry out the attack.
chain.effect: Larsan had opportunity and means to commit the crime.
required_evidence: Observation of Larsan’s behavior and cane
Discovery of eye-glasses in Larsan’s room

chain.observation: Mademoiselle Stangerson was attacked twice and showed signs of struggle and wounds. The arrangement of her apartment and the trust she placed in Darzac complicated the investigation.
chain.correction: The first attack was real; the second was a nightmare causing accidental gunshot.
chain.effect: Some evidence of struggle was misinterpreted as continuous attack.
required_evidence: Blood-stained hair found on overturned table
Bullet lodged in ceiling from accidental discharge

chain.observation: Larsan escaped the locked room and the château without being caught. The arrangement of the ladder and spike outside the apartment was discovered by the watch set on the terrace.
chain.correction: He used a prepared spike and ladder to climb the wall and re-enter through a window.
chain.effect: The escape was physical and planned, not supernatural or via secret passage.
required_evidence: Iron spike fitting hole in terrace cornice
Ladder found resting against terrace

chain.observation: Robert Darzac was absent from the château during attacks and had suspicious footprints. The post office and apartment watch trusted by the investigators confirmed the arrangement of his movements.
chain.correction: An accomplice impersonated Darzac to mislead investigators.
chain.effect: Doubts about Darzac’s guilt arise; he was framed.
required_evidence: Witness statement of railway employee seeing Darzac at station
Post office records of letter collection by lookalike
Trust in the apartment watch's testimony

chain.observation: Mademoiselle Stangerson and Larsan had secret past and connection. The arrangement of her apartment and the trust between her and Darzac was crucial to understanding her silence.
chain.correction: She was married to Larsan (Ballmeyer) and kept this secret to protect Darzac.
chain.effect: Mademoiselle’s silence and actions were motivated by fear and love.
required_evidence: Testimony of Darzac about Mademoiselle’s past
Rouletabille’s investigation in America about Ballmeyer

chain.observation: The apartment was under constant watch, and the arrangement of trusted observers ensured that any attempt to enter or leave would be noticed.
chain.correction: The arrangement of the watch over the apartment was essential to catching the culprit.
chain.effect: The trust placed in the observers and the arrangement of the watch provided the necessary evidence.
required_evidence: Testimony from the trusted watch about movements in and out of the apartment

herrings.description: The concierges were arrested as suspected accomplices due to suspicious behavior and presence near the pavilion at the time of the crime.
herrings.innocent_explanation: They were poaching on the estate and had no involvement in the crime.

herrings.description: The Green Man, the forest-keeper, was suspected after his body was found stabbed near the château.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was the victim of the murderer, killed during the escape attempt.

supporting_points: Footprints matching Darzac’s boots found near the scene
His absence from the château during the attacks
Larsan’s theory and police suspicion
Lack of alibi and silence during interrogation
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The footprints and evidence were manipulated by the real murderer to frame Darzac, who was innocent.

items.false_assumption: The little black book found and recovered early in the investigation was the genuine incriminating evidence.

chain.observation: The body of Antonio Bareda was found dead in a taxi cab with no visible wounds.
chain.correction: De Silva used a hypodermic needle with poison to kill Bareda silently.
chain.effect: The murder method was subtle and left no external marks.
required_evidence: Hypodermic needle found in De Silva's room
Doctor's report on Bareda's body showing no external wounds but symptoms of poisoning

chain.observation: A little black book was recovered but contained only flattering testimonials.
chain.correction: The recovered book was a forged copy; the original was hidden elsewhere.
chain.effect: The evidence initially found was misleading.
required_evidence: Estuban's analysis of the book's contents
De Silva's note about hiding the original book

chain.observation: Francisco de Socotra impersonated Antonio Bareda to mislead political authorities.
chain.correction: De Socotra used the forged book to deceive the President and others.
chain.effect: The political conspiracy involved impersonation and forgery.
required_evidence: Pa Simmons' surveillance report of de Socotra
Greg's observation of de Socotra carrying the forged book

chain.observation: Amy Wilmot was disguised as a boy and communicated secretly with Greg.
chain.correction: Amy was the niece of Bareda and opposed de Socotra's plans.
chain.effect: Amy was a key ally in recovering the evidence and exposing the conspiracy.
required_evidence: Notes exchanged between Amy and Greg
Amy's testimony and actions

chain.observation: De Silva attempted suicide and was found in a distressed state.
chain.correction: De Silva was a remorseful hired assassin who confessed to the murder.
chain.effect: De Silva's mental state confirmed his guilt and the murder method.
required_evidence: Doctor's report on De Silva's condition after suicide attempt
Hypodermic needle found in De Silva's room

chain.observation: De Socotra was confronted and escaped multiple times during the raid.
chain.correction: De Socotra's escape delayed justice but he was ultimately cornered.
chain.effect: The final confrontation was tense and required coordinated effort.
required_evidence: Greg and Estuban's raid reports
Witness accounts of de Socotra's escape

chain.observation: De Socotra died suddenly of heart failure after the confrontation.
chain.correction: De Socotra's death ended the political threat and allowed reform.
chain.effect: The villain's demise resolved the case and restored justice.
required_evidence: Doctor's report on de Socotra's death
Señora de Socotra's statements

herrings.description: Amy's wealthy fiancé who is suspected of betraying her to de Socotra.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His presence with de Socotra and his suspicious behavior suggest possible collusion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He acted out of fear and loyalty to protect Amy and was manipulated by de Socotra.

herrings.description: De Silva's attempted suicide and mysterious behavior cast suspicion on him as a murderer.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His nervousness and presence at key moments suggest guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was a remorseful hired assassin overwhelmed by guilt and fear.

supporting_points: Hickey sold the cab to Greg just before the body was found
He was evasive about the circumstances of the body
His nervous behavior suggested guilt
He disappeared after the murder
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Hickey had no motive or opportunity to commit the murder and was not involved in the political conspiracy

items.false_assumption: Dr. Ransford deliberately murdered John Braden by throwing him from the cathedral gallery.

chain.observation: Varner saw a gentleman's hand throw Braden from the gallery
chain.correction: The hand was likely Braden's own during a struggle or fall
chain.effect: Discredits direct murder accusation against Ransford
required_evidence: Varner's witness statement describing the hand and fall
Physical evidence of the open doorway and absence of other fingerprints or marks at the scene

chain.observation: Collishaw was poisoned by hydrocyanic acid
chain.correction: Poison was administered via a coated pill, not the tin bottle
chain.effect: Points to a medical man with access as the poisoner
required_evidence: Post-mortem report by Dr. Coates and Dr. Everest
Box of pills with Ransford's handwriting

chain.observation: Bryce withdrew fifty pounds in gold shortly before Collishaw's death
chain.correction: The gold was not hush-money but payment for information or other purpose
chain.effect: Bryce's innocence in poisoning is supported; suggests complex motives
required_evidence: Bank withdrawal records
Friendly Society deposit book showing Collishaw's fifty pounds

chain.observation: Braden had no papers on him except a scrap of Latin directions
chain.correction: The directions led to the hiding place of the Saxonsteade jewels
chain.effect: Reveals motive for Braden's visit and murder
required_evidence: Scrap of paper found in Braden's purse
Discovery of jewels buried in Paradise

chain.observation: Wraye and Flood were unknown to the police initially
chain.correction: They were identified as Mr. Folliot and Fladgate, involved in robbery and murder
chain.effect: Identifies true culprits behind the crimes
required_evidence: Glassdale's testimony identifying Wraye and Flood
Physical evidence of Flood's presence in the cathedral gallery at the time of Braden's death (e.g., witness statement or access record)

chain.observation: Ransford was agitated and suspected of murder
chain.correction: Ransford was protecting the children and seeking justice
chain.effect: Exonerates Ransford and clarifies his role
required_evidence: Ransford's testimony and explanation to police
Discovery of the Saxonsteade jewels in Paradise, confirming the real motive for the crimes

chain.observation: Bryce was manipulating suspicions and withholding evidence
chain.correction: Bryce's motives were personal ambition, not murder
chain.effect: Bryce is a schemer but not the murderer
required_evidence: Bryce's interactions with Mary Bewery
Bryce's gold withdrawal and lack of direct involvement in murders

herrings.description: Bryce's manipulations and false accusations against Ransford mislead the investigation.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Bryce acted out of personal ambition and desire to marry Mary, not as the murderer.

herrings.description: Varner's testimony about seeing a gentleman's hand throwing Braden is questioned and doubted.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The hand was likely Braden's own in a struggle or fall, not an assailant's.

supporting_points: Ransford was seen leaving the cathedral porch looking pale and agitated
Rumors and gossip linked him to the victim
He had access to the victim and the crime scenes
He was found in possession of pills linked to the poisoning
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Ransford had no motive to kill and was unaware of the true culprits; the evidence against him was circumstantial and manipulated by Bryce.

items.false_assumption: Van Dusen escaped Cell 13 solely by mental power without any outside assistance.

chain.observation: Van Dusen communicated with outside via linen notes tied to rats
chain.correction: He used a hidden drain pipe to send and receive messages
chain.effect: Established external communication despite prison isolation
required_evidence: Linen notes with money tied sent from Cell 13
Guard's report of rat with linen note outside prison

chain.observation: Gas lights in Henley's apartment went out despite locked doors
chain.correction: Gas jets were extinguished by blowing into gas pipes from adjacent apartment
chain.effect: Explained how gas was put out without physical entry
required_evidence: Loose gas jet tip found in Cabell's apartment
Mirror on flagpole used to watch Henley

chain.observation: Scarlet thread found on flagpole rope
chain.correction: Thread came from Cabell's bath robe worn by the valet
chain.effect: Linked valet Jean to the crime scene
required_evidence: Chemical test matching thread to bath robe
Valet's possession of bath robe with scarlet stripe

chain.observation: Handkerchief with violet perfume found near bank safe
chain.correction: Perfume linked to Louise Clarke, implicating her in the bank robbery
chain.effect: Identified inside accomplice in bank burglary
required_evidence: Perfume odor on handkerchief and on Dunston's handkerchief
Miss Clarke's change from violet to rose perfume

chain.observation: Grace Field disappeared; letter threatening her found
chain.correction: She was held captive by St. George, who attacked Willis
chain.effect: Connected disappearance and attack to St. George
required_evidence: Chloroform odor in studio closet
Blood-stained revolver found with St. George

chain.observation: St. George escaped hospital and was found raving mad
chain.correction: His mental collapse was due to attack and guilt over captivity
chain.effect: Explained his erratic behavior and connection to Grace Field
required_evidence: Hospital records of St. George's condition
Witness accounts of attack on Willis

chain.observation: Valet Jean's sullen and defiant behavior when accused
chain.correction: Physical evidence and witness statements linked Jean to the murder and attempted murder
chain.effect: Confirmed Jean as the culprit in Henley and Regnier cases
required_evidence: Scarlet thread from bath robe found on flagpole and chemical test matching it to Jean's robe
Witness statement describing Jean's actions and presence during the critical times

herrings.description: Cabell's rivalry over Miss Lipscomb and his sudden departure suggest guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Cabell was out of town and his valet was the actual culprit.

herrings.description: Curtis's jealousy and possession of the murder weapon implicate him in Marguerite Melrose's death.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Marguerite Melrose was alive and married to Don MacLean; the murder victim was Elizabeth Dow.

supporting_points: Cabell had a motive due to rivalry over Miss Lipscomb.
He was seen hurriedly packing to leave town after Henley was shot.
The scarlet thread matched his bath robe.
His valet was suspicious and had access.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Cabell was out of town during the critical times and had no opportunity to commit the crimes.

items.false_assumption: Stanley Rees disappeared voluntarily to avoid scandal or personal trouble.

chain.observation: Stanley Rees disappeared mysteriously from his hotel room leaving coat and hat behind
chain.correction: Rees was abducted and brought to Dredlinton House
chain.effect: Rees is a victim, not a voluntary runaway
required_evidence: Statement from hotel manager about Rees' disappearance and the time he was last seen leaving his room without coat or hat
Testimony of Rees' valet about the noise and missing master from the hotel room at the time of disappearance

chain.observation: Phipps and Dredlinton are missing and unaccounted for
chain.correction: They are held captive in Dredlinton House
chain.effect: All three directors are hostages
required_evidence: Servant Grant's testimony about seeing Phipps and Dredlinton inside the locked room during the night
Physical evidence of bindings and gags found in the room where the directors were held

chain.observation: Wingate openly threatens the directors and controls the house
chain.correction: Wingate is the orchestrator of the kidnapping
chain.effect: Wingate is the mastermind behind the blackmail
required_evidence: Servant's statement that Wingate gave all orders to the staff and controlled access to the directors' rooms during the captivity
Telephone records showing Wingate's exclusive use of the house line to communicate with outside parties during the hostage period

chain.observation: A coded cable message reveals a secret shipment of wheat
chain.correction: The shipment will break the wheat corner if shares are sold
chain.effect: The motive for the kidnapping is to force sale of shares
required_evidence: Josephine's reading of the decoded cable message about the Universal Line steamers and wheat cargo
Correspondence showing the shipment details and its impact on the wheat market

chain.observation: The directors refuse to sell wheat at a lower price
chain.correction: They are held hostage and threatened with death
chain.effect: Their compliance is coerced by Wingate
required_evidence: Hostage bindings and threats with pistol as described by the released directors
Telephone orders to Harrison to sell wheat at reduced price, placed from Dredlinton House during captivity

chain.observation: Lord Dredlinton dies suddenly during captivity
chain.correction: Death caused by exhaustion and heart disease exacerbated by stress
chain.effect: The hostage situation has fatal consequences
required_evidence: Doctor's report certifying cause of death as exhaustion and heart disease after examining Dredlinton's body
Observation of Dredlinton's deteriorating condition by the other captives and servants during captivity

chain.observation: After sale orders, the market collapses and wheat prices fall
chain.correction: The blackmail achieves its goal of breaking the corner
chain.effect: Wingate's plan succeeds
required_evidence: Telephone confirmation of sales to Harrison from Dredlinton House during the captivity window
Market price reports showing collapse of wheat prices immediately after the sale

herrings.description: Lord Dredlinton's drunken outbursts and aggressive behavior suggest he might be responsible for Rees' disappearance.
herrings.innocent_explanation: His drunkenness is genuine but he is himself a victim of the kidnapping and blackmail scheme.

herrings.description: Peter Phipps' ruthless market dealings and threats imply he might have orchestrated the disappearance to protect his interests.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Though involved in the scheme, Phipps is coerced and held hostage, not the mastermind.

supporting_points: Wingate is the enemy of the directors and openly threatens them
He is present at many key moments and has access to the house
He shows knowledge of the disappearance and market manipulation
He controls the servants and communications
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Wingate orchestrates the kidnapping but is not the victimizer; the actual blackmail and market manipulation are carried out by the directors themselves under duress.

items.false_assumption: Eileen Quentin is complicit in her husband's criminal activities.

chain.observation: Fingerprints on dispatch-box match Quentin's
chain.correction: Quentin tampered with victim's belongings
chain.effect: Links Quentin to victim and crime scene
required_evidence: Fingerprint analysis of dispatch-box
Quentin's fingerprints from tumbler in his room

chain.observation: Quentin tried to borrow money from Aylmer and Whitefield
chain.correction: Quentin was in financial difficulty and scheming
chain.effect: Motive for crime is financial gain
required_evidence: Quentin's proposals to Aylmer and Whitefield
Whitefield's receipt for loan

chain.observation: Quentin's pillow-case contained rare poison
chain.correction: Poisoning was method of murder
chain.effect: Explains sudden heart disease deaths
required_evidence: Toxicological report from Monsieur Dumont
Analysis of pillow-case from Whitefield's room

chain.observation: Eileen is not legally married to Quentin
chain.correction: Eileen is innocent and a victim
chain.effect: Removes suspicion of her complicity
required_evidence: Marriage records search
Eileen's written statement describing her relationship with Quentin

chain.observation: Quentin and Dicks associate with Ramon, a known criminal
chain.correction: Quentin is part of a criminal gang
chain.effect: Establishes criminal background and network
required_evidence: Duberry and Webber's surveillance reports
Police records on Ramon

chain.observation: Martyn abruptly leaves the group and is evasive
chain.correction: Martyn is not directly involved in murder
chain.effect: Focus shifts to Quentin as culprit
required_evidence: Martyn's statements and movements
Lack of evidence linking Martyn to poisoning

chain.observation: Quentin commits suicide upon arrest
chain.correction: Confession by act of suicide
chain.effect: Confirms guilt and ends investigation
required_evidence: Police report of Quentin's death
Monsieur Paillot's testimony

herrings.description: Martyn's rudeness and secretive meetings with Quentin and Dicks suggest he may be the criminal mastermind.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Martyn is a cynical friend with questionable past but not directly involved in the murder or poisoning.

herrings.description: Eileen's knowledge of Quentin's schemes and her mysterious behavior imply she is complicit in the crimes.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Eileen is a victim of Quentin's deception and unaware of his criminal activities.

supporting_points: Martyn shows hostility and rudeness towards Eileen
He is seen in secretive meetings with Quentin and Dicks
He abruptly leaves the group before the final events
His suspicious behavior suggests possible involvement
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No concrete evidence links Martyn directly to the poisoning or theft; he is more a reluctant associate than mastermind.

items.false_assumption: The thumbprint found in the safe was genuine and conclusively proved Reuben's guilt.

chain.observation: The thumbprint found in the safe was identified as Reuben Hornby's by Scotland Yard experts.
chain.correction: Thorndyke observed the print was larger than genuine prints and had an accidental mark from a loose fibre.
chain.effect: This suggested the print was a photo-mechanical forgery, not a genuine fingerprint.
required_evidence: Photograph of the thumbprint with micrometer scale
Examination of the 'Thumbograph' book containing genuine thumbprints

chain.observation: The blood on the paper was fresh and liquid, producing a clear print.
chain.correction: Medical expert Dr. Rowe testified that fresh blood cannot produce such a clear print without artificial treatment.
chain.effect: The blood was likely defibrinated or chemically treated, indicating artificial preparation for forgery.
required_evidence: Medical testimony on blood clotting and fingerprint clarity
Microscopic examination of blood smears on the paper

chain.observation: The 'Thumbograph' book had disappeared and reappeared mysteriously.
chain.correction: Mrs. Hornby confirmed the book was taken from her writing table and returned during her absence.
chain.effect: Someone had access to the book and could have used it to create the forged print.
required_evidence: Mrs. Hornby's testimony about the disappearance and return of the 'Thumbograph'
Physical custody records of the book

chain.observation: Walter Hornby recently purchased a typewriter and is skilled in photography.
chain.correction: The typewriter used to type a suspicious label was a rare literary model with a unique worn letter 'e' matching Walter's machine.
chain.effect: Walter had the means and skills to produce the forged fingerprint and tampered documents.
required_evidence: Typewritten label with unique typewriter characteristics
Testimony about Walter's typewriter purchase and photographic skills

chain.observation: Fingerprint experts confidently identified the print as genuine.
chain.correction: Thorndyke demonstrated that the experts could not distinguish the forged prints from genuine ones in a controlled test.
chain.effect: Fingerprint evidence alone is insufficient and can be fabricated to mislead experts.
required_evidence: Thorndyke's demonstration with forged and genuine prints
Expert witness testimony during trial

chain.observation: The forged prints were made with a single stamp, expected to be identical.
chain.correction: Thorndyke used multiple stamps from different impressions to avoid detection by experts.
chain.effect: The forgery was sophisticated enough to evade expert detection by mimicking natural variations.
required_evidence: Thorndyke's multiple stamp preparation
Expert witness confusion during trial

chain.observation: Walter Hornby was suspected due to his skills and suspicious behavior.
chain.correction: Walter's motive and opportunity aligned with the forgery and theft, implicating him as the true culprit.
chain.effect: Walter Hornby was identified as the actual thief and forger, framing Reuben.
required_evidence: Walter's access to 'Thumbograph' and typewriter
Discrepancies in Walter's statements and behavior

herrings.description: John Hornby's financial difficulties and possible motive to steal the diamonds.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He had no legal liability and no evidence linked him to the theft; his financial troubles were unrelated.

herrings.description: Walter Hornby's recent purchase of a typewriter and skill in photography suggested he might have forged documents and prints.
herrings.innocent_explanation: His skills and equipment were initially suspicious but ultimately used to uncover the forgery and frame Reuben.

supporting_points: The thumbprint found in the safe matched Reuben's left thumb exactly.
No forced entry was detected, implying the thief had a key or access.
Reuben had custody of the keys at times and was present at the premises.
Police and fingerprint experts testified to the print's authenticity.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The thumbprint was a photo-mechanical forgery made from the genuine print in the 'Thumbograph' book, not a real print made by Reuben.

items.false_assumption: Dr. Bliss was the sole murderer and acted without any accomplices or interference.

chain.observation: Scarab pin of Bliss found beside Kyle’s body
chain.correction: Pin was planted to implicate Bliss
chain.effect: Bliss’s guilt is not proven by pin alone
required_evidence: Testimony of Scarlett about pin last seen in Bliss’s study
Location of pin on scene inconsistent with natural loss

chain.observation: Bliss’s fingerprints on statue of Sakhmet
chain.correction: Bliss handled statue earlier to straighten it, not to kill
chain.effect: Fingerprints do not prove murder
required_evidence: Bliss’s own admission of adjusting statue before bedtime
Scarlett’s testimony on Bliss’s habit of orderliness

chain.observation: Bloody footprints of tennis shoe leading to Bliss’s study
chain.correction: Only one tennis shoe found downstairs; other shoe hidden upstairs
chain.effect: Footprints were staged to mislead
required_evidence: Discovery of left tennis shoe in Bliss’s bedroom
Butler’s testimony on locked front door

chain.observation: Opium found in Bliss’s coffee
chain.correction: Bliss drugged his own coffee to fake alibi
chain.effect: Bliss was not narcotized, but feigning
required_evidence: Hani’s admission of opium tin location
Chemical analysis of coffee residue

chain.observation: Forged hieroglyphic letter implicating Salveter
chain.correction: Letter was planted by Bliss to frame Salveter
chain.effect: Salveter’s guilt is doubtful
required_evidence: Reconstruction of letter from waste-basket fragments
Salveter’s testimony about original letter

chain.observation: Scarlett found unconscious in sarcophagus
chain.correction: Bliss attacked Scarlett to prevent exposure
chain.effect: Scarlett was victim, not culprit
required_evidence: Medical report on Scarlett’s injury
Vance’s discovery of letter in Scarlett’s pocket

chain.observation: Bliss’s death by falling statue of Anûbis
chain.correction: Hani killed Bliss to end the murderous plot
chain.effect: Bliss’s death was murder by Hani
required_evidence: Vance’s conversation with Hani about legal impossibility of convicting Bliss
Physical evidence of statue’s broken ankles and position over Bliss

herrings.description: Hani’s talk of the vengeance of Sakhmet and mystical retribution suggested he might be involved in a supernatural killing or be the murderer.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Hani used superstition as a cover to protect Salveter and Meryt-Amen and to mislead investigators.

herrings.description: Salveter’s hieroglyphic letter containing ominous words suggested he had a motive and was involved in the murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The letter was a linguistic exercise and was forged and planted by Bliss to implicate Salveter.

supporting_points: Salveter had a motive due to jealousy and inheritance
A forged hieroglyphic letter implicating Salveter was found
The dagger sheath was hidden in Salveter’s room
Salveter was evasive about his whereabouts during the murder
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The letter and dagger sheath were planted by Bliss to frame Salveter, and Salveter’s alibi was corroborated.

items.false_assumption: The murderer entered the house through the front door and chased Gwynne into the garden.

chain.observation: Osric Orm lingered in the garden for two hours without entering the house
chain.correction: His behavior was consistent with composing poetry, not committing murder
chain.effect: Orm's presence is explained, reducing suspicion
required_evidence: Witness testimony about Orm's behavior in the garden
Expert opinion on poet's habits

chain.observation: The front door was unlatched and mirror broken
chain.correction: The mirror was broken by a bullet, not a struggle
chain.effect: The struggle likely did not happen inside the house
required_evidence: Physical examination of broken mirror and bullet trajectory
Father Brown's analysis of the scene

chain.observation: Michael Flood entered and left the garden irregularly
chain.correction: Flood was a reporter scared by the murder, not a culprit
chain.effect: Flood is innocent and a witness
required_evidence: Flood's statements
Servant Green's testimony

chain.observation: John Bankes fled with jewels after a shooting
chain.correction: Bankes was the mastermind behind the theft and murder
chain.effect: Focus shifts to Bankes as the prime suspect
required_evidence: Jewelry memorandum and cipher notes
Fingerprints and footprints linking Bankes

chain.observation: The Master of the Mountain was seen taking the ruby
chain.correction: The theft was an illusion created by painted hand and sleight
chain.effect: Master of the Mountain is innocent
required_evidence: Witness accounts of the hand at the window
Father Brown's reenactment of the theft

chain.observation: Sir Arthur Vaudrey disappeared and was found dead with throat cut
chain.correction: He was killed by John Dalmon with a razor in a barber's shop
chain.effect: Dalmon is guilty of Vaudrey's murder, not disappearance
required_evidence: Barber Wicks's testimony
Blood and body position at the riverbank

chain.observation: Captain Musgrave fled the country after blackmail threats
chain.correction: He killed his father and disguised himself to secure inheritance
chain.effect: Musgrave is the culprit of the worst crime in the world
required_evidence: Family portraits showing resemblance
Old man's testimony and moat evidence

herrings.description: Michael Flood entered the garden irregularly and was found near the victim.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was a reporter trying to interview the victim and was scared by the murder.

herrings.description: The Master of the Mountain was suspected of stealing a valuable ruby at a bazaar.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He created an illusion of theft to impress others but did not actually steal the ruby.

supporting_points: He was seen entering the garden and lingering for two hours
He had no coherent explanation for his presence
The prosecution argued he had opportunity due to open doors
His eccentric behavior suggested possible motive
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He lacked motive and the ability to commit the crime in the time and manner suggested.

items.false_assumption: Purcell landed at Penzance and other ports after the yacht voyage and is alive.

chain.observation: Varney claims Purcell landed at Penzance and other ports during the expedition.
chain.correction: Scientific and testimonial evidence disproves these sightings and the expedition's reported conduct.
chain.effect: Purcell likely never landed and is dead.
required_evidence: Captain's report of the steamer Hedwig passenger list showing no Purcell and no record of his conduct during the expedition
Witness statements denying Purcell's presence at Falmouth and Ipswich, including details of the expedition's route and location

chain.observation: Letters purportedly from Purcell received after disappearance reference the expedition and his physical location.
chain.correction: Microscopic and forensic examination shows letters are forged and do not reveal Purcell's true location.
chain.effect: Letters are fabrications to conceal Purcell's death.
required_evidence: Microscopic analysis of postmarks on letters showing lithographic forgery and absence of physical handling from the claimed location
Comparison of handwriting and ink with known samples, including analysis of the expedition's trawl-rope and creeper references

chain.observation: Blood stain and hand print found on yacht's sail after the expedition.
chain.correction: Hand print matches Varney's maimed finger and the physical evidence from the trawl-rope and creeper used during the expedition.
chain.effect: Varney was present at the time of Purcell's death and involved.
required_evidence: Chemical test of blood stain on sail and physical residue from trawl-rope and creeper used in the expedition
Visual and microscopic comparison of hand print with Varney's finger, including analysis of conduct during the search

chain.observation: Missing ballast weight and cut rope from yacht, both used in the expedition's trawl-rope search.
chain.correction: Weight and rope likely used to sink Purcell's body, as revealed by the expedition's physical findings.
chain.effect: Body disposed of weighted to sink at sea bottom.
required_evidence: Inventory check of yacht gear showing missing weight and rope, including trawl-rope and creeper used in the expedition
Witness testimony of yacht condition before and after voyage, and conduct of the search expedition

chain.observation: Cork button with marine worm tube found on sea bottom during the expedition's trawl-rope search.
chain.correction: Button is from Purcell's oilskin coat and has been underwater for months, as revealed by the physical evidence collected by the creeper.
chain.effect: Purcell's coat and body have been at sea bottom near Wolf Rock.
required_evidence: Identification of button embroidery as Purcell's, recovered by creeper during the expedition
Expert analysis of marine worm tube composition and origin, and physical location of the find

chain.observation: Varney's sudden disappearance from social circles after the expedition's findings.
chain.correction: Varney's disappearance coincides with investigation progress and the reveal of physical evidence from the trawl-rope search.
chain.effect: Varney attempts to avoid detection and consequences.
required_evidence: Witness statements of Varney's last known whereabouts after the expedition's reveal
Correspondence and social visits records, including details of the search expedition's conduct

chain.observation: Varney appears on lugger near Wolf Rock during the search expedition using creeper and trawl-rope.
chain.correction: Varney's presence confirms proximity to crime scene and body disposal, as revealed by the expedition's physical findings.
chain.effect: Varney is implicated as murderer and responsible for body disposal.
required_evidence: Eyewitness account of Varney boarding search boat during the expedition and conduct at the location
Matching of hand print and blood evidence to Varney, as revealed by the physical evidence recovered by creeper and trawl-rope

herrings.description: Reports and Varney's testimony that Purcell was seen at Falmouth and Ipswich after the disappearance.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Varney, as the fabricator of these false sightings
herrings.innocent_explanation: These sightings were invented by Varney to mislead the investigation and divert suspicion from the murder.

herrings.description: The mysterious letter and enclosures received by Mr. Penfield from Purcell.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Purcell, suggesting illicit activities or secret communications
herrings.innocent_explanation: The letter contained forged bank-note blanks and was part of Varney's scheme to expose Purcell and cover up the murder.

supporting_points: Margaret's suspicions about her husband's disappearance
Her emotional distress and desire for freedom
Her possible motive related to Purcell's secretive and brutal nature
Her access to the letters and knowledge of the case
false_solution.the_one_flaw: There is no evidence that Margaret had opportunity or motive to commit the murder; all incriminating evidence points to Varney.

items.false_assumption: The murderer must have entered through the locked door or window.

chain.observation: The door and window of the victim's room were locked from the inside
chain.correction: There is a secret trap-door in the roof providing access
chain.effect: The murderer did not enter through conventional means
required_evidence: Inspection of the locked room and trap-door by Holmes
Witness statement from housekeeper Mrs. Bernstone about locked door

chain.observation: Footprints of a wooden stump and small naked feet found in the room
chain.correction: Two perpetrators: one with a wooden leg and a small accomplice
chain.effect: Identifies two distinct criminals with different physical characteristics
required_evidence: Footprint impressions in creosote and dust
Description of Tonga's small stature and wooden leg of Jonathan Small

chain.observation: Poisoned thorn found in victim's scalp
chain.correction: Murder was committed using a poisoned dart from a blow-pipe
chain.effect: Cause of death is poisoning, not blunt force trauma
required_evidence: Physical examination of the thorn
Toxicological analysis of poison

chain.observation: Rope found in the victim's room leading to the roof
chain.correction: Murderer climbed down the rope from the roof
chain.effect: Confirms secret access route and method of entry/exit
required_evidence: Rope found near trap-door
Holmes's demonstration of climbing method

chain.observation: Toby the dog tracked scent from creosote on the rope
chain.correction: The accomplice dipped foot in creosote to climb down
chain.effect: Identifies the accomplice's route and presence
required_evidence: Toby's tracking of creosote scent
Creosote stains on rope and footprints

chain.observation: Launch Aurora was missing and later found at Jacobson's Yard
chain.correction: Launch was used for escape and hidden at a boatyard
chain.effect: Escape route and method identified
required_evidence: Witness statement from Mrs. Smith about launch departure
Holmes's inquiry at Jacobson's Yard

chain.observation: Jonathan Small and Tonga captured after chase on Thames
chain.correction: They are the culprits responsible for murder and theft
chain.effect: Case solved with arrest of guilty parties
required_evidence: Eyewitness accounts of chase and capture
Physical evidence linking them to crime scene

herrings.description: Thaddeus Sholto's nervousness and quarrel with his brother suggest guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was anxious about the treasure and family disputes but was not the murderer.

herrings.description: The butler Lal Rao is suspected of complicity due to his presence and character.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was merely a loyal servant and had no involvement in the murder or theft.

supporting_points: He was the last person seen with Bartholomew
He had a motive related to the treasure
He was found in a disturbed state near the crime scene
He had access to the house and the victim
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was locked out of the victim's room at the time of death and had an alibi

items.false_assumption: No shot was fired because no noise or smoke was detected by witnesses.

chain.observation: A thirty-two-calibre bullet was found in the victim's neck with fabric impressions.
chain.correction: The bullet must have passed through a fabric matching the impressions.
chain.effect: Identifies the coat as the fabric through which the bullet was fired.
required_evidence: Thirty-two-calibre bullet with fabric impressions recovered from Kerr Parker's neck
Pongee silk from Mrs. Parker's automobile-coat with a bullet hole

chain.observation: No noise or smoke was reported by witnesses during the shooting.
chain.correction: A silencer was used to muffle the gunshot and prevent smoke.
chain.effect: Explains the silent nature of the shooting despite many witnesses.
required_evidence: Purchase records of silencer for thirty-two-calibre revolver by James Bruce
Demonstration of silenced revolver firing in laboratory

chain.observation: Mrs. Parker showed great emotion during the demonstration of the coat and bullet.
chain.correction: Emotional reaction due to grief, not guilt.
chain.effect: Removes suspicion from Mrs. Parker as the shooter.
required_evidence: Emotional response curves recorded during the demonstration
Witness testimony of Mrs. Parker's behavior after the murder

chain.observation: James Bruce was agitated during the demonstration and had access to the coat.
chain.correction: His agitation indicates guilt and opportunity.
chain.effect: Focuses suspicion on James Bruce as the murderer.
required_evidence: Emotional response curves showing agitation of James Bruce
Tracing of messenger calls leading to Bruce's apartment

chain.observation: No weapon was found at the scene.
chain.correction: The weapon was concealed and removed after the shooting.
chain.effect: Explains absence of weapon and supports theory of concealed silenced revolver.
required_evidence: Absence of revolver at the office
Purchase and tracing of silencer and revolver by police

chain.observation: A wet, pulp-like mass of paper was found in the wastebasket.
chain.correction: It was the remains of the note read by the victim.
chain.effect: Links the note to the murder context and suspects.
required_evidence: Microphotographs of fibers in the wet paper matching suspect's notepaper
Witness testimony about the note's existence and timing

chain.observation: The bullet hole in the coat was scorched and burned.
chain.correction: The bullet was fired through the coat, causing the hole.
chain.effect: Confirms the coat was used to conceal the weapon during shooting.
required_evidence: Physical examination of the coat showing bullet hole and scorch marks
Laboratory demonstration firing bullet through pongee coat

herrings.description: Mrs. Parker's strong emotional reaction during the scientific demonstration suggested guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Her reaction was due to shock and grief over her husband's death, not guilt.

herrings.description: A mysterious note and a red-haired actress suspected to be involved in the murder plot.
herrings.innocent_explanation: She confessed to involvement in a side plot unrelated to the murder and was not the shooter.

supporting_points: Mrs. Parker showed great emotion during the demonstration
She was present in the ladies' department near the time of the shot
The coat with the bullet hole belonged to her
She had motive related to financial and personal affairs
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No physical evidence or witness placed her firing the shot, and the silenced revolver was traced to James Bruce

items.false_assumption: The butler was guilty of the murder because he was found at the scene with no alibi.

chain.observation: The stab wound is on the left side of the victim's neck and shoulder.
chain.correction: Only a left-handed person could have delivered such a wound from the victim's position.
chain.effect: This excludes the butler, who is right-handed, as the murderer.
required_evidence: Medical report detailing the position and angle of the stab wound
Witness testimony about the victim's seating and room layout

chain.observation: The butler was found at the scene with no alibi and the drawer was forced open with an ice-pick from his pantry.
chain.correction: The forced drawer and presence are circumstantial and could be staged.
chain.effect: The butler's guilt is questionable; evidence may have been planted.
required_evidence: Analysis of the drawer forcing marks
Butler's testimony and alibi verification

chain.observation: A glove was dropped and picked up by Mr. Percy Thompson, who is left-handed.
chain.correction: The glove drop indicates the presence and involvement of Thompson.
chain.effect: Thompson's presence at the scene is confirmed and suspicious.
required_evidence: Witness statement about the glove drop
Physical glove with matching fingerprints

chain.observation: The will was altered from 30,000 to 50,000 dollars favoring Gosford.
chain.correction: Chemical reagent test revealed the alteration was recent and forged.
chain.effect: Gosford forged the will to claim a larger inheritance.
required_evidence: Chemical reagent test results on the will document
Expert handwriting analysis

chain.observation: The butler's attorney withdrew from the case citing loss of confidence.
chain.correction: The withdrawal was due to pressure and manipulation by Gosford.
chain.effect: The defense was compromised, affecting the trial's fairness.
required_evidence: Attorney's statements and court transcripts
Correspondence indicating external pressure

chain.observation: The young woman presents a detailed drawing of the crime scene and points out inconsistencies.
chain.correction: Her observations reveal the true sequence of events and the murderer's identity.
chain.effect: The court reconsiders the evidence and suspects Thompson.
required_evidence: Drawing on the menu card showing room layout
Courtroom testimony of the young woman

chain.observation: Thompson is left-handed and the wound matches left-handed attack.
chain.correction: This physical evidence directly implicates Thompson as the murderer.
chain.effect: Thompson is identified as the true culprit.
required_evidence: Medical wound analysis
Witness testimony about Thompson's handedness

herrings.description: The will was altered from 30,000 to 50,000 dollars favoring Gosford, suggesting a motive for forgery.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The will was forged by Gosford to claim more inheritance, unrelated to the murder itself.

herrings.description: Bloody footprints found at Benton Court were claimed to be of a barefoot assassin.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The footprints were fabricated using a hand to mislead investigators.

supporting_points: Presence at the crime scene with no alibi
Drawer pried open with an ice-pick from the butler's pantry
Strong circumstantial evidence and expert testimony
Prosecutor's confident case against the butler
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The wound's position and handedness do not match the butler, and planted evidence was fabricated.

items.false_assumption: The murderer escaped through the locked kitchen door or window.

chain.observation: The studio door and kitchen door were locked from inside with keys in place.
chain.correction: The murderer could not have escaped through these doors.
chain.effect: Eliminates normal exit routes for the murderer.
required_evidence: Police report on locked doors at the studio
Witness testimony of locked kitchen door with key inside

chain.observation: The window was open but led to a blank wall 60 feet above ground.
chain.correction: Escape through the window was physically impossible.
chain.effect: Rules out window as escape route.
required_evidence: Police measurement of window height and ledge
Observation of window open but no escape path

chain.observation: A lay figure dressed in clothes was found in the studio, with disturbed clothing and a torn piece of cotton.
chain.correction: The lay figure was used as a decoy outside the window.
chain.effect: Suggests deception involving the lay figure.
required_evidence: Torn cotton piece matching lay figure's covering
Dust and dirt stains on lay figure's leg

chain.observation: Fingerprints and stains on the lay figure's clothing.
chain.correction: The murderer wore the lay figure's clothes to disguise himself.
chain.effect: Identifies the murderer as the person disguised as the lay figure.
required_evidence: Stain patterns on lay figure's jacket and skirt
Witness testimony of lay figure's position outside window

chain.observation: Witnesses saw a man with a limp and distinctive features entering the studio.
chain.correction: The murderer was identified as Tricot, an accomplice of Quinlevin.
chain.effect: Identifies the culprit.
required_evidence: Witness identification of Tricot
Police record of Tricot's limp and physical description

chain.observation: Jim Horton and Piquette Morin were outside the studio during the murder.
chain.correction: They were not involved in the murder but discovered the body.
chain.effect: Exonerates Jim Horton and Piquette Morin.
required_evidence: Testimony of Jim Horton and Piquette Morin
Witness accounts of their location

chain.observation: Barry Quinlevin had motive and orchestrated the blackmail scheme.
chain.correction: He hired Tricot to commit the murder to protect his interests.
chain.effect: Establishes conspiracy and motive.
required_evidence: Letters from Barry Quinlevin
Testimony of Piquette Morin and others

herrings.description: Moira's sudden message to Jim Horton and her complex relationship with both brothers suggested she might be involved in the murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Moira was unaware of the murder plot and was herself a victim of the blackmail scheme and deception.

herrings.description: Harry Horton's erratic behavior, drinking, and absence of wounds raised suspicion about his role in the intrigue.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Harry was a cowardly deserter and victim of the murder, not the perpetrator.

supporting_points: Jim Horton was found at the scene shortly after the murder.
Jim had motive due to rivalry with his brother Harry.
Jim was impersonating Harry, creating suspicion.
Jim had opportunity as he was present in the studio.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Physical impossibility of escape from the locked studio without detection.

items.false_assumption: Frank Gough's quarrel and motive made him the obvious murderer.

chain.observation: Traces of muscarin alkaloid poison found in Jack's brain
chain.correction: Death caused by poison injection simultaneous with head injury
chain.effect: Murder involved medical knowledge and deliberate poisoning
required_evidence: Report of Sir Werner Scatterhyde, Home Office analyst
Medical testimony on poison effects and timing

chain.observation: Dr. Laidlaw seen entering Prior's Tower via secret passages
chain.correction: Laidlaw had opportunity to commit murder unseen
chain.effect: Laidlaw is a prime suspect with access
required_evidence: Witness statements of secret passage usage
Mr. Benson's discovery of secret passages

chain.observation: Lady Evenden's mental instability and secret meetings with Laidlaw
chain.correction: Lady Evenden under mental control, unreliable witness
chain.effect: Her testimony about the murder is compromised
required_evidence: Mr. Rushton Tring's psycho-analyst report
Wilfred Barlow's observations of Lady Evenden

chain.observation: Frank Gough had a quarrel with Jack and was alone after
chain.correction: Quarrel was reconciliatory and unrelated to murder
chain.effect: Frank's motive and opportunity are weakened
required_evidence: Frank's testimony about reconciliation
Roberto's and Thomason's witness statements

chain.observation: Laidlaw attempted to murder Mr. Benson and was later kidnapped, showing his willingness to evade capture and his violent tendencies
chain.correction: Laidlaw is dangerous and likely guilty
chain.effect: Confession and evidence can be extracted
required_evidence: Mr. Benson's testimony of attack and Laidlaw's attempt to evade capture
Physical evidence of violent tendencies: bruises and chloroform traces on Laidlaw after capture

chain.observation: Lady Evenden died from muscarin alkaloid poison
chain.correction: She was poisoned with the same substance, likely by herself
chain.effect: Her death ends her control and reveals the truth
required_evidence: Mr. Rushton Tring's analysis of poison
Discovery of hypodermic cylinder in Lady Evenden's room

chain.observation: Brenda Trenchard claims marriage to Jack and reveals kidnapping
chain.correction: Jack was married and murdered after the marriage
chain.effect: New heir emerges, complicating inheritance
required_evidence: Marriage certificate and testimony of Brenda Trenchard
Brenda's detailed account of kidnapping and imprisonment

herrings.description: Lady Evenden's mental instability and secret meetings with Dr. Laidlaw suggest she might be involved in the murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Lady Evenden was under mental control and drug influence by Laidlaw, unaware of the murder details and not involved in the killing.

herrings.description: A mysterious woman was seen in the Prior's Tower on the night of the murder, suggesting a possible accomplice or alternative suspect.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Unknown woman, possibly Lady Evenden or Jill Kilby
herrings.innocent_explanation: The woman was Jill Kilby, Lady Evenden's companion, who was present but innocent and frightened; no evidence linked her to the murder.

supporting_points: He had a quarrel with Jack Evenden the night before the murder.
He had a motive related to inheritance and family disputes.
Witnesses heard voices of Frank and Jack arguing.
Frank was found alone after the quarrel and before the murder discovery.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The quarrel was followed by a genuine reconciliation, and Frank lacked opportunity and knowledge of the secret passages used by the real murderer.

items.false_assumption: Roger Gretorex was the murderer because he was the last to see Jervis alive and had access to arsenic.

chain.observation: Roger Gretorex was the last to see Jervis alive and had arsenic in his surgery, but Ivy Lexton was also secretly present in the surgery and could obtain poison.
chain.correction: Ivy Lexton was seen alone in the surgery with the arsenic jar, showing she could secretly obtain it.
chain.effect: Shifts suspicion from Gretorex to Ivy and introduces her secret opportunity to obtain arsenic.
required_evidence: Mrs. Huntley’s sworn statement describing Ivy alone with arsenic jar in the surgery, confirming Ivy could secretly obtain poison
Nurse Bradfield’s testimony about visitors and Ivy’s absences, including times Ivy could have secretly obtained arsenic

chain.observation: Ivy Lexton claimed to have visited Gretorex only once with a friend, but evidence shows she could secretly obtain arsenic and administer it to her husband.
chain.correction: Mrs. Huntley and love letters prove Ivy visited multiple times alone, giving her the chance to secretly obtain and administer poison.
chain.effect: Reveals Ivy’s secret access and opportunity to administer arsenic to her husband.
required_evidence: Two love letters from Ivy to Roger Gretorex pieced together, referencing secret meetings and her ability to obtain poison
Mrs. Huntley’s statutory declaration describing Ivy’s secret visits and her ability to administer poison

chain.observation: Roger Gretorex was convicted based on circumstantial evidence and love motive, but Ivy Lexton had a strong motive to poison her husband.
chain.correction: New evidence shows Ivy’s motive and access to poison, and her ability to secretly administer it to her husband.
chain.effect: Undermines prosecution case against Gretorex and highlights Ivy’s motive and opportunity to administer arsenic.
required_evidence: Love letters from Ivy to Roger, revealing her motive and intent to obtain and administer poison
Mrs. Huntley’s testimony and statutory declaration about Ivy’s secret actions regarding her husband

chain.observation: Ivy Lexton appeared as a grieving widow and chief witness, but her behavior was manipulative and she could secretly administer poison.
chain.correction: Ivy’s behavior was manipulative and calculated, and she had the opportunity to secretly administer arsenic to her husband.
chain.effect: Suggests Ivy’s guilt and ability to deceive and secretly administer poison.
required_evidence: Ivy’s admissions during interrogation and trial about her secret actions regarding her husband
Observations of her social behavior and financial dealings, including her ability to secretly administer poison

chain.observation: Miles Rushworth was a wealthy admirer with no apparent motive, but Ivy’s secret actions regarding her husband went unnoticed.
chain.correction: Rushworth’s cables and financial support show his involvement but innocence, while Ivy’s secret ability to obtain and administer poison was overlooked.
chain.effect: Rushworth is a witness and protector, not a culprit, and Ivy’s secret actions regarding her husband become more suspicious.
required_evidence: Miles Rushworth’s telegrams and cables, showing his absence and Ivy’s secret communications
Testimony of his whereabouts during crime, confirming he could not have administered poison to Ivy’s husband

chain.observation: Post-mortem revealed arsenic poisoning but no direct evidence of administration, and Ivy could secretly obtain and administer poison to her husband.
chain.correction: Ivy’s secret visits and possession of poison establish method, and her ability to secretly administer arsenic to her husband is confirmed.
chain.effect: Completes the chain of evidence against Ivy, showing she could secretly obtain and administer poison to her husband.
required_evidence: Mrs. Huntley’s statement of seeing Ivy with arsenic, confirming Ivy could secretly obtain poison
Bolster bag with poison traces found in Ivy’s possession, showing she could administer poison to her husband

chain.observation: Roger Gretorex refused to testify, possibly to protect Ivy’s secret actions regarding her husband.
chain.correction: He suspected Ivy’s guilt and protected her, knowing she could secretly obtain and administer poison to her husband.
chain.effect: Explains Gretorex’s silence and supports his innocence, while highlighting Ivy’s secret actions regarding her husband.
required_evidence: Roger Gretorex’s letter to Ivy, referencing her secret actions regarding her husband
Testimony of Mrs. Gretorex and Enid Dent about Roger’s knowledge of Ivy’s ability to secretly obtain and administer poison to her husband

herrings.description: Roger Gretorex’s love for Ivy and his access to arsenic made him the obvious suspect.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Though he loved Ivy and had arsenic, he had no motive to kill Jervis and was unaware of Ivy’s poisoning.

herrings.description: Rumors and suspicions about Miles Rushworth being Ivy’s secret lover and possible murderer.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Miles Rushworth was wealthy, kind, and away in South Africa during the crime, with no opportunity or motive.

supporting_points: He was the last person to see Jervis Lexton alive besides nurse and cook
He had arsenic in his surgery and was familiar with poisons
He was passionately in love with Ivy Lexton
He refused to testify, which was seen as an admission of guilt
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No direct evidence linked him to the administration of arsenic, and new evidence showed Ivy’s secret visits and possession of poison.

items.false_assumption: David Hume-Frazer was guilty of murdering his cousin Sir Alan.

chain.observation: David Hume-Frazer was found asleep in the library at 1 a.m.
chain.correction: A man resembling David was seen near the house at the same time
chain.effect: David's alibi is not absolute; a double may exist
required_evidence: Footman's testimony of David asleep in library
Poacher 'Rabbit Jack's' witness statement of a man like David

chain.observation: The drawer in Sir Alan's desk was forcibly opened and documents stolen
chain.correction: The documents were used for blackmail and motive for murder
chain.effect: Murder was motivated by theft of incriminating papers
required_evidence: Physical evidence of broken drawer
Family documents found with Ooma

chain.observation: Giovanni Capella was hostile and had motive
chain.correction: Capella was in Naples at time of murder and later killed by Ooma
chain.effect: Capella is innocent of Sir Alan's murder
required_evidence: Travel records of Capella to Naples
Holden's report of Capella's death

chain.observation: Numagawa Jiro had knowledge of the Ko-Katana and wrote letters; he was involved in the arrangement and securing of the typewriter used for anonymous letters.
chain.correction: Jiro was an unwitting accomplice manipulated by Ooma, who arranged for Jiro to dispose of the typewriter and secure the weapon for Ooma's use.
chain.effect: Jiro is innocent but involved in the arrangement and securing of key objects used in the crime.
required_evidence: Jiro's testimony and letters describing the arrangement and disposal of the typewriter and the securing of the Ko-Katana for Ooma's possession
Receipt for the sale of the typewriter and physical trace of the Ko-Katana's transfer

chain.observation: Ooma resembles the Hume-Frazer family and was seen near Beechcroft; he challenged the household by entering the library and was cornered by Brett's team.
chain.correction: Ooma is the true murderer using resemblance to confuse witnesses and challenging the household by arranging to be present in the library, where he was cornered and secured.
chain.effect: Ooma is the culprit, revealed by his identity and possession of the murder weapon.
required_evidence: Physical resemblance noted by witnesses and arrangement of the confrontation in the library
Inventory of Ooma's possessions at the time of being cornered, including the Ko-Katana sword and hypodermic syringe

chain.observation: Two attacks on David and Robert Hume-Frazer were made by a man like them; the attacks were arranged to challenge their safety and secure Ooma's escape.
chain.correction: Ooma attempted to kill them to cover his crime, arranging the attacks as a challenge to the investigation and to secure his own position.
chain.effect: Ooma is dangerous and must be apprehended; his possession of the weapon and arrangement of the attacks are key evidence.
required_evidence: Witness statements of attacks describing the arrangement and challenge posed by the assailant
Injuries and syringe found at the scene, confirming Ooma's possession of the weapon

chain.observation: Ooma injected himself with snake poison during arrest, revealing his identity and intent to avoid capture.
chain.correction: Ooma intended suicide to avoid capture, revealing his guilt and confirming his possession of the murder weapon and poison.
chain.effect: Ooma dies before trial but confesses; the challenge of securing him and the arrangement of the confrontation are confirmed.
required_evidence: Hypodermic syringe found at scene, confirming Ooma's possession of the weapon and poison
Doctor's report of cause of death, revealing the identity of the poison and confirming the arrangement of Ooma's suicide

herrings.description: Giovanni Capella, the Italian husband of Margaret, is suspected due to his hostile behavior and possible financial motives.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Giovanni's quarrel with Margaret and his passion for Helen Layton
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was away in Naples at the time of the murder and later killed by Ooma.

herrings.description: Numagawa Jiro, a Japanese man, is suspected due to his connection with the Ko-Katana and involvement in typewritten letters.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His knowledge of the sword and suspicious behavior with his wife
herrings.innocent_explanation: He was an unwitting tool of Ooma and acted under duress.

supporting_points: David was found asleep in the library at the time of the murder
The stolen documents were missing while David was alone in the room
Witnesses saw a man resembling David near the crime scene
David had a motive related to family disputes and inheritance
false_solution.the_one_flaw: David had a solid alibi of being asleep and was unaware of the murder until after it happened

items.false_assumption: Mary Pinder was guilty of murder and the evidence against her was conclusive.

chain.observation: Lois has a star-shaped scar matching Mary Pinder’s baby scar

required_evidence: Description of scar on Lois’s arm and prison doctor’s account, including the sequence of events leading to the identification of the scar
Lois’s visit to Telsbury Prison and reading of Mary Pinder’s case, as documented in the event records

chain.observation: Countess of Moron has a hidden safe disguised as a book with electric shock
chain.correction: Countess uses extreme measures to protect secrets and intimidate
chain.effect: Indicates Countess’s willingness to harm servants or intruders
required_evidence: Michael Dorn’s discovery of the electrified book safe and the sequence of his investigation into the safe’s mechanism
Countess’s refusal to reveal contents and reaction, as recorded in the event transcript

chain.observation: Poisoned chocolates sent to Lois and her near-fatal car accidents
chain.correction: Attempts on Lois’s life are deliberate and connected to Countess’s plot
chain.effect: Confirms active efforts to eliminate Lois
required_evidence: Michael Dorn’s investigation and removal of chocolates, including the sequence of events and physical trace of hydrocyanic acid
Witness accounts of car collisions and injuries, as documented in the event records

chain.observation: Lois and Mary Pinder are detained at Gallows Farm under Dr. Tappatt, in an event involving abduction and detention
chain.correction: They are held against their will in a disguised mental home, and the sequence of their abduction and detention is orchestrated by the Countess and her accomplices
chain.effect: Reveals the physical captivity and abuse, and the wrongful imprisonment of both women
required_evidence: Descriptions of Gallows Farm and locked rooms, including physical traces of detention and imprisonment
Michael Dorn’s search and confrontation with Dr. Tappatt, as documented in the event sequence

chain.observation: Chesney Praye demands Lois marry him to secure her and her mother’s release, as part of the orchestrated conspiracy
chain.correction: Praye uses coercion and blackmail as part of the conspiracy, and his actions are part of the event sequence leading to the exposure of the plot
chain.effect: Exposes Praye’s opportunistic and villainous role in the wrongful imprisonment and abduction
required_evidence: Lois’s refusal and Praye’s threats, as documented in the event transcript and sequence
Special marriage licence and telegram to vicar, as physical evidence of the orchestrated plan

chain.observation: Countess offers to pay Mary Pinder to leave and keep silent, attempting to plant the idea of escape and silence
chain.correction: Countess seeks to buy silence and secure her position, furthering the wrongful imprisonment and abduction
chain.effect: Shows Countess’s manipulative and controlling nature, and her orchestration of the event sequence
required_evidence: Countess’s conversation with Mary Pinder, as recorded in the event transcript
Mary Pinder’s refusal and recounting of truth, as documented in the event sequence

chain.observation: Michael Dorn rescues Lois and Mary after fire and confrontation, ending the sequence of abduction and detention
chain.correction: Dorn’s persistence leads to exposure and collapse of conspiracy, and the wrongful imprisonment is ended
chain.effect: Resolution of the case and liberation of victims, and the event sequence is completed
required_evidence: Fire at Gallows Farm and escape, as documented in the event records and physical traces of detention
Confrontation with Chesney Praye and Countess, as recorded in the event transcript and sequence

herrings.description: Michael Dorn’s persistent following of Lois and his intrusion into her room suggested he might be a threat or culprit.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Dorn was protecting Lois and investigating the conspiracy; his actions were motivated by concern and duty.

herrings.description: Selwyn Moron’s childish outbursts and opposition to his mother suggested he might be involved in the plot or acting suspiciously.

supporting_points: Lois was arrested for attempted murder of John Braime.
She was found near the scene of the butler’s injury.
Her presence at suspicious locations and association with the Countess.
Her erratic behavior and supposed delusions.

items.false_assumption: The victim's death and the murderer's guilt can be conclusively proven by circumstantial evidence alone.

Police officers' testimony about Ancona's presence

chain.observation: Ancona's despair and confession-like behavior

chain.effect: Public and jury convinced of guilt

Circumstantial evidence of motive

chain.observation: Legal requirement for direct proof of death or criminal violence

Absence of corpse or eyewitness of killing

chain.observation: Telegram received by Samuel Walcott threatening exposure

chain.effect: Establishes motive for murder
required_evidence: Telegram text in Spanish
Walcott's reaction and panic

chain.observation: Mason's legal argument about escape from punishment
chain.correction: Legal loopholes exploited
chain.effect: Culprit escapes criminal liability
required_evidence: Mason's courtroom speech
Judge's ruling on corpus delicti

chain.observation: Ancona's use of acid and chemical means
chain.correction: Body dissolved to prevent discovery
chain.effect: No direct proof of death
required_evidence: Description of chemical process in bath-room
Absence of body despite search

herrings.description: Samuel Walcott (Richard Warren) is suspected due to his false identity and possible motive.

herrings.innocent_explanation: He did not kill Nina San Croix; she was killed by Victor Ancona.

herrings.description: The complete disappearance of Nina San Croix's body suggests supernatural or impossible concealment.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Implies an elaborate cover-up or unknown accomplice.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Victor Ancona dissolved the body using acid and chemical means.

supporting_points: He had motive, as Nina San Croix threatened to expose his past crimes.
He received a telegram from Nina San Croix threatening exposure.
He panicked and acted suspiciously after the telegram.
He was present in the city and had opportunity.

items.false_assumption: Gabrielle Engledue was dead and the girl seen alive was a different person or imposter.

chain.observation: Hugh Garfield was drugged and lost memory after visiting De Gex's house
chain.correction: The drug was orosin administered in coffee and atmosphere

Witness testimony of Garfield's symptoms and loss of consciousness

chain.observation: Gabrielle Engledue was declared dead and cremated

Gabrielle Tennison's mental condition and testimony

chain.observation: Oswald De Gex denies knowledge of Gabrielle Engledue
chain.correction: De Gex is the mastermind behind the poisoning and murder
chain.effect: De Gex attempts to mislead investigators and cover his tracks
required_evidence: Intercepted telegrams showing De Gex's communication with suspects about Gabrielle's movement
Testimonies of servants and associates regarding De Gex's instructions and evasions

chain.observation: Dead bandit Despujol and motor-bandit Sanz are associates of De Gex

Arrest records and confessions detailing communication between Sanz, Despujol, and De Gex

chain.observation: Baron van Veltrup died suddenly with heart failure diagnosis

Exhumation and toxicological analysis of glove fragments

chain.observation: Sample cake of toilet soap contained sharp steel points

chain.effect: Another assassination attempt on Garfield was foiled
required_evidence: Chemical analysis by Professor Vega of the soap and steel points
Discovery of soap sample sent to Garfield's address

chain.observation: Gabrielle Tennison recovered memory after treatment by Professor Gourbeil
chain.correction: Orosin poisoning effects can be partially reversed in rare cases
chain.effect: Gabrielle is able to testify and reveal the conspiracy
required_evidence: Medical reports from Lyons detailing Gabrielle's recovery
Gabrielle's own testimony about her memory and identity

herrings.description: Gaston Suzor, posing as a French banker, is suspected of being a conspirator but his exact role is unclear.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Oswald De Gex and his network
herrings.innocent_explanation: Suzor is an agent of De Gex, but not the direct murderer or poisoner.

herrings.description: Rodriquez Despujol, a notorious Spanish criminal and assassin, is implicated in the murders and attempts on Garfield's life.

items.false_assumption: Parrawhite escaped to America and is alive, avoiding capture.

Pratt's testimony at the inquest regarding his actions and presence after Bartle's death

Discovery of Parrawhite's weighted body in quarry pit, confirming his presence at the scene
