required_evidence: Murgatroyd's shop records and testimony about advertising the passage and the presence of Pratt during the arrangement
Byner's investigation of shipping records and monitoring of reactions to the advertisement

chain.observation: Mrs. Mallathorpe locked the foot-bridge gates and wrote to Pratt, and her presence was monitored by estate staff.
chain.correction: She intended to have the bridge repaired and warned Pratt.
chain.effect: No murder attempt by Mrs. Mallathorpe.
required_evidence: Hoskins the woodman's testimony about warning Mrs. Mallathorpe and monitoring her presence at the bridge
Estate carpenter's statement about bridge condition and the advertisement for repairs

chain.observation: Pratt held power of attorney and controlled Mrs. Mallathorpe's affairs, advertising his authority and monitoring her reactions.
chain.correction: Pratt used blackmail and forged documents to gain control.
chain.effect: Pratt exploited Mrs. Mallathorpe's fear.
required_evidence: Power of attorney documents and the advertisement of Pratt's new authority in the local paper
Esther Mawson's intercepted correspondence and the monitoring of Pratt's presence at key meetings

chain.observation: Duplicate will found in John Mallathorpe's clothes, and its presence was advertised to the family and monitored for reactions.
chain.correction: Duplicate will invalidates Pratt's blackmail.
chain.effect: Restores rightful inheritance to Mallathorpe family.
required_evidence: Mrs. Gaukrodger's discovery of duplicate will and her statement about its presence in the clothing
Cobcroft's testimony about will signing before chimney accident and the advertisement of the will's existence

chain.observation: Pratt found dead in locked room with revolver wound, after his presence was monitored and his reaction to the investigation was observed.
chain.correction: Pratt committed suicide to avoid arrest.
chain.effect: Culprit removed from scene, case closed.
required_evidence: Police report on Pratt's death and the monitoring of his presence at the house
Esther Mawson's account of drugging Pratt and observing his reaction to the advertisements and investigation

herrings.description: The old foot-bridge was in dangerous condition and locked by Mrs. Mallathorpe, suggesting a possible murder trap.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mrs. Mallathorpe intended to have the bridge repaired and locked it for safety; the collapse was accidental.

herrings.description: Murgatroyd's telegram claimed Parrawhite left for America, implying he escaped.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The telegram was a fabrication arranged by Pratt to fake Parrawhite's escape and cover up the murder.

supporting_points: Mrs. Mallathorpe was found near the scene of her son's death and appeared frightened
She had motive to suppress the will to keep the estate
She locked the foot-bridge gates and wrote a suspicious letter to Pratt
Local gossip and suspicion pointed to her involvement
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No concrete evidence linked her to the murder or theft; the will was stolen by Pratt and Parrawhite was killed by Pratt to silence him.

items.false_assumption: The murder was committed by someone who boarded the yacht before Templeton returned.

chain.observation: Walking-stick found in dinghy did not belong to Templeton and its location was arranged to incriminate another.
chain.correction: The stick belonged to the murderer who left it behind to mislead and was aware of its location.
chain.effect: Focused suspicion on a left-handed man carrying a walking-stick and revealed the culprit's attempt to arrange evidence.
required_evidence: Housekeeper’s statement denying stick belonged to Moss and confirming Norwood's stick was missing from his umbrella stand on Sunday morning
Observation of Norwood using left hand to draw cork and carry stick, and being seen near the dinghy at the relevant time

chain.observation: Cigar band found at scene was changed during inquest, revealing a deliberate attempt to mislead.
chain.correction: Coroner Norwood swapped the band to mislead investigators and was aware of the incriminating evidence.
chain.effect: Initial suspicion on Grayson and others smoking similar cigars, but the act revealed the culprit's manipulation.
required_evidence: Witnesses noting cigar band change at inquest and Norwood's handling of the evidence tray
Discovery of identical cigar boxes in Norwood’s house and a record of the band swap

chain.observation: Templeton had diamonds but only one found on body; the rest were missing, and the culprit arranged to obtain them.
chain.correction: Diamonds were handed over to Moss earlier, and the culprit was not aware the diamond bag remained.
chain.effect: Robbery was not the primary motive, and the culprit's lack of awareness of the diamond bag's location is revealed.
required_evidence: Moss’s testimony about receiving diamonds and giving receipt, showing the arrangement of the transaction
Discovery of diamond bag in Moss’s possession and Templeton's receipt book with the transaction recorded

chain.observation: Norwood was wealthy and respected coroner, but secretly arranged to obtain incriminating papers and was aware of the risk.
chain.correction: Norwood was financially ruined and embezzled money, and the incriminating papers threatened to reveal his crimes.
chain.effect: Motive for murder was to prevent exposure and blackmail, and the culprit's secret was the driving force.
required_evidence: Bank records showing Norwood's financial difficulties and bankruptcy risk, and a letter arranging a meeting with Templeton
Ezra Grice’s written statement describing Norwood's embezzlement and the incriminating documents

chain.observation: Moss fled suddenly before murder discovery, but was not aware of the murder at the time.
chain.correction: Moss fled out of fear, not guilt, and his location was confirmed by access records.
chain.effect: Moss was cleared as suspect, and the access record revealed his innocence.
required_evidence: Hotel records confirming Moss’s presence Sunday night, showing his location
Witness statements corroborating Moss’s alibi and his awareness of the murder only after the fact

chain.observation: Grayson left suddenly and had no alibi for murder time, but was not aware of the murder or the location of the crime.
chain.correction: Grayson was at Selham and had witnesses, and access records revealed his absence from the scene.
chain.effect: Grayson was cleared as suspect, and the access record revealed his innocence.
required_evidence: Police surveillance and witness statements at Selham confirming Grayson's location at the time of the murder
Landlady’s testimony about Grayson’s presence and his lack of awareness of the murder until later

chain.observation: Norwood’s walking-stick matched the one found in dinghy, and he arranged to plant a dummy stick as incriminating evidence.
chain.correction: Norwood planted a dummy stick and kept original, revealing his attempt to incriminate others and his awareness of the evidence's location.
chain.effect: Direct evidence linking Norwood to the crime scene, and the arrangement of the stick revealed the culprit's manipulation.
required_evidence: Housekeeper’s recognition of Norwood’s stick and its absence from his umbrella stand, showing the arrangement
Colson’s controlled placement of dummy stick in dinghy and observation of Norwood attempting to retrieve it, revealing the culprit's awareness and intent

herrings.description: Harold Grayson’s sudden departure and cigar evidence suggested guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Grayson left early due to personal reasons unrelated to the murder and was confirmed to be elsewhere during the crime.

herrings.description: Isaac Moss’s abrupt departure and nervous behavior raised suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Moss fled out of fear after discovering Templeton’s body and was later corroborated to have an alibi at the hotel.

supporting_points: Sudden departure from Marsh Quay
Possession of cigars matching the cigar band found
Lack of alibi for the time of murder
Avoidance of Templeton during his stay
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Grayson was proven to have been elsewhere during the murder and did not have access to the yacht at the critical time.

items.false_assumption: Miriam Ward was the murderer because she was the last person with Paul Abbott and was chloroformed to cover the crime.

chain.observation: Miriam was chloroformed and unconscious during the murder
chain.correction: She was incapacitated and could not have committed the murder
chain.effect: Exonerates Miriam as the culprit
required_evidence: Cotton with chloroform odor found under the bed
Miriam's own testimony of being chloroformed

chain.observation: Betty Carter denied being at Abbott's Lodge on the night of the murder
chain.correction: Betty admitted later she was present and married Paul Abbott
chain.effect: Removes suspicion from Betty
required_evidence: Telegram from Betty Carter to Paul Abbott sent on the night of the murder
Marriage certificate signed by Doctor Nash and witnessed by Alan Mason

chain.observation: Alan Mason was found hiding in Paul's bed wearing a beard
chain.correction: Alan was hiding to avoid disturbing the marriage ceremony
chain.effect: Alan's presence explained, no motive for murder
required_evidence: Muddy shoes found on the veranda roof matching Alan Mason's size and recent use
Description of the marriage ceremony from Doctor Nash's written statement

chain.observation: Bloodstained nut pick found in the sunparlor
chain.correction: Nut pick was the murder weapon used by Doctor Roberts
chain.effect: Identifies murder weapon and links to culprit
required_evidence: Nut pick with blood stains
Doctor Roberts' fingerprints on the nut pick handle

chain.observation: Coded letters with unusual postage stamps found
chain.correction: Letters contain a code revealing the hiding place of the Paltoff diamond
chain.effect: Reveals motive related to diamond theft
required_evidence: Decoded messages from the letters showing the hiding place
Thirteenth letter envelope with code and matching stamps

chain.observation: Doctor Roberts was seen with the letters and acted suspiciously
chain.correction: Roberts was the murderer and tried to decode the letters to find the diamond
chain.effect: Identifies Roberts as the culprit
required_evidence: Roberts caught in Mrs. Nash's bedroom with the thirteenth letter envelope and a perforation gauge
Perforation gauge with Doctor Roberts' initials found at the scene

chain.observation: Paul Abbott was found stabbed with no external blood stains
chain.correction: The wound was internal, explaining the lack of blood on sheets
chain.effect: Clarifies cause of death and scene
required_evidence: Autopsy report by Coroner Dixon detailing internal bleeding
Bloodstained sheets and bedclothes examination showing minimal external stains

herrings.description: Betty Carter denies being at Abbott's Lodge on the night of the murder, casting suspicion on her.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Betty was protecting her reputation and inheritance rights; she was indeed present and married Paul Abbott.

herrings.description: Alan Mason impersonates Paul Abbott by wearing a beard and hiding in the bed, suggesting possible guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Alan was hiding to avoid upsetting Betty and Paul during their marriage ceremony and had no involvement in the murder.

supporting_points: She was the last known person with Paul Abbott
She was chloroformed and unconscious during the murder
She found a strange man in the bed instead of Paul
Her statements about Betty Carter's visit were initially disbelieved
false_solution.the_one_flaw: She was chloroformed by the real murderer and had no motive or opportunity to kill Paul Abbott.

items.false_assumption: The deaths were caused by an escaped black mamba snake biting the victims.

chain.observation: Victims showed puncture wounds typical of snake bites but no snake or dart was found.
chain.correction: The wounds were caused by tiny venom darts that melted after delivery.
chain.effect: Disproves natural snake attack theory.
required_evidence: Search of crime scenes showing no physical darts
Laboratory discovery of frozen venom dart moulds

chain.observation: Mirabelle Leicester was brought into Oberzohn’s laboratory under suspicious circumstances.
chain.correction: She was targeted due to her inheritance of a valuable gold concession.
chain.effect: Establishes motive for Oberzohn’s actions.
required_evidence: Letters and telegrams about concession renewal
Barberton’s letter describing gold find

chain.observation: Montague Newton died suddenly at the theatre with snake bite wounds.
chain.correction: He was assassinated using the same venom dart method.
chain.effect: Shows Monty was a victim, not culprit.
required_evidence: Medical examination of Monty’s wounds
Witness accounts of theatre events

chain.observation: Oberzohn’s factory and house contained many deadly snakes and venom extraction equipment.
chain.correction: Oberzohn used these to produce the venom for the darts.
chain.effect: Links Oberzohn to the murder weapon.
required_evidence: Discovery of venom extraction apparatus
Frozen venom darts moulds found in laboratory

chain.observation: Letters in Braille and documents reveal the gold concession’s value and renewal deadline.
chain.correction: Oberzohn’s motive was to prevent renewal by detaining Mirabelle.
chain.effect: Confirms financial motive.
required_evidence: Braille letters from Barberton
Official concession renewal documents

chain.observation: Elijah Washington survived a venom dart attack and is immune to snake venom.
chain.correction: His survival disproves natural snake bite and supports artificial venom use.
chain.effect: Supports venom dart theory.
required_evidence: Washington’s medical records
Witness testimony of attack

chain.observation: Oberzohn was found dead with symptoms of venom dart poisoning.
chain.correction: He was killed by his own venom darts during the final confrontation.
chain.effect: Ends Oberzohn’s threat and confirms method.
required_evidence: Autopsy report
Discovery of venom dart cigarette holder

herrings.description: Montague Newton’s gambling losses and erratic behavior suggest possible guilt.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Montague was manipulated and ultimately killed by Oberzohn’s gang.

herrings.description: Joan Newton’s role as Monty’s sister and her involvement in the plot raise suspicion.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Joan was coerced and fearful, acting under duress without true culpability.

supporting_points: Monty was present at key locations and had motive for financial gain
He was involved in suspicious activities and had conflicts with investigators
His sudden death at the theatre seemed suspicious
He had opportunity to harm Mirabelle and others
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Montague Newton was actually a victim of the venom dart assassination, not the perpetrator.

items.false_assumption: Lewis Parker accidentally shot Doctor Gaskell while hunting quail at dawn.

chain.observation: Lewis was found shooting near the dead body at 5:00 AM.
chain.correction: The body was already cold and dead before Lewis fired.
chain.effect: Lewis could not have been the murderer at the time of death.
required_evidence: George Uhlman's witness statement of body temperature and time
Coroner Burgess' autopsy report on time of death

chain.observation: Aunt Mary is paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair.
chain.correction: She was seen walking and moving about at night.
chain.effect: Her paralysis is hysterical and intermittent.
required_evidence: George Uhlman and Doctor Somers' eyewitness accounts of Aunt Mary walking
Miss Christie's testimony about Aunt Mary's nighttime activity

chain.observation: Poltergeist disturbances are supernatural.
chain.correction: The disturbances are caused by Aunt Mary during somnambulistic episodes.
chain.effect: The ghostly phenomena have a human origin.
required_evidence: Doctor Somers' observation of Aunt Mary acting as Poltergeist
Physical evidence of broken dishes and stolen items

chain.observation: Ralph Satterfield is hostile and involved in bootlegging, and was seen outside the house imitating a whistle to provoke a reaction from the residents.
chain.correction: He is intimidated and not the murderer.
chain.effect: Satterfield is a red herring.
required_evidence: Revenue agent's report on bootlegging operations and Satterfield's presence outside the house
Witness statement describing Satterfield imitating a quail's whistle to provoke Aunt Mary

chain.observation: Roaring Lafe Rutledge threatened Gaskell and was near the scene, and was observed outside the house attempting to provoke a confrontation.
chain.correction: He did not shoot Gaskell but was the leader of bootleggers.
chain.effect: Rutledge is a suspect but not the murderer.
required_evidence: Government raid and arrest records showing Rutledge's presence outside the house
Witness statement describing Rutledge's attempt to provoke Gaskell with a whistle

chain.observation: Aunt Mary fired a shotgun at the quail near her window after being provoked by an imitation whistle from outside.
chain.correction: She shot Doctor Gaskell earlier in a fit of rage.
chain.effect: Aunt Mary is the murderer.
required_evidence: Doctor Somers and George Uhlman's eyewitness accounts of Aunt Mary firing the shotgun after being provoked by the quail whistle imitation
Physical examination of the shotgun showing it was recently fired

chain.observation: Aunt Mary died from a shotgun wound to the temple after being provoked by an imitation quail whistle outside her window.
chain.correction: The gun malfunctioned and caused accidental self-inflicted death.
chain.effect: Her death was accidental during an attempted second shooting.
required_evidence: Doctor Somers' medical examination of Aunt Mary after the accidental shooting provoked by the whistle
Physical examination of the shotgun revealing the malfunction that caused the fatal wound

herrings.description: Ralph Satterfield, a bootlegger and enemy of Gaskell, is suspected due to his grudge and involvement with moonshine.
herrings.points_at_suspect: His threats against Gaskell and leadership of a lynch mob suggest motive and opportunity.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Though involved in illicit liquor trade, he did not kill Gaskell and was intimidated into silence.

herrings.description: Roaring Lafe Rutledge, a feared mountain moonshiner, is suspected of killing Gaskell due to threats and violent reputation.
herrings.points_at_suspect: He threatened Gaskell and was found with the bootleggers; his presence near the crime scene is suspicious.
herrings.innocent_explanation: He admitted intent but claimed he did not shoot Gaskell and was captured before he could harm anyone.

supporting_points: Lewis was found standing over the body with the shotgun.
He had a known angry quarrel with Doctor Gaskell.
The shotgun shells matched the shot extracted from the body.
Witnesses heard the gunshot and saw Lewis nearby.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The timeline and physical evidence do not prove Lewis was the shooter at the time of death; the body was already dead and cold when he fired.

items.false_assumption: Joe Richards was the murderer because he possessed the stolen bonds and watch.

chain.observation: Joe Richards possessed Troy Valve bonds stolen from Robert Hale's safe on Tuesday night.
chain.correction: The bonds were stolen by Jim Turner and sold by Richards, who was unaware of their origin.
chain.effect: Richards' financial troubles are explained but do not prove guilt in murder.
required_evidence: Testimony of Frank Latimer about bond sale on Tuesday evening
Inventory of bonds missing from safe after Tuesday night

chain.observation: Austin Hale's antique watch was found in Richards' possession with repair tag dated Wednesday.
chain.correction: Richards left the watch for repair after finding it on Austin's body to conceal evidence.
chain.effect: Watch possession is explained as an attempt to cover up discovery, not murder.
required_evidence: Watchmaker Jennings' testimony about Wednesday morning delivery
Richards' account of events after finding Austin's body on Wednesday

chain.observation: Polly Davis disappeared after the murder and had suspicious behavior on Tuesday night.
chain.correction: Polly fled out of fear and suspicion, not guilt.
chain.effect: Polly is cleared as a suspect for murder.
required_evidence: Polly's letter to her mother describing her movement on Tuesday night
Mrs. Davis' testimony about Polly's whereabouts on Wednesday

chain.observation: John Hale claimed to be at French Embassy during murder time on Tuesday night.
chain.correction: John Hale returned home secretly to meet Austin and committed the murder.
chain.effect: John Hale's alibi is disproved, making him the murderer.
required_evidence: Witness testimony of John Hale's arrival at the house late Tuesday night
Bloodstained sword cane found in John's possession after Wednesday morning search

chain.observation: Bloodstains found on John Hale's sword cane after Tuesday night incident.
chain.correction: The cane concealed a rapier used to kill Austin Hale.
chain.effect: Identifies murder weapon and links it to John Hale.
required_evidence: Autopsy report describing wound consistent with rapier on Wednesday
Examination of sword cane revealing concealed blade and blood after Tuesday night

chain.observation: Judith Richards was found bound, gagged, and blindfolded in her boudoir on Wednesday morning, unable to focus or move.
chain.correction: Jim Turner attempted to silence Judith to prevent discovery of his theft and identity.
chain.effect: Reveals Turner's role as accomplice and thief.
required_evidence: Judith's testimony of abduction and inability to focus or move on Tuesday night
Physical evidence of bindings and gag found in boudoir after Wednesday morning

chain.observation: Dictograph device found in Judith's boudoir recorded conversations from Tuesday night to Wednesday morning.
chain.correction: Robert Hale installed it to secretly monitor conversations and gather evidence.
chain.effect: Provides surveillance evidence aiding investigation.
required_evidence: Testimony of Robert Hale about dictograph installation on Tuesday
Recorded conversations implicating suspects between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning

herrings.description: Polly Davis disappears after the murder, leading to suspicion she killed Austin Hale.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Polly fled due to fear of being implicated and to protect herself, not because she was guilty.

herrings.description: Joe Richards' financial difficulties and sale of Judith's bonds suggest a motive for murder.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Richards sold the bonds to cover losses but did not commit murder; he was unaware of the murderer's identity.

supporting_points: Possession of stolen Troy Valve bonds belonging to Judith.
Possession of Austin Hale's watch with his name on the repair tag.
Unexplained absence from the club for over an hour during the murder time.
Suspicious behavior and refusal to explain possession of the watch.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: No direct evidence links Richards to the murder weapon or the act of killing; the murder weapon was a rapier concealed in John Hale's cane.

items.false_assumption: The bloodstain on the window sill was made by the murderer escaping through the window.

chain.observation: Bloodstain on window sill matches Barker's bloodstained slippers
chain.correction: Bloodstain was placed deliberately by Barker
chain.effect: Discredits escape through window theory
required_evidence: Slippers found under hall chair stained with blood
Blood mark on window sill matching slipper sole
Barker was suspected of staging the blood mark, making him a suspect

chain.observation: Missing dumb-bell from the study
chain.correction: Dumb-bell used as weight to sink bundle in moat
chain.effect: Suggests something was hidden in the moat
required_evidence: Recovered bundle weighted with dumb-bell from moat
Missing dumb-bell reported by Ames
The bundle was placed by an agent acting on behalf of Douglas

chain.observation: Suit of clothes found in bundle in moat
chain.correction: Clothes belonged to the dead man found, not Douglas
chain.effect: Victim was not John Douglas but the assassin
required_evidence: Tailor's label 'Neal, Outfitter, Vermissa, U.S.A.' on coat
Clothing matching description of assassin's outfit
The assassin was a Pinkerton target, and Douglas was a Pinkerton agent

chain.observation: Douglas's body not found, only the dead man in clothes
chain.correction: Douglas was hidden in secret room in manor
chain.effect: Douglas is alive and in hiding
required_evidence: Secret hiding place in manor house known to Ames
Douglas's reappearance at the end
Douglas's infiltration of the manor was confirmed by Holmes

chain.observation: Mrs. Douglas and Barker's suspicious behavior
chain.correction: They conspired to protect Douglas and stage the scene
chain.effect: They are accomplices, not murderers
required_evidence: Their coordinated stories and actions
Holmes's deduction of their conspiracy
Mrs. Douglas was invited to participate in the concealment

chain.observation: Assassin's weapon was a sawed-off American shotgun
chain.correction: Assassin was American and came prepared for murder
chain.effect: Links crime to American criminal elements
required_evidence: Shotgun barrel marked 'PEN' for Pennsylvania Small Arms Company
Description of assassin's clothing and weapon
The assassin was suspected to be part of the Scowrers

chain.observation: Cipher message warning Holmes of danger to Douglas
chain.correction: Message was from informant Birdy Edwards (Douglas's real identity)
chain.effect: Douglas was under threat from criminal gang
required_evidence: Cipher decoded referencing Douglas and Birlstone
Letter from Porlock warning Holmes
The message revealed the infiltration of the lodge and confirmed the threat

chain.observation: Birdy Edwards was a Pinkerton agent who infiltrated the Scowrers
chain.correction: Birdy Edwards's infiltration was confirmed by the lodge's own suspecting members
chain.effect: Birdy Edwards's true identity was revealed
required_evidence: Birdy Edwards was invited to a secluded room by McMurdo
McMurdo suspected Birdy Edwards was a Pinkerton agent
The lodge confirmed Birdy Edwards's infiltration

herrings.description: A bicycle found near the manor suggested the murderer fled on it.
herrings.points_at_suspect: An unknown outsider arriving by bicycle
herrings.innocent_explanation: The murderer left the bicycle deliberately to mislead the investigation.

herrings.description: A bloodstain on the window sill implied the murderer escaped through the window.
herrings.points_at_suspect: An intruder escaping the locked manor
herrings.innocent_explanation: The blood mark was made by Barker to fake the escape route.

supporting_points: She was present at the manor during the murder.
She displayed unusual composure and secrecy.
The missing wedding ring suggested a personal motive.
Her relationship with Barker was suspicious.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: She lacked opportunity and motive to commit murder and was protecting her husband.

items.false_assumption: Betty Varian killed her father and then disappeared by hiding or suicide.

chain.observation: No secret passage found in house despite thorough search
chain.correction: Secret passage is a natural tunnel through cave and well outside house structure
chain.effect: Explains how intruder entered and exited undetected
required_evidence: Old contractor’s plans of the house
Carpenters’ demolition and search reports

chain.observation: Green stain on Martha’s hand and on Zizi’s frock
chain.correction: Stain matches mossy stones in the well and tunnel
chain.effect: Links Martha’s murder and intruder’s use of secret passage
required_evidence: Green smear on Martha’s left palm
Green stain on Zizi’s frock after cellar exploration

chain.observation: Yellow satin pillow found in kitchen floor
chain.correction: Pillow dropped during struggle when Betty was abducted
chain.effect: Confirms Betty was carried through kitchen and cellar
required_evidence: Yellow pillow embroidery and hairpin found
Witness testimony about pillow’s usual location

chain.observation: String of yellow beads broken and scattered in kitchen
chain.correction: Beads broke during Betty’s abduction struggle
chain.effect: Physical evidence of struggle and abduction route
required_evidence: Yellow beads found under furniture in kitchen
Testimony of servants and investigators

chain.observation: Lawrence North’s room shows signs of struggle but no forced exit
chain.correction: North staged his own disappearance to mislead investigators
chain.effect: North is suspect, not victim
required_evidence: Overturned chair and scratches in North’s room
Note left by North: 'They’ve got me. L. N.'

chain.observation: Ransom letters and telegrams received by Minna Varian
chain.correction: Letters are from Lawrence North, the kidnapper and blackmailer
chain.effect: Identifies the criminal and motive
required_evidence: Typed ransom letters signed 'Step'
Blackmail letter signed 'Step'

chain.observation: Discovery of secret tunnel connecting well and cave to ocean
chain.correction: Tunnel used by criminal for secret ingress and egress
chain.effect: Explains how intruder avoided detection
required_evidence: Pennington Wise’s exploration and clearance of tunnel
Carpenters’ report on no secret passage in house

herrings.description: The exhaustive search for a secret passage in the house that repeatedly failed to find any hidden rooms or doors.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Suggested that no intruder could have entered, implicating Betty.
herrings.innocent_explanation: The secret passage was a natural tunnel through the cave and well outside the house structure.

herrings.description: A woman claimed to have seen Betty Varian speaking silently in a moving picture crowd scene.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Suggested Betty was alive and possibly involved in the mystery or hiding.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Betty was indeed alive but confined and allowed limited exercise, and the scene was a chance occurrence.

supporting_points: She was missing at the time of the murder.
No weapon was found at the scene, implying she might have hidden it.
She had known quarrels with her father.
The locked house suggested no other intruder.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The existence of a secret passage and the presence of another culprit who staged his own disappearance.

items.false_assumption: John Boulnois was the murderer of Sir Claude Champion.

chain.observation: James Todhunter was found tied with knots he could undo himself
chain.correction: The ropes were self-tied as part of conjuring practice
chain.effect: Mr Glass was a fictitious blackmailer; the struggle was staged
required_evidence: Examination of knots on Todhunter's ropes for self-tying patterns and looseness
Todhunter's own admission of conjuring practice and ventriloquism to Maggie MacNab

chain.observation: The black figure in the theatre passage was seen by multiple witnesses
chain.correction: The figure was a reflection in a mirror
chain.effect: The supposed mysterious figure was an optical illusion
required_evidence: Layout and angles of mirrors in the theatre dressing rooms and passage
Testimony of Father Brown about seeing himself in the mirror during the investigation

chain.observation: Sir Claude Champion was stabbed with a sword and John Boulnois was absent
chain.correction: Sir Claude committed suicide with the sword
chain.effect: Boulnois was innocent of murder despite appearances
required_evidence: Fingerprints on the sword halfway down the blade, not on the hilt
Witness testimony of Mrs Boulnois and Father Brown's moral analysis of Sir Claude's jealousy

chain.observation: Colonel Cray was poisoned and silverware was missing
chain.correction: The poisoning was done via the cruet-stand with Indian poison
chain.effect: The burglary was a cover-up for attempted murder
required_evidence: Presence of Indian poison and emetics in the cruet-stand on the dining table
Dr Oman’s observation of the poison book open on the table near the scene

chain.observation: Prince Otto was found shot with no firearms allowed in the principality
chain.correction: He was strangled with his own military scarf
chain.effect: The murder was disguised as a shooting
required_evidence: Condition of the scarf with a bullet hole and bloodstains
Testimony about the hermit Paul Arnhold and his servants' movements during the murder

chain.observation: The hotel proprietor was found dead and a secret society was suspected
chain.correction: The secret society used assassination during noisy events to conceal crimes
chain.effect: The murder was committed amidst crowd distractions
required_evidence: Witness accounts of the bandstand and the timing of the murder during the music
Discovery of the hotel proprietor’s body and the black society’s involvement in the crowd

chain.observation: The note about the secret drawer was inaccurate
chain.correction: The note was a deliberate forgery to mislead foreign spies
chain.effect: Dr Hirsch was not a traitor but part of a complex deception
required_evidence: Inspection of the secret drawer at the War Office showing no formula present
Analysis of the forged note’s errors in location and handwriting

herrings.description: The mysterious Mr Glass who supposedly blackmailed James Todhunter and was involved in a violent struggle.
herrings.points_at_suspect: James Todhunter as victim of blackmail and possible murderer
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mr Glass never existed; the noises and voices were conjuring tricks by Todhunter himself.

herrings.description: Ezza Montano, the self-styled King of Thieves, who captured the Harrogate family and staged a ransom demand.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Montano as a dangerous brigand and criminal mastermind
herrings.innocent_explanation: Montano was an actor and courier playing a role; the kidnapping was a staged event with no real threat.

supporting_points: Caught struggling with Isidore Bruno over the dagger
Had a motive of jealousy over Aurora Rome
Was present at the scene with no solid alibi at the time of death
Was seen agitated and passionate during the events
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The dagger was used by Parkinson to kill Aurora Rome, and Cutler was only involved in the struggle, not the murder.

items.false_assumption: John Carsdale killed Sydney Werrick during a confrontation at Mrs. Walsingham’s flat.

chain.observation: Burgoyne’s necklace was valued as paste by jeweller Levanter.
chain.correction: The necklace given to Burgoyne was a perfect paste duplicate.
chain.effect: Suspected theft and substitution of the real necklace.
required_evidence: Mr. Levanter’s valuation report of the necklace
Captain Burgoyne’s testimony of the necklace’s authenticity

chain.observation: Mrs. Walsingham pawned a diamond necklace for a small loan.
chain.correction: The pawned necklace was the real one stolen from Leverton’s safe.
chain.effect: Mrs. Walsingham is implicated in the theft.
required_evidence: Pawnshop records of the necklace
Mrs. Walsingham’s admission of possession

chain.observation: Sydney Werrick was found shot dead in Mrs. Walsingham’s flat.
chain.correction: Mrs. Walsingham shot Werrick in self-defense during a confrontation.
chain.effect: Murder was not premeditated by Carsdale or others.
required_evidence: Police surgeon’s report on time of death
Carsdale’s testimony of arrival after shooting

chain.observation: Mrs. Walsingham fled disguised as a nun and hid in Shrewsbury’s flat.
chain.correction: She attempted to escape detection but was aided by Kedgin.
chain.effect: Kedgin’s involvement in aiding escape and theft is suspected.
required_evidence: Witness reports of nun disguise
Inventory of missing items from Shrewsbury's flat

chain.observation: Valuables and jewelry disappeared from Shrewsbury’s flat.
chain.correction: Kedgin stole valuables to finance escape and cover tracks.
chain.effect: Kedgin is a secondary culprit and murderer of Mrs. Walsingham.
required_evidence: Inventory of missing items
Discovery of Mrs. Walsingham’s body in empty house

chain.observation: Carsdale possessed securities and tickets for flight.
chain.correction: Carsdale planned to flee with Mrs. Walsingham but was detained.
chain.effect: Carsdale’s fraud and flight plans are confirmed.
required_evidence: Bank records of securities withdrawal
Tickets for Southampton steamer found on Carsdale

chain.observation: Frances Leverton holds proof of Carsdale’s fraud.
chain.correction: Legal pressure from Winch and Leverton’s estate forces Carsdale’s surrender.
chain.effect: Carsdale loses control over Shrewsbury’s fortune.
required_evidence: Legal documents proving fraud
Mr. Winch’s confrontation with Carsdale

herrings.description: Sandy Kinahan was reported dead in Nevada, which was used to mislead Mrs. Walsingham and Carsdale.
herrings.points_at_suspect: Mrs. Walsingham and Carsdale, as they believed the threat was gone.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Kinahan was alive and returned to London, complicating the situation but not directly involved in the theft or murder.

herrings.description: Frances Leverton’s stern attitude and investigation suggested she might be involved in the theft or fraud.
herrings.points_at_suspect: John Carsdale and Mrs. Walsingham, as Frances was hostile to them and had motive.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Frances was acting to protect her father’s estate and uncover the truth, not to commit any crime.

supporting_points: He was present at key moments and had access to the necklace.
He was the first to raise suspicions about the necklace's authenticity.
He had a close relationship with Frances Leverton, who was investigating the fraud.
He was seen near the scene of the murder and was questioned by police.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Burgoyne's actions were motivated by investigation, not concealment, and he had no opportunity to commit the theft or murder.

items.false_assumption: The death of Hartley Parrish was a straightforward suicide caused by business worries.

chain.observation: Bude hears voices in the locked library shortly after Greve passes.
chain.correction: Voices were between Parrish and Jeekes, not Greve.
chain.effect: Greve’s presence in the library is disproved.
required_evidence: Bude’s witness statement about hearing voices
Horace Trevert’s testimony about entering through the window

chain.observation: Only one shot was heard by Mary Trevert.
chain.correction: Two shots were fired; one silenced, one loud.
chain.effect: Implies presence of two pistols and a struggle.
required_evidence: Mary Trevert’s testimony about hearing a hiss before the shot
Bullet mark on rosery tree indicating a shot fired from window

chain.observation: Parrish’s pistol found without silencer in his hand.
chain.correction: Silencer was removed by murderer to disguise the loud shot.
chain.effect: Murder staged as suicide using Parrish’s pistol.
required_evidence: Jay’s testimony about missing silencer
Silencer found in the shrubbery outside the library window

chain.observation: Jeekes was in London and then in Rotterdam following Mary.
chain.correction: Jeekes was spying and acting under Marbran’s orders.
chain.effect: Jeekes had motive and opportunity to murder Parrish.
required_evidence: Telegram from Rotterdam police confirming Jeekes’s presence at Villa Bergendal
Manderton’s investigation and telegram about pistol purchase

chain.observation: Letter from Elias van der Spyck & Co. found on Parrish’s desk.
chain.correction: Letter was coded blackmail threatening Parrish’s life.
chain.effect: Provides motive for murder.
required_evidence: Decoded letter using slotted sheet
Dulkinghorn’s expert analysis

chain.observation: Jeekes found dead by hanging at Villa Bergendal.
chain.correction: Jeekes committed suicide after confessing murder.
chain.effect: Confession confirms murder and clears others.
required_evidence: Jeekes’s last statement
Manderton’s and Dutch police’s discovery of body

chain.observation: Marbran fled the country after murder.
chain.correction: Marbran was the mastermind but escaped justice.
chain.effect: Only Jeekes was caught and confessed.
required_evidence: Manderton’s testimony about Marbran’s flight
Ticket stubs and passport records showing Marbran’s departure

herrings.description: Robin Greve is suspected due to his argument with Parrish and the butler hearing voices after he passed.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Greve did not enter the library and the voices were from Jeekes and Parrish during the murder.

herrings.description: Mary Trevert’s engagement to Parrish and her previous relationship with Greve create suspicion and emotional motives.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Mary was a witness and had no motive or opportunity; Greve was innocent and wrongly suspected.

supporting_points: Bude testified hearing voices in the library shortly after Greve passed him.
Greve had a known rivalry and confrontation with Parrish over Mary Trevert.
Greve was unaccounted for during the time of the murder and had opportunity.
Greve’s denial of visiting Parrish was contradicted by servants’ testimony.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Greve had a solid alibi and no physical evidence linked him to the murder; the voices heard were misattributed and the real culprit was Jeekes.

items.false_assumption: The dead man in Cathcart Square was Reginald Davis who committed suicide out of fear of capture.

chain.observation: Body found with letters addressed to Reginald Davis and a suicide note in his name; initial investigation did not monitor the condition of the body for movement or verify the identity beyond surface resemblance.
chain.correction: Reginald Davis was later found alive, so the letters and note were planted and the opportunity for misidentification was exploited.
chain.effect: The identity of the dead man is questioned, and the need to verify movement and condition of the body is established.
required_evidence: Letters addressed to Reginald Davis found on the body and the suicide note, both of which were later revealed as forgeries
Reginald Davis's reappearance and testimony, which provided a concrete opportunity to reveal the misidentification

chain.observation: Caretaker Miles was absent and window broken, but surveillance and movement records were used to monitor his opportunity and verify his alibi condition.
chain.correction: Miles had a credible alibi supported by witnesses and movement logs, eliminating his opportunity.
chain.effect: Caretaker is cleared as suspect; his movements and condition at the time are verified.
required_evidence: Miles's alibi testimony from friend at Shepperton, including movement records and time-stamped statements
Testimony of constables Brown and younger colleague, who monitored Miles's movements and verified his condition

chain.observation: Norah Burton's close association with known criminals and suspicious behavior was monitored through detective surveillance, revealing clandestine movement and opportunity.
chain.correction: Detective Bryant confirms Norah Burton is the same person as Stella Keane, and her movements were verified to coincide with key events.
chain.effect: Norah identified as a suspect with criminal past and monitored opportunity.
required_evidence: Detective Bryant's identification of Norah Burton as Stella Keane, supported by surveillance of her movements
Surveillance reports of meetings between Norah and George Burton, verifying their opportunity and motive

chain.observation: George Burton operates a bucket-shop and has a criminal record; his movements and meetings with Norah were monitored to verify opportunity and motive.
chain.correction: George Burton is confirmed as the same person as George Dutton, and his movements were tracked to confirm his presence at key times.
chain.effect: George Burton identified as accomplice with verified opportunity and motive.
required_evidence: Detective Bryant's identification of George Dutton as George Burton, including movement logs and surveillance records
City office records of George Dutton, showing his movements and opportunity to meet Norah

chain.observation: Major Hugh Murchison disappeared suddenly and belongings left at station; detectives monitored the movement of his luggage and verified the condition of his possessions.
chain.correction: Body exhumed and identified as Major Murchison, not Reginald Davis, using witness statements and verification of physical condition.
chain.effect: Victim identity confirmed as Murchison, confirming murder and revealing the opportunity for the culprits.
required_evidence: Exhumation and identification of body by multiple witnesses including Guy Spencer, verifying the condition and identity
Hotel manager's testimony about Murchison's departure, monitoring his last known movements

chain.observation: Diary found in victim's luggage detailing events leading to murder; detectives monitored the movement of the diary and verified its condition as evidence.
chain.correction: Diary entries implicate Norah and George in murder plot, revealing their motive and opportunity.
chain.effect: Strong evidence against Norah and George, revealing their motive and monitored opportunity.
required_evidence: Diary entries recovered from victim's luggage, showing movement and condition of the evidence
Detective Bryant's analysis of diary, verifying the motive and opportunity described

chain.observation: Surveillance shows Norah and George meeting clandestinely and exchanging envelopes; detectives monitored their movement and verified the condition of the exchanges.
chain.correction: Envelope exchanges likely payments or bribes related to crime, revealing ongoing opportunity and motive.
chain.effect: Confirms ongoing criminal collaboration, monitored opportunity, and motive.
required_evidence: Detective Parkinson's surveillance reports, documenting movement and condition of meetings
Witness statements of meetings at City restaurants, verifying opportunity and motive

herrings.description: Caretaker Miles was suspected due to his absence and broken window but had a credible alibi.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Miles was on holiday with a friend and had no involvement in the murder.

herrings.description: Jack Pomfret's suicide was initially thought to be related to the murder mystery.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Pomfret's suicide was due to despair after discovering Norah's criminal past, not the murder itself.

supporting_points: Broken window pane suggested forced entry.
Caretaker was absent during the murder.
Caretaker had a weak character and was suspected of lying.
Caretaker had no alibi for the night.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Miles had a solid alibi supported by witnesses and was not involved in the crime.

items.false_assumption: Daniel Craig is guilty of the murder for which he was imprisoned.

chain.observation: Craig was found in the punishment cell with saws and a cat wearing a collar of steel saws.
chain.correction: The saws were smuggled in to aid his escape, not for self-harm.
chain.effect: Confirmed the planned prison break and Craig’s leadership role.
required_evidence: Description of the steel saw collar on the cat
Whispered instructions from Jim Bartow to Craig

chain.observation: Craig subdued the guards and took control of the prison.
chain.correction: Craig used stealth and surprise, not brute force alone.
chain.effect: Showed Craig’s strategic mind and ability to command.
required_evidence: Narrative of Craig’s capture of guards
Eddie Yarmouth’s assistance

chain.observation: Craig escaped and assumed a new identity outside prison.
chain.correction: Craig’s escape was aided by allies and disguises.
chain.effect: Allowed Craig to operate freely and gather information.
required_evidence: Craig’s use of guard’s uniform
Joan Gracie’s aid and letters

chain.observation: Craig systematically tracked fugitives using underworld contacts.
chain.correction: Craig combined criminal knowledge with law enforcement cooperation.
chain.effect: Enabled him to capture dangerous criminals effectively.
required_evidence: Craig’s meetings with Artie the lawyer and district attorney
Information from Mr. Sanders and others

chain.observation: Count Wolf was captured at Marebello’s residence.
chain.correction: Craig used a bluff and physical confrontation to subdue Wolf.
chain.effect: Final capture of the main antagonist.
required_evidence: Description of the ballroom and confrontation
Craig’s slap and subsequent fight

chain.observation: Count Wolf escaped shackles and fled down elevator shaft.
chain.correction: Craig pursued and fought Wolf on top of elevator car.
chain.effect: Demonstrated Craig’s determination and physical prowess.
required_evidence: Elevator shaft struggle description
Witnesses’ reactions and sounds

chain.observation: Craig returned with Wolf and other fugitives to law enforcement.
chain.correction: Craig coordinated with district attorney and newspaper editor for arrests.
chain.effect: Closure of the case and restoration of order.
required_evidence: Courtney’s newspaper office preparations
Major Gracie and Colonel Bird’s involvement

herrings.description: Samuel Green's vendetta against Craig and his suspicious behavior suggest he might be the mastermind behind the chaos.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Green acted out of personal resentment but was not involved in the original murder or the prison break; he was manipulated by his own emotions and family issues.

herrings.description: Harry, the Goose, initially appears threatening and untrustworthy, possibly a traitor or accomplice to the criminals.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Harry is a cowardly and self-interested man but ultimately is captured and controlled by Craig, posing no real threat to the investigation.

supporting_points: Green was the disgraced ex-warden seeking revenge
He organized a posse to capture Craig
He had motive to frame Craig
He was present at key moments of pursuit
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Green lacked concrete evidence and was ultimately revealed to be misled by his own biases and family secrets.

items.false_assumption: The man in white was an innocent outsider unrelated to the family or staff.

chain.observation: Only the replicas and not the real medallions were initially stolen.
chain.correction: The theft of replicas was a deliberate misdirection.
chain.effect: The real medallions were secretly substituted and later removed.
required_evidence: Examination of medallions with drilled holes distinguishing real from replicas
Inventory logbook showing the sequence of medallion removals and substitutions

chain.observation: Morden’s hand was cut and wrapped in a handkerchief.
chain.correction: The injury was self-inflicted to create an alibi.
chain.effect: Morden’s story about the murder scene is partially fabricated.
required_evidence: Blood patterns on the floor and glass case
Morden’s inconsistent testimony and fingerprint analysis

chain.observation: Maurice disappeared mysteriously and was found dead in a secret chamber.
chain.correction: Maurice committed suicide due to agoraphobia.
chain.effect: His disappearance was not a murder or escape but self-inflicted.
required_evidence: Discovery of secret passage and underground chamber
Medical and behavioral evidence of agoraphobia

chain.observation: A man in white costume escaped capture by diving into the lake.
chain.correction: The man was Brackley using a living statue disguise.
chain.effect: The escape was a planned trick to evade police.
required_evidence: Witnesses’ description of living statue movement
Recovery of white costume and injuries on Brackley

chain.observation: Foss was murdered with a Japanese sword bearing Maurice’s fingerprints.
chain.correction: Maurice handled the sword but did not kill Foss; Marden killed Foss.
chain.effect: Morden is the murderer, using the sword and framing Maurice.
required_evidence: Fingerprint analysis on sword and pistol
Marden’s presence and behavior at murder scene

chain.observation: The otophone was used to pick the safe lock.
chain.correction: The gang planned a second burglary to retrieve the real medallions.
chain.effect: The otophone was a tool for the gang’s burglary attempt.
required_evidence: Otophone device and its use in opening the safe
Guard’s testimony and police surveillance

chain.observation: Cecil claimed to arrive by first train but was found to have been present earlier.
chain.correction: Cecil lied about his arrival to conceal knowledge of secret passages.
chain.effect: Cecil knew about family secrets but was not involved in crimes.
required_evidence: Telephone records and train schedules
Sir Clinton’s map and secret passage discovery

herrings.description: Cecil’s bitter resentment towards Maurice and his hostile attitude suggested he might have motive for foul play.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Cecil’s resentment was personal and did not extend to criminal actions; he was not involved in the theft or murders.

herrings.description: Maurice was found in a white Pierrot costume and was suspected of being the man in white involved in the theft.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Maurice was suffering from agoraphobia and ultimately committed suicide; he was not involved in the theft or murders.

supporting_points: Polegate planned the practical joke that led to the theft.
He was near the museum during the theft and had opportunity.
He was evasive about his actions and whereabouts.
He was suspected by Inspector Armadale based on circumstantial evidence.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Polegate handed over the real medallions promptly and had no motive or evidence linking him to the murders or the real theft.

items.false_assumption: The khaki tunic found in the victim's hand belonged to Arthur Clarke and proved his guilt.

chain.observation: Khaki tunic found in victim's hand with torn sleeve matching cloth piece and the blackmail letter mentioned in Mary Clarke's possession.
chain.correction: Tunic is too small for Arthur Clarke and is an old school tunic; the blackmail letter is a compromising document (compromis) that others had motive to suppress.
chain.effect: Arthur Clarke cannot have worn the tunic at the time of murder, and the blackmail (compromis) letter provides motive for others.
required_evidence: Testimony of April St. Jude about Arthur's size and tunic fitting, and the existence of the blackmail letter among Mary Clarke's effects
Physical examination of the khaki tunic showing size discrepancy and the letter's handwriting analysis

chain.observation: Lord Foremeere seen coming out of smoking-room at 7 pm with wet clothes, after having entered Hardacres earlier that evening.
chain.correction: Wet clothes indicate he had been outside or involved in the murder scene, and his entering the house was not observed by others.
chain.effect: Lord Foremeere's alibi is suspicious and he had opportunity to commit the murder.
required_evidence: Butler Spinks's testimony about carrying Lord Foremeere's coat and hat, and the timing of his entry into the house
Observation of wet boots and clothes by witnesses, and the lack of a credible explanation for his movements

chain.observation: Victim died of gas poisoning in locked room, with the blackmail letter (compromis) missing from her effects.
chain.correction: Victim was stunned by a blow before gas was turned on, and the letter was taken by the murderer.
chain.effect: Murder was premeditated and staged to look like suicide, and the missing letter (compromis) suggests motive.
required_evidence: Medical evidence of blow to back of head and absence of the blackmail letter from Mary Clarke's belongings
Locked parlour door with key hidden in tunic pocket

chain.observation: Arthur Clarke claimed to be at Meere Court until 7 pm, and did not enter Hardacres at the relevant time.
chain.correction: Conflicting testimonies about Arthur's departure time, but no evidence he entered the house during the murder window.
chain.effect: Arthur's alibi is uncertain but supported by Lady Foremeere, and he could not have entered Hardacres to commit the crime.
required_evidence: Lady Foremeere's sworn testimony about Arthur's visit and his not entering Hardacres
Servants' statements about party timing and Arthur's presence elsewhere

chain.observation: Key to locked parlour door found in tunic pocket, and the blackmail letter (compromis) not found.
chain.correction: Key was planted to implicate Arthur Clarke, and the missing letter suggests the murderer had access and motive.
chain.effect: Evidence is fabricated to mislead investigation, and the blackmail letter's absence points away from Arthur.
required_evidence: Location of tunic in Arthur's room drawer and the fact that the letter was not among Mary Clarke's papers
Physical impossibility of Arthur wearing tunic at time and handwriting comparison of the blackmail letter

chain.observation: Lord Foremeere died accidentally by shooting himself after the murder was discovered.
chain.correction: His death prevented further investigation, but his motive (the blackmail letter/compromis) and opportunity are clear.
chain.effect: Murderer escapes justice but truth revealed posthumously; the blackmail letter's disappearance is explained.
required_evidence: Valet's testimony about accidental shooting and Lord Foremeere's agitation over the blackmail letter
Police visit to Meere Court with coat and hat, and search for the missing letter

chain.observation: Public suspects Lady Foremeere as murderer due to rumors about the blackmail letter (compromis).
chain.correction: No evidence supports Lady Foremeere's guilt, and she did not enter Hardacres or possess the letter.
chain.effect: Focus shifts to Lord Foremeere as true culprit, who had both motive (blackmail/compromis) and opportunity to enter.
required_evidence: Lady Foremeere's testimony and alibi, and her lack of access to the letter
Lack of motive or opportunity for Lady Foremeere, and confirmation she did not enter Hardacres

herrings.description: April St. Jude's contradictory testimony about Arthur Clarke's departure time created confusion about his alibi.
herrings.innocent_explanation: April was trying to protect Arthur out of love and was mistaken about the time.

herrings.description: Lord Foremeere's wet coat, hat, and boots hidden in the smoking-room suggested suspicious behavior.
herrings.innocent_explanation: Concealment was to fake an alibi and mislead investigators about his movements.

supporting_points: The torn khaki tunic with the key was found in the victim's hand
Arthur had motive related to love and money
Witnesses initially placed Arthur near the scene
Arthur's initial inconsistent statements raised suspicion
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The tunic was too small for Arthur and was an old school tunic, not the one he wore recently
